Glossary

Every term the site defines, collected from the definition boxes in the articles themselves. A term is defined in exactly one place, and this is the link to it.

ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWZ

A

A posteriori
Knowledge or justification that depends on experience for its warrant. Also called empirical knowledge.Defined in A Priori and A Posteriori · Epistemology · Intermediate
A priori
Knowledge or justification that does not depend on experience for its warrant. Experience may be needed to acquire the concepts involved, but plays no part in supporting the claim once the concepts are in hand.Defined in A Priori and A Posteriori · Epistemology · Intermediate
A priori argument
An argument whose premises can be known without appeal to experience of how the world happens to be, resting instead on concepts, definitions, or truths of reason.Defined in Ontological Arguments · Theism · Intermediate
A-theory
The view that temporal facts include tensed facts that cannot be reduced to the earlier-and-later relations: there is a real, objective difference between what is past, present and future, and that difference is not merely a matter of perspective.Defined in Theories of Time · Metaphysics · Intermediate
Abduction
An inference from a body of evidence to a hypothesis on the grounds that the hypothesis would explain the evidence better than the alternatives. Also called inference to the best explanation.Defined in Deductive and Inductive Support · Logic · Beginner
absolute creationism
The thesis that abstract objects exist and are created by God, so that numbers, properties, propositions, and possible worlds are among the things brought into being by divine creative activity. It preserves aseity by refusing to make an exception for the abstract: everything distinct from God depends on God, without qualification.Defined in Aseity and the Bootstrapping Problem · Theism · Advanced
Abstract object
An object of the sort that has no such place: the number seven, the proposition that grass is green, the game of chess as distinct from any particular playing of it.Defined in Abstract and Concrete · Metaphysics · Beginner
Abstract world
A possible world that is an abstract object, such as a set of propositions or a state of affairs, and that stands to a way things could have been roughly as a complete description stands to what it describes. Exactly one abstract world is actual: the one that represents the concrete universe correctly.Defined in Modal Realism and Ersatzism · Metaphysics · Intermediate
Access consciousness
The property a mental state has when its content is available to the rest of the system: poised for use in reasoning, for the direct control of action, and for report.Defined in Consciousness Versus Cognition · Philosophy of Mind · Beginner
Access internalism
The view that a factor can justify a belief only if the believer has reflective access to it, so that on reflection alone the believer could become aware of what justifies them.Defined in Internalism versus Externalism · Epistemology · Intermediate
Accessibility relation
A two-place relation on the set of worlds, written $R$, where $Rwv$ says that $v$ is accessible from $w$. The clauses for the operators are then relativised to it: $\Box \varphi$ is true at $w$ when $\varphi$ is true at every world accessible from $w$, and $\Diamond \varphi$ is true at $w$ when $\varphi$ is true at at least one world accessible from $w$. Worlds not accessible from $w$ are simply not consulted in evaluating a modal formula at $w$.Defined in Modal Logic: Possible Worlds Semantics · Logic · Intermediate
accidental necessity
The kind of necessity a proposition acquires simply by being about the past. A proposition can be contingent in itself, in the sense that things could have gone otherwise, while being accidentally necessary now, because there is no longer anything anyone can do to make it false. That Caesar crossed the Rubicon was once an open question and is now beyond anyone's power to affect, including God's. The name marks that the necessity is not built into the content of the proposition but attaches to it by the accident of its subject matter having become past.Defined in Divine Foreknowledge and Freedom · Theism · Advanced
Accidental property
A property a thing has but could have lacked. Nearly everything true of an ordinary object is accidental to it in this sense.Defined in Essence and Accident · Metaphysics · Beginner
Accuracy dominance
One credence function accuracy-dominates another if it is at least as accurate at every possible world and strictly more accurate at some. It strictly dominates if it is strictly more accurate at every world.Defined in Accuracy-First Epistemology · Epistemology · Advanced
Accuracy-first epistemology
The programme of deriving norms for credences from a single underlying value: accuracy, or closeness to the truth. It holds that the only fundamental epistemic good is having credences close to the truth values of the propositions they concern, and that all other norms of credence are justified by showing that obeying them promotes accuracy.Defined in Accuracy-First Epistemology · Epistemology · Advanced
Acts and omissions doctrine
The claim that there is a moral difference between performing an act that produces a result and omitting an act that would have prevented that result, so that the two can differ in permissibility even where the result and the agent's state of mind are the same.Defined in Doing, Allowing, and Double Effect · Applied Ethics · Beginner
Actual infinite
A completed totality with infinitely many members, as distinct from a potential infinite, which is a process or collection that can always be extended further without ever being finished.Defined in Cosmological Arguments · Theism · Intermediate
Adams' thesis
The claim that the assertibility of an indicative conditional goes by the conditional probability of the consequent given the antecedent, rather than by the probability of any proposition the conditional expresses. Proposed by Ernest Adams in 1965 and 1975.Defined in Conditionals and the Triviality Results · Logic · Advanced
adaptive but false belief
A belief that contributes to the survival and reproduction of the organism that holds it while being false. Its possibility is the pivot of the evolutionary argument: if a system of largely false beliefs could generate the same fitness-enhancing behaviour as a system of largely true ones, then selection for behaviour does not amount to selection for truth, and the adaptiveness of our faculties gives no direct evidence of their accuracy.Defined in The Evolutionary Argument Against Naturalism · Theism · Advanced
Adequate set
A set of connectives that is functionally complete. The two terms are used interchangeably, with "adequate set" more common when the set itself is the subject and "functional completeness" more common when the property is.Defined in Truth-Functional Completeness · Logic · Intermediate
Affirming the consequent
The invalid form that takes a conditional and the truth of its consequent, and concludes the truth of its antecedent: from $P \rightarrow Q$ and $Q$, to $P$.Defined in Common Formal Fallacies · Logic · Beginner
Agnosticism
Either the condition of a person who suspends judgement about whether God exists, or the claim that nobody is justified in believing either that God exists or that God does not.Defined in Theism, Atheism, and Agnosticism · Theism · Beginner
Agrippa's trilemma
The claim that any attempt to justify a belief must end in an infinite regress, in a circle, or in an unsupported assumption, and that none of the three delivers justification.Defined in The Regress Problem · Epistemology · Beginner
Ampliative inference
An inference whose conclusion says more than its premises do, so that the conclusion could be false even if every premise is true. Every inductive inference is ampliative, and no valid argument is.Defined in Deductive and Inductive Support · Logic · Beginner
analogy of being
The doctrine that terms applied to God and creatures are used neither in the same sense nor in unrelated senses, but in related senses, because of a real relation between God and creatures. On the analogy of attribution, a term applies primarily to one thing and derivatively to others related to it, as "healthy" applies primarily to an organism and derivatively to a diet that produces health. On the analogy of proportionality, a term applies to each thing in the way proper to what that thing is, so that God's wisdom is to God as human wisdom is to a human. Aquinas develops the account in the first part of the Summa Theologiae, question 13, arguing that names are said of God and creatures analogically, and that the perfection named exists more properly in God, though our understanding of it begins from creatures.Defined in Religious Language · Theism · Advanced
Analysis of knowledge
The project of stating conditions that are individually necessary and jointly sufficient for someone to know that something is the case, thereby saying what knowing consists in.Defined in The JTB Analysis · Epistemology · Beginner
Analytic truth
A proposition true solely in virtue of the meanings of its constituent terms, so that understanding it is sufficient for seeing that it is true. Standard examples are that all bachelors are unmarried and that no square is round.Defined in The Analytic/Synthetic Distinction and Quine's Attack · Epistemology · Intermediate
Anarchism
The position that the state is unjustified and should be abolished or dispensed with, and that the goods it supposedly provides can be secured by voluntary and non-coercive association instead.Defined in What a State Is For · Political Philosophy · Beginner
Animalism
The view that each of us is a human animal, so that the persistence conditions of a person are those of the organism and are fixed by biological continuity, not psychological continuity.Defined in Personal Identity · Metaphysics · Intermediate
Annihilationism
The view that those not finally united with God simply cease to exist, so that immortality is a gift conditional on that union rather than a property everyone has.Defined in Death and the Afterlife · Theism · Intermediate
Anthropic principle
The principle that our observations of the universe are inevitably restricted to conditions compatible with the existence of observers, so that finding conditions suitable for us carries a built-in selection effect.Defined in Design and Fine-Tuning Arguments · Theism · Intermediate
anthropomorphism objection
The charge that a conception of God has been built by taking human characteristics and enlarging them, so that what the conception describes is a magnified person rather than the ultimate reality it claims to describe. Directed against theistic personalism, the objection is that its God differs from us only in scale, and that a difference of scale is not the difference religion has always claimed. The objection is old: Xenophanes observed in the sixth century that people picture the gods with their own features, and remarked that horses and oxen would draw gods shaped like horses and oxen.Defined in Classical Theism Against Theistic Personalism · Theism · Advanced
Anti-luminosity argument
Williamson's argument that no non-trivial condition is luminous, where a condition is luminous if, whenever it obtains, one is in a position to know that it obtains. The argument uses a margin-for-error principle for knowledge, applied to a gradual series of cases, to show that even conditions like feeling cold can obtain without one's being in a position to know it.Defined in Knowledge-First Epistemology and Anti-Luminosity · Epistemology · Advanced
Anti-reductionism about testimony
The view that testimony is a basic source of justification in its own right. A hearer is entitled to accept what they are told without positive reasons for trusting the speaker, provided they have no reasons against doing so.Defined in Testimony and Disagreement · Epistemology · Intermediate
anti-theism
The view that God's existence would make things worse, or does make things worse, than they otherwise would be. It is not the claim that God does not exist, and it is not the claim that God is not good. An anti-theist may accept that God is perfectly good and still hold that certain goods available in a godless world are unavailable in a world with God, so that something of value is lost. The position was named and developed by Kahane, taking its cue from remarks by Thomas Nagel.Defined in The Axiology of Theism · Theism · Advanced
anti-theodicy
The position that the project of justifying God's permission of evil should not be undertaken, rather than merely that it has not yet succeeded. Its proponents, among them Kenneth Surin in Theology and the Problem of Evil (Basil Blackwell, 1986), Terrence Tilley in The Evils of Theodicy (Georgetown University Press, 1991), and D. Z. Phillips in The Problem of Evil and the Problem of God (SCM Press, 2004), hold that theodicy misconceives what religious belief is, treats suffering as a theoretical problem when it is a practical and moral one, and produces a distorted relation to the suffering of others in those who practise it.Defined in Horrendous Evils and Anti-Theodicy · Theism · Advanced
apophatic theology
Theology conducted through denial, on which what can be known about God is what God is not. Positive statements are treated as at best provisional and at worst misleading, because every affirmative predicate carries a creaturely condition that God does not satisfy. The apophatic theologian regards the sequence of denials as itself a form of knowledge, a progressive refusal to rest in any concept, rather than as an admission that theology has nothing to work with.Defined in Religious Language · Theism · Advanced
Applied ethics
The part of moral philosophy that addresses particular practical questions, asking what may or must be done in a specified kind of situation rather than what makes actions right in general.Defined in From Theory to Cases · Applied Ethics · Beginner
Argument
A set of statements, one of which (the conclusion) is presented as being supported by the others (the premises).Defined in What an Argument Is · Logic · Beginner
Argument from analogy
The inference that since one's own mental states are correlated with certain bodily conditions and behaviour, and other creatures exhibit relevantly similar bodies and behaviour, they probably have similar mental states.Defined in The Problem of Other Minds · Philosophy of Mind · Beginner
Argument from design
The argument that certain features of the natural world exhibit the marks of contrivance found in artefacts, and are therefore best explained by a designer.Defined in Design and Fine-Tuning Arguments · Theism · Intermediate
argument from divine hiddenness
J. L. Schellenberg's argument that the existence of nonresistant nonbelief is incompatible with the existence of a perfectly loving God. If perfect love entails openness to relationship, and openness to relationship entails ensuring that the person is able to believe, then a perfectly loving God would see to it that no nonresistant person lacks belief. Since some nonresistant people do lack belief, there is no perfectly loving God, and therefore, on any conception of God on which God is perfectly loving, no God.Defined in The Problem of Divine Hiddenness · Theism · Advanced
argument from pain and pleasure
Draper's argument that the observed facts about the distribution and biological integration of pain and pleasure are antecedently much more probable on the hypothesis of indifference than on theism, and that they therefore constitute significant evidence against theism. The conclusion is that theism is less probable than it would otherwise have been, not that theism is false, and Draper explicitly allows that other evidence might outweigh it.Defined in Draper's Argument from Pain and Pleasure · Theism · Advanced
Aristotelian essence
Essence understood as what a thing is, the content of its real definition, rather than as the collection of properties the thing has necessarily. On this conception the essential properties are those that belong to the thing's nature, and the thing's necessary properties are a wider class that includes whatever its nature, together with the natures of other things, makes unavoidable.Defined in Essence Is Not Modality · Metaphysics · Advanced
Arithmetical completeness
The property a modal system has when it derives exactly those formulas all of whose arithmetical interpretations are provable in Peano arithmetic. Solovay proved in 1976 that $\mathsf{GL}$ has it.Defined in Provability Logic and Löb's Theorem · Logic · Advanced
Arithmetical comprehension
The principle asserting the existence of every set definable by a formula containing no set quantifiers, though possibly containing set parameters. Added to the base theory it gives the system ACA-zero, whose first-order consequences are exactly those of Peano arithmetic.Defined in Reverse Mathematics · Logic · Advanced
Arithmetical interpretation
An assignment of a sentence of arithmetic to each propositional variable of the modal language, extended to all formulas by commuting with the connectives and by sending $\Box A$ to the arithmetised statement that the sentence assigned to $A$ is provable in Peano arithmetic. Every modal formula thereby becomes a sentence of arithmetic, one for each choice of assignment.Defined in Provability Logic and Löb's Theorem · Logic · Advanced
aseity
The property of existing from oneself, of having one's existence and nature from no source outside oneself. A being with aseity does not depend on anything for existing, for being the kind of thing it is, or for having the features it has. The doctrine that God has aseity is the strongest form of the independence claim: everything other than God depends on God, and God depends on nothing.Defined in Aseity and the Bootstrapping Problem · Theism · Advanced
aseity bootstrapping problem
The objection that God cannot create the properties his own creative activity presupposes. To create anything, God must already be omnipotent, must already have the property of being a creator, and must already be the kind of thing that can act. If those properties are among the things God creates, then God must have them before he creates them, and the account is circular. If they are not, then some properties are uncreated and aseity fails in the way absolute creationism was introduced to prevent.Defined in Aseity and the Bootstrapping Problem · Theism · Advanced
Assumption
A formula written down without justification, for the sake of argument, opening a subproof in which it and everything derived from it are available. An assumption differs from a premise in that it carries no commitment: the argument does not claim it is true, only that something follows from it.Defined in Natural Deduction · Logic · Intermediate
Atheism
The proposition that God does not exist: the denial of theism.Defined in Theism, Atheism, and Agnosticism · Theism · Beginner
Atomic formula
A sentence letter standing alone. Atomic formulas have no connectives and no proper parts that are themselves formulas, which is what makes them the base case of the grammar. A formula that is not atomic is compound, and every compound formula has exactly one main connective.Defined in Propositional Logic and Well-Formed Formulas · Logic · Intermediate
Attribute incompatibility
An argument that two or more of the properties ascribed to God cannot both be instantiated by the same being, so that nothing answers to the description and God as classically conceived does not exist.Defined in Divine Attributes and Their Tensions · Theism · Intermediate
axiology of theism
The study of what difference in value God's existence would make, as distinct from whether God exists. The question was given its modern form by Guy Kahane in "Should We Want God to Exist?" in Philosophy and Phenomenological Research in 2011, and the literature that followed treats the existential question and the axiological question as fully independent: one can hold that God exists and that this is in some respect regrettable, or that God does not exist and that this is a loss.Defined in The Axiology of Theism · Theism · Advanced
Axiom schema
A pattern with metalinguistic variables in place of formulas, every uniform substitution of formulas for which is an axiom. A schema stands for infinitely many axioms, so a system described as having three axioms in fact has infinitely many, arranged in three families. The alternative is to state finitely many axioms and add a rule permitting substitution, which shifts the same work from the axioms to the rules.Defined in Axiomatic Systems and the Deduction Theorem · Logic · Intermediate

B

B-theory
The view that the earlier-than, later-than and simultaneous-with relations are all there is to the order of time. Pastness, presentness and futurity are not objective features of events, and so nothing is privileged as the present.Defined in Theories of Time · Metaphysics · Intermediate
Barcan formula
The schema $\Diamond \exists x\, \varphi \rightarrow \exists x\, \Diamond \varphi$, equivalently $\forall x\, \Box \varphi \rightarrow \Box \forall x\, \varphi$. It says that if there might have been something satisfying a condition, then something actually existing might have satisfied it, and it is valid on exactly the models whose domains do not grow along the accessibility relation.Defined in Quantified Modal Logic and the Barcan Formulas · Logic · Advanced
Bare particular
A particular that has properties but has no nature of its own: nothing about what it is in itself makes it red or round or iron, and two bare particulars differ only numerically. The postbox is, on this view, a bare particular together with the properties it instantiates.Defined in Substance and Bundle Theories · Metaphysics · Intermediate
Basic belief
A belief that is justified without deriving its justification from other beliefs. If there are such beliefs, the chain of reasons can stop at one without stopping arbitrarily.Defined in The Regress Problem · Epistemology · Beginner
Bayes factor
The factor by which a body of evidence multiplies the prior odds to give the posterior odds. For two hypotheses that each fix a definite probability for the evidence, it is identical to the likelihood ratio.Defined in Bayesian Natural Theology · Theism · Advanced
Bayes's theorem
The result that $P(h \mid e) = P(e \mid h) \cdot P(h) / P(e)$, which expresses the probability of a hypothesis given evidence in terms of the probability of that evidence given the hypothesis, the prior probability of the hypothesis, and the overall probability of the evidence.Defined in Bayesian Confidence and Credence, Introduced · Epistemology · Intermediate
Bayesian theodicy
A theodicy assessed not as a demonstration that some good justifies the evil, but as a hypothesis that raises the probability of the observed evils given theism. Its function within a probabilistic argument is to narrow the likelihood gap, and it can perform that function without being known to be true, since what matters is the probability it confers rather than its establishment. The trade-off is that a theodicy specific enough to raise the likelihood substantially is a further claim, so the conjunction of theism with it has a lower prior than theism alone.Defined in The Probabilistic Problem of Evil · Theism · Advanced
Behavioural evidence
The observable facts about a creature that bear on what mental states it has: what it does, how it responds, what it says, and how its body is built and behaves.Defined in The Problem of Other Minds · Philosophy of Mind · Beginner
Being
The condition of being something at all, as opposed to nothing. In most contemporary writing "being" and "existence" are used interchangeably; a minority tradition keeps them apart, so that some things can have being without existing.Defined in What 'Exists' Means · Ontology · Beginner
being among beings
The status classical theism denies to God: membership in the class of existing things, alongside stars, numbers, and people, differing from other members in degree rather than in kind. On the classical view God is not the greatest item in the inventory of what exists but the source of there being an inventory at all. Aquinas marks this by identifying God with subsistent existence itself rather than with something that has existence, which is the doctrinal use of the essence-existence distinction.Defined in Classical Theism Against Theistic Personalism · Theism · Advanced
Belief
Taking something to be the case. To believe that P is to hold P as true, which is compatible with being wrong, being unsure, and never having examined the matter.Defined in Knowledge, Belief, and Opinion · Epistemology · Beginner
Benardete paradox
Any of a family of cases in which infinitely many agents or objects are each conditioned to act only if no earlier one has acted, and in which there is no earliest, so that the situation is inconsistent although each agent's own instruction is unobjectionable.Defined in Grim Reaper Paradoxes and Causal Finitism · Theism · Advanced
Benefit
A change that leaves a being better off in some respect it has a stake in: the mirror image of a setback to its interests.Defined in Harm, Benefit, and Consent · Applied Ethics · Beginner
Bergmann's skeptical theses
Michael Bergmann's formulation of what the skeptical theist is committed to, given in "Skeptical Theism and Rowe's New Evidential Argument from Evil" in Noûs in 2001 and extended in "Skeptical Theism and the Problem of Evil" in The Oxford Handbook of Philosophical Theology (Oxford University Press, 2009). The theses deny that our samples are representative: that the goods we know of are representative of the goods there are, that the evils we know of are representative of the evils there are, that the entailment relations we grasp between goods and the permission of evils are representative of those that obtain, and, in the extended version, that our grasp of the total moral value of possible states of affairs is representative of the whole.Defined in Skeptical Theism and Its Costs · Theism · Advanced
Bertrand's paradox
A demonstration, due to Joseph Bertrand in 1889, that the principle of indifference gives different answers to a single question depending on which quantity is treated as uniformly distributed. The standard version asks for the probability that a chord drawn at random in a circle is longer than the side of the inscribed equilateral triangle, and three equally natural constructions give three different values.Defined in Probability as an Extension of Logic · Logic · Intermediate
best possible world
The world, among all the worlds an omnipotent being could bring about, that is better than every other. Leibniz argued in the Théodicée of 1710 that since God is omnipotent, omniscient, and perfectly good, God surveys all the possibilities and brings about the best of them, from which it follows that this world, whatever its apparent defects, is the best available. The phrase has since become detached from Leibniz's system and is used for the general assumption that there is such a world to be chosen.Defined in The No-Best-World Problem · Theism · Advanced
BHK interpretation
The Brouwer-Heyting-Kolmogorov reading of the connectives in terms of proofs rather than truth: a proof of $\varphi \land \psi$ is a pair of proofs; a proof of $\varphi \lor \psi$ is a proof of one disjunct together with an indication of which; a proof of $\varphi \rightarrow \psi$ is a construction transforming any proof of $\varphi$ into one of $\psi$; a proof of $\exists x\, \varphi$ is an object together with a proof that it satisfies $\varphi$; and $\neg \varphi$ abbreviates $\varphi \rightarrow \bot$.Defined in Intuitionistic Logic and Kripke Semantics · Logic · Advanced
Biconditional
The truth function written $P \leftrightarrow Q$ and read "$P$ if and only if $Q$": true when the two parts have the same truth value, and false when they differ.Defined in Statements and Connectives · Logic · Beginner
Binary truth function
A truth function taking two arguments. Since two arguments admit four combinations of truth values and each combination can be sent to either value independently, there are exactly sixteen binary truth functions, and each corresponds to one possible filling of the four-row output column of a truth table.Defined in The Sixteen Binary Connectives · Logic · Intermediate
Biological continuity
The continuation of one and the same life: the ongoing self-maintaining organisation of an organism, through metabolism, growth and repair. A later organism is biologically continuous with an earlier one when it is the later stage of that very life.Defined in Personal Identity · Metaphysics · Intermediate
biological role of pain
The fact that pain and pleasure in living organisms are systematically integrated into goal-directed biological systems: they are triggered by conditions that bear on survival and reproduction, they motivate behaviour that tends to preserve the organism, and their intensity and duration track biological stakes rather than moral ones. Tissue damage hurts, nutrition and mating are pleasant, and the correlation is not incidental but is what one would expect of a trait shaped by differential reproductive success.Defined in Draper's Argument from Pain and Pleasure · Theism · Advanced
Bodily resurrection
The view that persons do not survive death at all, and that God restores them to existence embodied at some later time.Defined in Death and the Afterlife · Theism · Intermediate
Bound variable
An occurrence of a variable that falls within the scope of a quantifier using that same variable. A bound occurrence contributes nothing on its own and could be replaced throughout by any other unused variable without changing what the formula says, so $\forall x Fx$ and $\forall y Fy$ are the same claim differently written.Defined in Predicate Logic · Logic · Intermediate
Brain in a vat
The modern version of the deceiver hypothesis: that you are a disembodied brain in a nutrient bath, receiving electrical stimulation that produces exactly the experiences you are now having.Defined in Skepticism, First Encounter · Epistemology · Beginner
Branch closure
The state of a branch that contains both some formula and its negation. Such a branch describes an impossible interpretation and is marked closed, and no further work is done on it. A tableau all of whose branches are closed is itself closed, and a branch on which every formula has been decomposed and which has not closed is open.Defined in Semantic Tableaux · Logic · Intermediate
Bundle theory
The view that an ordinary particular is nothing over and above its properties: a thing is a bundle of properties, held together by a relation of compresence, and there is no substratum in addition.Defined in Substance and Bundle Theories · Metaphysics · Intermediate
Burden of proof
The obligation, in a dispute, to make the case for one's position, borne by whichever party would lose if no argument at all were offered.Defined in Theism, Atheism, and Agnosticism · Theism · Beginner

C

Canonical model
An interpretation built directly out of a maximal consistent set, in which the truth values of the atomic formulas are read off membership in the set. The defining property of such a model, established by induction over formulas, is that a formula is true in it exactly when the formula belongs to the set that generated it.Defined in Soundness and Completeness Proofs · Logic · Advanced
Canonicity
A modal logic is canonical when its canonical frame, whose worlds are the maximal consistent sets of formulas of the logic and whose accessibility relation holds between two sets when everything necessitated in the first belongs to the second, validates all the logic's axioms. A canonical logic is complete with respect to the class of frames its axioms define.Defined in Correspondence Theory · Logic · Advanced
Cardinality
The size of a set, understood so that two sets have the same cardinality exactly when there is a bijection between them. For finite sets this agrees with counting. For infinite sets it is the definition rather than an approximation to one, since there is nothing else available, and it has consequences that finite intuition does not prepare anyone for.Defined in Basic Set Theory for Logicians · Logic · Intermediate
Cartesian doubt
The procedure of provisionally rejecting any belief that admits of the slightest doubt, in order to find out what survives. The doubts are deliberately extreme, because the point is to test the foundations rather than to describe anyone's actual uncertainty.Defined in Skepticism, First Encounter · Epistemology · Beginner
Casuistry
Moral reasoning that works outward from settled paradigm cases, deciding a new case by comparing it with cases already resolved and judging how far the differences between them matter.Defined in From Theory to Cases · Applied Ethics · Beginner
Categoricity
The property a theory has, relative to a cardinal, when all of its models of that cardinality are isomorphic. A theory categorical in some infinite cardinal and having no finite models is complete, since two models of a sentence-disputing pair could be brought down or up to that cardinality and would then have to be isomorphic.Defined in Model Theory: Types, Quantifier Elimination, Categoricity · Logic · Advanced
Category
One of the most general kinds a thing can belong to, such that everything falls under some category and the categories are not themselves species of anything more general.Defined in What Metaphysics Asks · Metaphysics · Beginner
Causal chain
A sequence of occurrences in which each depends on the one before it. Causation is then taken to hold between the ends of such a chain, not only between adjacent links.Defined in Causation, First Pass · Metaphysics · Beginner
Causal finitism
The thesis that nothing can be affected by infinitely many causes, so that every event has only finitely many causal antecedents.Defined in Grim Reaper Paradoxes and Causal Finitism · Theism · Advanced
Causal inefficacy
The inability to cause anything or to be affected by anything: standing outside the causal order entirely.Defined in Abstract and Concrete · Metaphysics · Beginner
Causal overdetermination
A case in which an effect has two or more separate causes, each of which was by itself enough to produce it, so that the effect would have occurred even if either one had been missing.Defined in Theories of Causation · Metaphysics · Intermediate
Causal series per se
A causal series in which each member's causing depends on the simultaneous causing of the member before it, so that the later members have no causal power of their own but only what is being conferred on them.Defined in Cosmological Arguments · Theism · Intermediate
Causation
The relation that holds between one occurrence and another when the first brings about, produces, or is responsible for the second.Defined in Causation, First Pass · Metaphysics · Beginner
Cause
The occurrence that does the bringing about: the striking of the match, the impact of the ball, the passing of the law.Defined in Causation, First Pass · Metaphysics · Beginner
Change
A persisting thing having a property at one time and lacking it at another. Change requires numerical identity across the two times, since otherwise there is no one thing that has altered.Defined in Change and Identity Over Time · Metaphysics · Beginner
Church-Turing thesis
The claim that the functions computable by any effective procedure whatever are exactly the recursive functions. It is not a theorem and cannot be one, since one side of the identification is an informal notion and no proof can connect an informal notion to a mathematical one. It is supported by the convergence of independently motivated analyses on the same class, by the failure of every attempt to define a procedure falling outside it, and by ninety years of use.Defined in Computability, Decidability, and Church's Theorem · Logic · Advanced
Church's theorem
The result that the set of valid first-order sentences is not decidable: no procedure takes an arbitrary sentence of first-order logic and determines in finitely many steps whether it is valid. The set is recursively enumerable, since completeness allows the derivations to be listed, so the failure is exactly the failure of the complement to be listable.Defined in Computability, Decidability, and Church's Theorem · Logic · Advanced
Claim right
A right that another party has a duty to you: you have a claim right that someone do or refrain from something exactly when they have a duty to you to do or refrain from it.Defined in Rights, Introduced · Political Philosophy · Beginner
Classical theism
The conception of God developed in Jewish, Christian, and Islamic philosophical theology, on which God is one, without a body, the creator of everything other than himself, and possessed of every perfection to the highest degree.Defined in What God Is Claimed to Be · Theism · Beginner
Close possible world
A way things might have been that differs minimally from how they actually are. Modal epistemology uses closeness as a measure of how easily something could have happened: an outcome that occurs in a close world is one that could easily have occurred.Defined in Safety and Sensitivity Conditions · Epistemology · Intermediate
Closure denial
The position that knowledge is not always preserved under known entailment, so that one may know an ordinary proposition without knowing the denial of a sceptical hypothesis it entails.Defined in Epistemic Closure and Its Denial · Epistemology · Intermediate
Coarse-grained event
A coarse-grained event is one individuated by something looser than its properties, such as its causes and effects (Davidson 1969) or the spatiotemporal region it occupies (Quine 1985). On this view Brutus's stabbing of Caesar and Brutus's killing of Caesar are one event, described in two ways.Defined in Facts, Events, and States of Affairs · Metaphysics · Intermediate
Coercion
Getting someone to act by threatening them with a consequence they will want to avoid, so that the option they would otherwise have taken is made unattractive or removed.Defined in Authority and Legitimacy · Political Philosophy · Beginner
Cognition
The mind's information-handling: taking in, storing, representing, transforming, and using information to guide behaviour. Perception, memory, inference, categorisation, and language use are cognitive processes.Defined in Consciousness Versus Cognition · Philosophy of Mind · Beginner
Cognitive science of religion
The research programme explaining religious belief as a by-product of ordinary cognitive systems that evolved for other purposes, rather than as an adaptation for religion or as a product of reasoning.Defined in Natural Explanations of Religious Belief · Theism · Intermediate
Coherence
The relation among the members of a set of beliefs consisting in logical consistency together with positive relations of explanation, inference, and mutual support, and the absence of unexplained anomalies.Defined in Foundationalism, Coherentism, Infinitism · Epistemology · Intermediate
Coherentism
The view that no belief is justified independently of others, and that justification is a property a body of beliefs has in virtue of how its members fit together. It takes the second horn and denies that the circularity involved is vicious.Defined in Foundationalism, Coherentism, Infinitism · Epistemology · Intermediate
Coincident objects
Numerically distinct material objects that occupy exactly the same region of space at the same time and are made of exactly the same matter at that time. If the argument from squashing is sound, the statue and the lump are coincident objects.Defined in The Problem of Material Constitution · Metaphysics · Advanced
Compactness theorem
The result that a set of first-order sentences has a model if and only if every finite subset of it has a model. One direction is immediate, since a model of the whole set is a model of each part. The other direction is the substantial one: satisfiability, which is a condition on an infinite collection, is settled entirely by conditions on its finite parts.Defined in Compactness and Löwenheim-Skolem · Logic · Advanced
Compatibilism
The thesis that free will, and the moral responsibility that depends on it, is compatible with the truth of determinism. The compatibilist holds that an agent can act freely in a deterministic world.Defined in Free Will and Determinism · Metaphysics · Intermediate
Complete type
A maximal consistent set of formulas in a fixed finite number of free variables, consistent with a given theory. A type is realised in a model when some tuple of elements satisfies every formula in it, and omitted when no tuple does.Defined in Model Theory: Types, Quantifier Elimination, Categoricity · Logic · Advanced
Completeness theorem
The claim that every semantic consequence is derivable: whenever every interpretation making a set of premises true makes a conclusion true, a derivation of that conclusion from those premises exists. A proof system with this property leaves no valid argument out, so the failure to find a derivation is evidence that none exists rather than a comment on the searcher.Defined in Soundness and Completeness, Informally · Logic · Intermediate
Comprehension schema
The schema asserting, for each formula $\varphi$ of the language, that there exists a relation holding of exactly the tuples satisfying it: $\exists X\,\forall \bar{x}\,(X\bar{x} \leftrightarrow \varphi(\bar{x}))$. Full comprehension permits $\varphi$ to contain second-order quantifiers, in which case the schema is impredicative, since the relation asserted to exist is in the range of quantifiers occurring in the condition defining it.Defined in Second-Order and Higher-Order Logic · Logic · Advanced
Conceptual truth
A truth held to follow from the content of the concepts involved rather than from empirical fact. Often used interchangeably with analytic truth, though writers who distinguish them treat conceptual truth as the broader notion, covering cases where the connection between concepts is not a matter of definition.Defined in The Analytic/Synthetic Distinction and Quine's Attack · Epistemology · Intermediate
Conciliationism
The view that on discovering that an epistemic peer disagrees with you, you should move your credence substantially towards theirs. In its strongest form, the equal weight view, each peer's opinion counts for the same, and each should adopt the average or suspend judgement.Defined in Testimony and Disagreement · Epistemology · Intermediate
Conclusion
The statement an argument is trying to establish, on the strength of its premises.Defined in What an Argument Is · Logic · Beginner
Concrete object
An object of the sort that has a place in the world's causal and spatial order: the mug, the mountain, the electron, the eruption.Defined in Abstract and Concrete · Metaphysics · Beginner
Concrete world
A possible world that is a concrete object: a maximal whole of spatiotemporally related parts, like the universe we inhabit, with inhabitants of its own, and spatiotemporally and causally isolated from every other world.Defined in Modal Realism and Ersatzism · Metaphysics · Intermediate
concurrentism
The position that God does more than sustain creatures: he concurs immediately in every creaturely act, so that each natural effect is produced by God and by the creature together, and neither would produce it alone. The creature's contribution is genuine and specific, determining what sort of effect occurs, while God's contribution is general and required for any effect to occur at all. This is the mainstream scholastic view, developed with most care by Francisco Suárez.Defined in Existential Inertia and Divine Conservation · Theism · Advanced
Conditional probability
The probability of one proposition on the supposition that another holds, written $P(h \mid e)$ and defined as $P(h \wedge e) / P(e)$ whenever $P(e) > 0$.Defined in Bayesian Confidence and Credence, Introduced · Epistemology · Intermediate
Conditional proof
The introduction rule for the conditional. Assume the antecedent, derive the consequent within the subproof, then discharge the assumption and write the conditional at the outer level. The rule is what makes the conditional provable at all, since without it a conditional could only ever be carried down from a premise.Defined in Natural Deduction · Logic · Intermediate
Conditionalization
The rule that when an agent learns a proposition $E$ with certainty and learns nothing stronger, their new credence in any proposition $H$ should equal their old conditional credence in $H$ given $E$. In symbols, $c_{\text{new}}(H) = c_{\text{old}}(H \mid E)$.Defined in Formal Epistemology: Probabilism and Updating · Epistemology · Advanced
Confabulation
The production of a sincere, confident report that is not based on the process it purports to report, and which the subject does not recognise as invented.Defined in Introspection and Its Limits · Philosophy of Mind · Beginner
Confirmation
The relation that holds between a piece of evidence and a hypothesis when the evidence supports the hypothesis, making it more credible than it would otherwise be. Confirmation can be qualitative (whether E supports H at all) or quantitative (how much E supports H).Defined in Confirmation Theory, Ravens, and Grue · Epistemology · Advanced
Confirmation holism
The thesis that empirical evidence bears on bodies of belief as wholes rather than on individual statements, so that no single statement has its own confirming or disconfirming observations.Defined in The Analytic/Synthetic Distinction and Quine's Attack · Epistemology · Intermediate
Conflicting claims objection
The argument that since religious experiences across different traditions support incompatible claims about what is experienced, they cannot all be veridical, and no way of privileging one tradition's experiences is available that does not assume what is in question.Defined in Religious Experience · Theism · Intermediate
Conjunction
The truth function written $P \land Q$ and read "$P$ and $Q$": true when both parts are true, and false otherwise.Defined in Statements and Connectives · Logic · Beginner
Conjunction closure
The principle that if it is rational to believe $p$ and rational to believe $q$, it is rational to believe $p \land q$. A system of rational belief closed under conjunction permits one to combine any beliefs into a single belief.Defined in Lottery, Preface, and the Threshold View of Belief · Epistemology · Advanced
Consciousness
An umbrella term covering several distinct phenomena: a creature's being awake and responsive, a creature's being aware of something, a mental state's being available to the rest of the mind, and there being something it is like to undergo a state.Defined in Consciousness Versus Cognition · Philosophy of Mind · Beginner
Consequentialism
The family of theories on which the rightness of an action is determined entirely by its outcomes. Nothing about an act matters morally except the state of the world it brings about.Defined in Consequences, Rules, and Character · Ethics · Beginner
Consistency
The property a set of formulas has when no contradiction is derivable from it. This is a syntactic condition, concerning what can be written down, and it is to be distinguished from satisfiability, which is the semantic condition of having a model. A set with a model is consistent in any sound system, since a contradiction derived from it would have to be true on that model.Defined in Soundness and Completeness, Informally · Logic · Intermediate
Constant domain semantics
The interpretation on which every world of a model shares a single domain of quantification, so that the same objects exist at every world. Quantifiers are evaluated against that fixed domain regardless of which world is under consideration.Defined in Quantified Modal Logic and the Barcan Formulas · Logic · Advanced
Constitution without identity
The view that constitution is a relation between numerically distinct things: the lump constitutes the statue, the two coincide, and they are not identical. Its defenders usually add that constitution is more than mere coincidence, a relation of unity close enough to explain why the two share so much.Defined in The Problem of Material Constitution · Metaphysics · Advanced
Constitutionalism
The doctrine that the powers of government should be defined and limited by fundamental law, so that there are things the state may not do however it decides to do them and whatever majority supports it.Defined in Law and the Rule of Law · Political Philosophy · Beginner
Constructive proof
A proof that exhibits what it asserts to exist. A constructive proof of a disjunction specifies a true disjunct and a constructive proof of an existential specifies a witness, so the proofs are algorithms in a sense that can be made exact.Defined in Intuitionistic Logic and Kripke Semantics · Logic · Advanced
Contextualism
The view that the truth conditions of knowledge attributions vary with the context of the attributor. A sentence of the form "S knows that p" can be true as uttered in one conversation and false as uttered in another, about the same subject at the same time, because the word "knows" picks out different relations in different contexts.Defined in Contextualism, Invariantism, and Pragmatic Encroachment · Epistemology · Advanced
Contingency
A formula whose truth table column is true in at least one row and false in at least one row. Its value depends on how things stand, not on its form alone.Defined in Truth Tables · Logic · Beginner
Contingent truth
A truth that is not necessary: something that is the case but could have failed to be the case.Defined in Possibility and Necessity, Informally · Metaphysics · Beginner
Continuum of inductive methods
The one-parameter family of confirmation functions introduced by Carnap in 1952, in which the probability that the next individual has a property observed in $n_{i}$ of $n$ cases, with $k$ properties in the language, is $(n_{i} + \lambda / k) / (n + \lambda)$. The parameter $\lambda$ measures how much weight is given to the language's structure as against the observed frequency.Defined in Inductive Logic and the Carnap Programme · Logic · Advanced
Contraction
The structural rule permitting two occurrences of the same formula to be identified: from $\Gamma, \varphi, \varphi \vdash \psi$ infer $\Gamma, \varphi \vdash \psi$. It expresses the assumption that having a premise once is having it as many times as needed, and it is the rule that makes the Curry paradox derivable in a theory with naive comprehension.Defined in Substructural Logics · Logic · Advanced
Contradiction
A formula whose truth table column is false in every row. A contradiction cannot be true, whatever the letters in it stand for.Defined in Truth Tables · Logic · Beginner
Contrary-to-duty paradox
The difficulty of representing an obligation conditional on the violation of another obligation. Chisholm's 1963 example, that one ought to go to the neighbours' assistance, that if one goes one ought to tell them one is coming, that if one does not go one ought not to tell them, and that one does not go, is consistent and intuitively independent, and every natural formalisation in the standard system is either inconsistent or renders one premise redundant.Defined in Temporal, Deontic, and Epistemic Logic · Logic · Advanced
Converse Barcan formula
The schema $\exists x\, \Diamond \varphi \rightarrow \Diamond \exists x\, \varphi$, equivalently $\Box \forall x\, \varphi \rightarrow \forall x\, \Box \varphi$. It is valid on exactly the models whose domains do not shrink along the accessibility relation, and it follows from the ordinary quantifier axioms together with necessitation in any system with the distribution schema.Defined in Quantified Modal Logic and the Barcan Formulas · Logic · Advanced
CORNEA
Wykstra's Condition on Reasonable Epistemic Access: one is entitled to claim, on the basis of some situation one has examined, that it appears there is no such-and-such, only if it is reasonable to believe that if there were such a thing, the situation would likely have looked different in some way one could detect. The condition is not specific to religion; it is offered as a general constraint on when the failure to observe something counts as evidence of its absence.Defined in The Probabilistic Problem of Evil · Theism · Advanced
Corrective justice
Justice in the rectification of a wrong: restoring the injured party, so far as possible, to the position they would have occupied had the wrong not been done.Defined in What Justice Requires · Political Philosophy · Beginner
Correspondence
A modal formula and a condition on the accessibility relation correspond when the formula is valid on exactly the frames satisfying the condition. The correspondence is a biconditional between a modal fact and a relational one, proved in both directions.Defined in Correspondence Theory · Logic · Advanced
Cosmological argument
An argument from the existence of the universe, or from some completely general feature of it, to a cause or explanation lying outside it.Defined in Cosmological Arguments · Theism · Intermediate
Countability
The feature a kind has when it makes sense to ask how many of them there are, and there is a determinate answer.Defined in Identity and Individuation · Ontology · Beginner
Countable set
A set that is either finite or can be put into a bijection with the natural numbers. A countable infinite set can be arranged in a list with a first member, a second, and so on, such that every member appears somewhere in the list. A set that cannot be so arranged is uncountable.Defined in Basic Set Theory for Logicians · Logic · Intermediate
Counterexample
A possible situation in which all of an argument's premises are true and its conclusion is false. An argument is invalid exactly when it has one.Defined in Validity and Soundness · Logic · Beginner
Counterfactual
A conditional whose antecedent is supposed for the sake of argument, typically contrary to fact, and which asserts that the consequent holds under that supposition. The standard semantics evaluates it by considering the most similar situations in which the antecedent is true.Defined in Safety and Sensitivity Conditions · Epistemology · Intermediate
Counterfactual account of harm
The view that an act harms a person when it leaves them worse off than they would have been had the act not been performed, so that harm is measured against what would otherwise have happened.Defined in Harm, Benefit, and Consent · Applied Ethics · Beginner
Counterfactual analysis of causation
The view that one event causes another when, if the first had not occurred, the second would not have occurred. The effect depends counterfactually on the cause.Defined in Theories of Causation · Metaphysics · Intermediate
counterfactuals of freedom
The propositions middle knowledge is knowledge of: conditionals stating what a particular creature would freely do if placed in a particular fully specified circumstance. They are contingent, since the creature could have done otherwise in that circumstance, and they are not up to God, since the freedom of the act requires that the creature and not God settles it. If such propositions are true prior to creation, they constitute a fixed landscape that God must work with rather than a set of options God can select among.Defined in Divine Foreknowledge and Freedom · Theism · Advanced
Countermodel
An interpretation on which every premise of an argument is true and its conclusion false. An argument is invalid precisely when it has one, and exhibiting a countermodel is the standard way of establishing invalidity, since it settles the matter outright rather than reporting a failure to find a proof.Defined in Semantic Tableaux · Logic · Intermediate
Counterpart theory
Lewis's account of de re modality, first set out in "Counterpart Theory and Quantified Modal Logic" (1968). Each individual exists in only one world. Its counterparts in other worlds are the individuals there that resemble it closely enough, in the respects that matter. An individual could have been a certain way if and only if some counterpart of it is that way.Defined in Modal Realism and Ersatzism · Metaphysics · Intermediate
Cox's theorem
The result that any measure of plausibility satisfying a short list of structural requirements is a rescaling of a probability measure. The requirements are that degrees of plausibility be represented by real numbers, that the plausibility of a conjunction depend in a fixed way on the plausibility of one conjunct and of the other given the first, that the plausibility of a negation depend in a fixed way on the plausibility of what is negated, and that the assignment be consistent, in that two routes to the same value must agree. Cox published the argument in 1946.Defined in Probability as an Extension of Logic · Logic · Intermediate
Creation ex nihilo
The doctrine that God brings things into existence without working on any pre-existing material and without producing them out of God's own substance.Defined in Creation, Conservation, and Providence · Theism · Beginner
Credence
A degree of belief represented numerically on a scale from 0 to 1, where 0 is certainty that the proposition is false and 1 is certainty that it is true.Defined in Bayesian Confidence and Credence, Introduced · Epistemology · Intermediate
Credibility deficit
The condition of being given less credibility than one's evidence and competence warrant. A credibility deficit is not unjust merely by being mistaken; it becomes unjust when it results from prejudice.Defined in Epistemic Injustice · Epistemology · Intermediate
Criterion of identity
A principle stating, for things of a given kind, the condition under which one of them is the same as another. Sets have a well-known one: the same set when the same members.Defined in Identity and Individuation · Ontology · Beginner
Criterion of the mental
A condition whose satisfaction counts as grounds for applying a mental term, in virtue of what the term means rather than in virtue of an empirical correlation.Defined in The Problem of Other Minds · Philosophy of Mind · Beginner
culpable nonbelief
Nonbelief for which the nonbeliever is responsible, because it arises from some form of resistance: refusal to attend to the evidence, unwillingness to accept the moral demands belief would bring, or a disposition of the will turned against God. The theist who denies the hiddenness argument's third premise holds that all nonbelief is of this kind, and so that the category of nonresistant nonbelief is empty.Defined in The Problem of Divine Hiddenness · Theism · Advanced
Cumulative case argument
An argument that no single consideration establishes a conclusion, while several independent considerations, each inconclusive by itself, together support it.Defined in How Arguments About God Work · Theism · Beginner
Curry-Howard correspondence
The identification of proofs with terms and propositions with types, under which a proof of a formula is a term whose type is that formula, and reduction of terms corresponds exactly to the simplification of proofs. Observed by Haskell Curry for the implicational fragment in the 1930s and extended by William Howard in a 1969 manuscript circulated for a decade before its 1980 publication.Defined in The Curry-Howard Correspondence · Logic · Advanced
Cut elimination
Gentzen's Hauptsatz: every proof in the sequent calculus can be transformed into a proof of the same sequent that uses no cuts. The cut rule is therefore admissible rather than necessary, adding nothing to what the system proves, and the transformation is effective, taking a given proof to a cut-free one by a procedure that terminates.Defined in Sequent Calculus and Cut Elimination · Logic · Advanced
Cut rule
The rule permitting a formula proved on the right of one sequent to be discharged on the left of another: from a proof of Δ together with φ, and a proof that φ together with Γ yields Δ, infer that Γ yields Δ with φ gone. The formula cut away appears in both premises and in neither conclusion, which distinguishes cut from every other rule in the system.Defined in Sequent Calculus and Cut Elimination · Logic · Advanced

D

De dicto modality
Modality attributed to a whole proposition (a dictum): the claim that a proposition as a whole is necessary or possible. "Necessarily, every bachelor is unmarried" says of the proposition that every bachelor is unmarried that it could not have been false.Defined in Modality and Possible Worlds · Metaphysics · Intermediate
De re modality
Modality attributed to a particular thing (a res): the claim that a given object has a property necessarily or possibly. "Socrates is necessarily human" says of Socrates himself that he could not have failed to be human.Defined in Modality and Possible Worlds · Metaphysics · Intermediate
Debunking argument
An argument that a belief is unjustified because the best explanation of why people hold it makes no reference to the belief's being true.Defined in Natural Explanations of Religious Belief · Theism · Intermediate
Decidability
The property a set has when some procedure determines membership in it: given any object, the procedure halts and answers correctly, yes or no. A property is decidable when the set of things having it is, and a theory is decidable when the set of its theorems is. The requirement that the procedure halt on every input is what distinguishes this from mere search.Defined in Computability, Decidability, and Church's Theorem · Logic · Advanced
Decision-making capacity
The ability to make a particular decision at a particular time: to understand the relevant information, appreciate how it applies to oneself, reason with it, and express a choice.Defined in Harm, Benefit, and Consent · Applied Ethics · Beginner
Deduction theorem
The result that if $\varphi$ can be derived from a set of premises together with $\psi$, then $\psi \rightarrow \varphi$ can be derived from that set alone. Written with the turnstile: if $\Gamma, \psi \vdash \varphi$ then $\Gamma \vdash \psi \rightarrow \varphi$. It is a theorem about the system rather than a rule within it, and it holds despite the system having no assumptions and no discharge.Defined in Axiomatic Systems and the Deduction Theorem · Logic · Intermediate
Deductive argument
An argument put forward as valid: one whose premises are meant to guarantee the conclusion, so that accepting the premises and rejecting the conclusion would be inconsistent. A deductive argument that fails its own standard is not a weak argument, it is an invalid one.Defined in Deductive and Inductive Support · Logic · Beginner
Defeasibility analysis
The proposal that knowledge is justified true belief for which there exists no true proposition that, had the believer been aware of it, would have destroyed the justification. Such a proposition is a defeater.Defined in Gettier Cases and Post-Gettier Repairs · Epistemology · Intermediate
defeat within a life
The relation that must hold between a horrendous evil and the goods of the life containing it if that life is to be a great good to the person whose life it is. Following Roderick Chisholm's "The Defeat of Good and Evil" in the Proceedings and Addresses of the American Philosophical Association in 1968, a bad thing is balanced off when some separate good outweighs it in a sum, and defeated when it is integrated into a larger whole whose value depends on its presence, so that the whole is better for containing it than it would be without. Adams argues that horrendous evils require defeat within the individual's own life and that balancing off is not enough.Defined in Horrendous Evils and Anti-Theodicy · Theism · Advanced
defeater
Something a person acquires that removes the warrant a belief would otherwise have. A rebutting defeater is evidence that the belief is false. An undercutting defeater does not indicate falsity but removes the connection between the belief and its ground, as learning that the lighting is coloured undercuts a belief about an object's colour without showing the belief wrong. A belief can be properly basic and warranted at one time and lose that status when a defeater is acquired, which is why proper basicality is not immunity.Defined in Reformed Epistemology and Proper Function · Theism · Advanced
Defence
A response to the problem of evil that describes a way in which God's permitting evil could be consistent with God's goodness, without claiming that this is in fact God's reason.Defined in The Problem of Evil · Theism · Intermediate
Definite description
A phrase of the form "the such-and-such", which purports to pick out exactly one thing by describing it rather than by naming it. Definite descriptions behave like names in a sentence, occupying the same positions and appearing to refer, and the question of whether they really are a kind of name is the question this article turns on.Defined in Identity and Definite Descriptions · Logic · Intermediate
Degree of belief
The strength with which a person holds a proposition, understood as admitting of gradations rather than being all or nothing.Defined in Bayesian Confidence and Credence, Introduced · Epistemology · Intermediate
deism
The view that a creator brought the world into being and established its order but does not intervene in it, perform miracles, issue revelations, or respond to prayer. It was the dominant heterodox position of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, argued for in John Toland's Christianity Not Mysterious of 1696 and Matthew Tindal's Christianity as Old as the Creation of 1730, both published anonymously, which held that reason establishes everything in religion worth having and that revelation adds nothing.Defined in Philosophy of Religion Beyond Monotheism · Theism · Advanced
Demonstrative argument
An argument whose premises are held to be certain and whose conclusion follows from them necessarily, so that anyone who accepts the premises cannot consistently deny the conclusion.Defined in How Arguments About God Work · Theism · Beginner
Denying the antecedent
The invalid form that takes a conditional and the falsity of its antecedent, and concludes the falsity of its consequent: from $P \rightarrow Q$ and $\neg P$, to $\neg Q$.Defined in Common Formal Fallacies · Logic · Beginner
Deontic logic
The modal treatment of obligation and permission, with the box read as what ought to be the case and the accessibility relation running to the deontically ideal alternatives. The standard system, usually called SDL, is the normal modal logic D, whose characteristic axiom says that what is obligatory is permitted.Defined in Temporal, Deontic, and Epistemic Logic · Logic · Advanced
Deontology
The family of theories on which some actions are right or wrong in virtue of what they are, independent of their consequences. Certain acts are constrained or required whatever the outcomes.Defined in Consequences, Rules, and Character · Ethics · Beginner
Derivation
A finite sequence of formulas in which each member is an axiom, a premise, or follows from earlier members by a rule of the system. The last member is the formula derived. Nothing may be assumed temporarily and nothing is ever discharged, so every line of a derivation is asserted outright and depends on the premises alone.Defined in Axiomatic Systems and the Deduction Theorem · Logic · Intermediate
Descriptive claim
A claim about how things are, were, or will be. It reports, predicts, or explains, and it is assessed by finding out whether the world matches it.Defined in Descriptive and Normative Claims · Ethics · Beginner
Desert
What a person is owed in virtue of something they have done or some way they have been: their effort, their contribution, their conduct, or their character.Defined in What Justice Requires · Political Philosophy · Beginner
Designated value
A truth value counted as success for the purposes of defining validity. An argument is valid when every assignment giving all premises a designated value gives the conclusion one, so the choice of designated values fixes the consequence relation independently of the truth tables.Defined in Many-Valued Logics · Logic · Advanced
Desire
A propositional attitude whose content specifies a way the world is to be made, rather than a way the world is taken to be. Desires motivate action, and they are satisfied or frustrated rather than true or false.Defined in What a Mental State Is · Philosophy of Mind · Beginner
Determinism
The thesis that the state of the world at any one time, together with the laws of nature, entails the state of the world at every other time. Given the past and the laws, exactly one future is possible.Defined in Free Will and Determinism · Metaphysics · Intermediate
Diagonal lemma
The result that for any formula ψ with one free variable, in a theory capable of representing the recursive functions, there is a sentence φ such that the theory proves φ if and only if it proves ψ applied to the code of φ. Every property expressible in the language has a sentence that ascribes that property to itself.Defined in Gödel's Incompleteness Theorems · Logic · Advanced
Dialetheism
The thesis that some contradictions are true, so that certain sentences are both true and false. Defended principally by Graham Priest, it is a metaphysical position, distinct from the logical thesis of paraconsistency, which concerns only the consequence relation and carries no commitment to any contradiction being true.Defined in Relevance Logic and Paraconsistency · Logic · Advanced
Discharge
The act of closing a subproof and drawing a conclusion that no longer depends on the assumption that opened it. The conclusion is written outside the subproof, and from that point on neither the assumption nor any line inside the subproof may be cited. Every rule that makes an assumption also discharges it, so no assumption is ever left standing at the end of a completed proof.Defined in Natural Deduction · Logic · Intermediate
Disjunction
The truth function written $P \lor Q$ and read "$P$ or $Q$": true when at least one part is true, and false only when both are false.Defined in Statements and Connectives · Logic · Beginner
Disjunctive normal form
A formula that is a disjunction of one or more disjuncts, each of which is a conjunction of one or more literals, where a literal is a sentence letter or the negation of one. Every truth function is expressed by some formula in this form, and the construction below produces one from a truth table directly.Defined in Truth-Functional Completeness · Logic · Intermediate
Disjunctive syllogism
The valid form that takes a disjunction together with the denial of one disjunct and yields the other: from $P \lor Q$ and $\neg P$, infer $Q$.Defined in Basic Inference Rules · Logic · Beginner
Dispositional state
A mental state a subject has without it being currently active: a standing belief or preference the subject would produce or act on given the right occasion, but which is doing nothing at present.Defined in What a Mental State Is · Philosophy of Mind · Beginner
Distributive justice
The question of how the benefits and burdens of social cooperation ought to be allocated among the people who take part in it: who is entitled to what, and on what basis.Defined in Liberty, Equality, and Justice as Three Demands · Political Philosophy · Beginner
Divine command theory
The view that moral obligations are constituted by God's commands, so that an action is obligatory because God commands it and wrong because God forbids it.Defined in Moral Arguments · Theism · Intermediate
divine conceptualism
The view that abstract objects are constituents of the divine mind rather than independent entities: propositions are God's thoughts, properties are God's concepts, and possible worlds are the ways God conceives things might be. Since they are not distinct from God, they do not need to be created, and aseity is preserved without any act of creation being required to explain them.Defined in Aseity and the Bootstrapping Problem · Theism · Advanced
Divine conservation
The action by which God maintains a thing in existence over time, so that the thing would cease to exist at once if the action stopped.Defined in Creation, Conservation, and Providence · Theism · Beginner
Divine freedom
The question whether God can act freely, given that a being who is essentially omnipotent and essentially perfectly good appears to have no alternative but to do the best available thing.Defined in Divine Attributes and Their Tensions · Theism · Intermediate
divine love thesis
The claim that a perfectly loving God would always be open to personal relationship with any finite person capable of such a relationship, so long as that person is not resisting it. The thesis is offered not as an empirical observation about God but as an analysis of what perfect love comes to, drawing on the least controversial features of love as it appears between persons: that a loving parent is available to a child, that unavailability requires justification, and that love which withholds itself without reason is not love.Defined in The Problem of Divine Hiddenness · Theism · Advanced
divine simplicity
The doctrine that God has no parts and no internal composition of any kind. God is not composed of matter and form, of a subject and its properties, of an essence and an existence that instantiates it, or of a genus and a differentia. The consequence usually drawn is the identity thesis: God's attributes are not distinct things God has but are identical with God and therefore with each other. God's goodness is God's power is God's knowledge is God.Defined in Simplicity, Timelessness, and Impassibility · Theism · Advanced
divine timelessness
The doctrine that God has no temporal location, no duration measured in earlier and later, and no succession of states. God does not exist at a time, was not around before the world, and will not still be around afterwards. On the traditional formulation God possesses the whole of his life at once rather than living through it in parts.Defined in Simplicity, Timelessness, and Impassibility · Theism · Advanced
Doctrine of double effect
The principle that an act with a foreseen bad effect may be permissible when the bad effect is not intended, either as an end or as a means, provided the act is otherwise acceptable and the good achieved is proportionate to the harm.Defined in The Trolley Problem as a Diagnostic · Ethics · Beginner
Doing and allowing
The distinction between bringing a harm about and failing to prevent one. It underlies the widely held view that killing is harder to justify than letting die, even when the outcome is the same.Defined in The Trolley Problem as a Diagnostic · Ethics · Beginner
Domain of discourse
The collection of objects that an interpretation of a formula is about, over which its quantifiers range. Every interpretation fixes one, and it is required to be non-empty. A claim that everything is thus and so is a claim about the domain and nothing outside it, so the same formula can be true under one interpretation and false under another purely because the domain has changed.Defined in Predicate Logic · Logic · Intermediate
Dominant sortal
Of the sortals an object falls under at a time, the one that fixes its persistence conditions and so its modal profile. On Michael Burke's account, the dominant sortal is the one whose satisfaction carries with it the widest range of properties, so that "statue", which brings a shape, an origin in a design and a place in a practice, dominates "lump of clay".Defined in The Problem of Material Constitution · Metaphysics · Advanced
Doxastic attitude
A stance a person can take toward a claim: believing it, disbelieving it, or suspending judgement about it. Suspension is a genuine third attitude rather than the absence of the first two.Defined in What Justification Is · Epistemology · Beginner
Doxastic basing
The relation between a belief and the reasons the believer actually holds it on. A belief is based on a reason when that reason is what sustains it, as opposed to merely being available to the believer or being a good reason that someone might give.Defined in Foundationalism, Coherentism, Infinitism · Epistemology · Intermediate
Doxastic voluntarism
The view that belief is subject to the will, so that a person can decide to believe a proposition and thereby believe it.Defined in Pragmatic Arguments for Belief · Theism · Intermediate
Dream argument
The argument that since dreaming can be qualitatively indistinguishable from waking, no present experience establishes that one is awake, and so no experience establishes that things are as they appear.Defined in Skepticism, First Encounter · Epistemology · Beginner
Dualism
The view that the mental and the physical are fundamentally different in kind, so that mental phenomena are not reducible to, or identical with, anything physical.Defined in The Mind-Body Problem Stated · Philosophy of Mind · Beginner
Dutch book
A set of bets, each of which an agent regards as fair given their credences, that together guarantee the agent a net loss however the world turns out.Defined in Formal Epistemology: Probabilism and Updating · Epistemology · Advanced
Duty of rescue
The obligation to assist a person in serious and immediate peril where one is in a position to help and the cost or risk to oneself is small.Defined in Rights, Duties, and Going Beyond Duty · Applied Ethics · Beginner

E

Effect
The occurrence brought about: the lighting, the breaking of the window, the fall in emissions.Defined in Causation, First Pass · Metaphysics · Beginner
Elementary equivalence
The relation holding between two structures when exactly the same first-order sentences are true in both. It is implied by isomorphism, since an isomorphism preserves every property expressible in the language, and it does not imply isomorphism, as the results above make plain.Defined in Compactness and Löwenheim-Skolem · Logic · Advanced
Elimination rule
A rule licensing an inference from a formula whose main connective is a given one to a formula in which it no longer appears as the main connective. The rule states what may be drawn from a compound of that kind, and so states what having asserted it commits one to.Defined in Natural Deduction · Logic · Intermediate
Empty domain
A model with no objects at all, excluded by the classical definition of a model and permitted in free logic. In such a model every universally quantified sentence is true and every existentially quantified one is false, and the logic that results is called universally free or inclusive.Defined in Free Logic · Logic · Advanced
Endurantism
The view that an object persists by being wholly present at each moment at which it exists. On this view the poker on Monday and the poker on Tuesday are not two portions of anything: each is the whole poker, numerically the very same object, present twice.Defined in Persistence: Endurantism and Perdurantism · Metaphysics · Intermediate
Enumerative induction
The simplest inductive form: from the observation that all examined members of a class have a property, to the conclusion that all members do, or that the next one will.Defined in The Problem of Induction · Epistemology · Intermediate
Epistemic access
