The relation a believer stands in to a justifying factor when that factor is available to them on reflection, without further investigation of the world.Defined in Internalism versus Externalism · Epistemology · Intermediate
Epistemic closure
The principle that knowledge is preserved under known entailment: if a person knows one proposition and competently deduces a second from it while retaining knowledge of the first, they know the second.Defined in Epistemic Closure and Its Denial · Epistemology · Intermediate
Epistemic injustice
A wrong done to someone specifically in their capacity as a knower. Fricker distinguishes two central forms: testimonial injustice, which occurs in the assessment of what someone says, and hermeneutical injustice, which occurs in the shared resources for making sense of experience.Defined in Epistemic Injustice · Epistemology · Intermediate
Epistemic logic
The modal treatment of knowledge and belief, with the box read as knowing and the accessibility relation running to the worlds an agent cannot distinguish from the actual one. Hintikka's Knowledge and Belief of 1962 is the founding work; knowledge is usually modelled by S4 or S5 and belief by KD45.Defined in Temporal, Deontic, and Epistemic Logic · Logic · Advanced
Epistemic luck
The condition of holding a true belief where the truth is not attributable to the believer's evidence, faculties, or competence. Knowledge is standardly taken to exclude it, though not every kind of luck in the neighbourhood is excluded.Defined in Gettier Cases and Post-Gettier Repairs · Epistemology · Intermediate
Epistemic peer
A person who is your equal with respect to a question: they have the same evidence, and they are as intelligent, careful, and free from bias in assessing it as you are.Defined in Testimony and Disagreement · Epistemology · Intermediate
Epistemic reason
A consideration that bears on whether a claim is true. Evidence, observation, testimony from someone in a position to know, and inference from other things believed are the usual sorts.Defined in What Justification Is · Epistemology · Beginner
Epistemic regress
The chain of supporting reasons generated when each justifying belief is itself asked to be justified, and the demand is repeated on whatever answers it.Defined in The Regress Problem · Epistemology · Beginner
Epistemic standards
The level of epistemic position a subject must meet for a knowledge attribution to count as true in a given context. On contextualist views these standards are set by features of the attributor's conversation, such as which possibilities of error have been mentioned or what depends on getting the answer right.Defined in Contextualism, Invariantism, and Pragmatic Encroachment · Epistemology · Advanced
Epistemic utility
The value of a credal state from a purely epistemic point of view. Epistemic utility theory treats the choice of credences as analogous to a practical decision, with epistemic utility in place of practical utility, and applies the principles of decision theory to determine which credences are rational. In accuracy-first epistemology, epistemic utility is accuracy.Defined in Accuracy-First Epistemology · Epistemology · Advanced
Epistemic value
The kind of value that belongs to cognitive states and achievements in virtue of their relation to cognitive goals such as truth, understanding and knowledge, as opposed to their practical, moral or aesthetic value.Defined in Epistemic Value and the Swamping Problem · Epistemology · Advanced
Epistemicism about vagueness
The theory that vague predicates have sharp boundaries and that vagueness is ignorance of where they lie. Defended by Timothy Williamson in 1994 and by Roy Sorensen, it retains classical logic and bivalence in full and locates the phenomenon in an epistemic principle rather than in semantics.Defined in Vagueness and the Sorites · Logic · Advanced
Epistemological disjunctivism
The view, developed by John McDowell and systematically defended by Duncan Pritchard, that in paradigm cases of perceptual knowledge the subject's rational support for their belief is both factive and reflectively accessible. The support consists in the subject's seeing that p, which entails p and is something the subject can know by reflection that they have.Defined in Epistemological Disjunctivism and the New Evil Demon · Epistemology · Advanced
Equality
The demand that people be treated as of equal standing, or that some benefit or burden be distributed evenly among them, depending on which respect is in question.Defined in Liberty, Equality, and Justice as Three Demands · Political Philosophy · Beginner
Ersatzism
The view that possible worlds are abstract objects that exist in the actual world and represent ways things could have been, rather than being further universes. "There could have been a talking donkey" is true because some abstract world represents that there is one. The name is Lewis's: an ersatz world is a substitute for the real thing.Defined in Modal Realism and Ersatzism · Metaphysics · Intermediate
Essence
The collection of a thing's essential properties, taken as an answer to the question of what that thing is.Defined in Essence and Accident · Metaphysics · Beginner
Essential dependence
Dependence of one thing on another that holds in virtue of what the first thing is: x essentially depends on y when y figures in the essence, or real definition, of x, so that a full statement of what x is must mention y. This is the account Kit Fine gave in "Ontological Dependence" (1995).Defined in Ontological Dependence · Metaphysics · Advanced
Essential property
A property a thing could not have lacked while existing. If having it is necessary for that very thing to be, the property is essential to it.Defined in Essence and Accident · Metaphysics · Beginner
Essentialism
The view that some things have some of their properties essentially, in the de re sense: a particular object could not have existed without a given property, whatever description is used to pick it out. Essentialism in the interesting sense claims this for properties that say something about what the object is, not only for trivial ones such as being self-identical.Defined in Essentialism and the Argument from Origins · Metaphysics · Intermediate
Essentialist source of necessity
The view that metaphysical necessity has its source in essence: a proposition is metaphysically necessary because it is true in virtue of the natures of things. On Fine's formulation, the metaphysically necessary truths are those true in virtue of the natures of all objects whatever, and the truths that hold in virtue of the nature of some particular object form a part of them.Defined in Essence Is Not Modality · Metaphysics · Advanced
Eternalism
The view that all times are equally real: past, present and future things all exist, and the present is not special in respect of existence.Defined in Theories of Time · Metaphysics · Intermediate
Euthyphro dilemma
The question, put to any view that grounds morality in a divine will, whether something is right because God commands it or God commands it because it is right, with each answer said to be unacceptable.Defined in Moral Arguments · Theism · Intermediate
Evaluative claim
A claim that something is good, bad, better, worse, admirable, or contemptible. It grades rather than instructs.Defined in Descriptive and Normative Claims · Ethics · Beginner
Event
A happening: something that occurs rather than something that persists. The eruption, the meeting, the collision of two cars at a particular time and place.Defined in Candidate Existents · Ontology · Beginner
Evidence as knowledge
Williamson's thesis, often written E = K, that a subject's evidence consists of exactly the propositions the subject knows. Something is part of your evidence if and only if you know it.Defined in Knowledge-First Epistemology and Anti-Luminosity · Epistemology · Advanced
Evidential aggregation
The combination of several independent pieces of evidence into a single verdict, by multiplying their individual Bayes factors together.Defined in Bayesian Natural Theology · Theism · Advanced
evidential atheology
Argument against the existence of God that proceeds by treating some feature of the world as evidence, and claiming that the evidence lowers the probability of theism, rather than by claiming that the feature is logically incompatible with theism. Its conclusion is comparative and defeasible: it says that the evidence counts against theism to some degree, which leaves open that other evidence counts in favour and that the total balance could go either way.Defined in Draper's Argument from Pain and Pleasure · Theism · Advanced
Evidential problem of evil
The argument that the amount, the kinds, and the distribution of suffering, while not logically incompatible with the existence of God, constitute strong evidence against it.Defined in The Problem of Evil · Theism · Intermediate
Evidentialism
The view that a belief is justified only in proportion to the evidence supporting it, so that religious belief is rational only if the available evidence supports it.Defined in Faith and Reason · Theism · Beginner
evolutionary argument against naturalism
Alvin Plantinga's argument that the conjunction of naturalism with the claim that human cognitive faculties arose through unguided evolution gives one no reason to think those faculties are reliable, and that recognising this gives the naturalist a defeater for all of their beliefs. Since the belief in naturalism is among them, the position defeats itself. Plantinga developed it in the final chapter of Warrant and Proper Function (Oxford University Press, 1993) and restated it at length in Where the Conflict Really Lies: Science, Religion, and Naturalism (Oxford University Press, 2011).Defined in The Evolutionary Argument Against Naturalism · Theism · Advanced
Exchange
The structural rule permitting the formulas in a sequent to be reordered. It expresses the assumption that premises form a set or multiset rather than a sequence, and dropping it leaves order significant, which is what a grammar needs.Defined in Substructural Logics · Logic · Advanced
Exchangeability
The property a probability assignment has when the probability of a sequence of outcomes depends only on how many of each kind occur, not on their order. De Finetti's representation theorem of 1937 shows that an exchangeable assignment is a mixture of independent identically distributed ones, so that a subjectivist who treats individuals symmetrically behaves as though estimating an unknown objective chance.Defined in Inductive Logic and the Carnap Programme · Logic · Advanced
Excluded middle
The schema $\varphi \lor \neg \varphi$. Classically valid because every sentence has one of two truth values, it is rejected by intuitionists on the ground that asserting a disjunction requires a method of determining which disjunct holds, and no such method is available in general.Defined in Intuitionistic Logic and Kripke Semantics · Logic · Advanced
Existence
What something has when it is one of the things there are. To say that a thing exists is to say that the world includes it. Whether saying so also describes the thing is a further question, taken up later in this tier.Defined in What 'Exists' Means · Ontology · Beginner
Existence as a predicate
The disputed claim that existing is a property a thing can have or lack, so that it may be included in or omitted from the concept of a thing.Defined in Ontological Arguments · Theism · Intermediate
Existence claim
A sentence asserting that there is at least one thing of a given kind, such as "there are prime numbers greater than a million" or "there is no largest prime".Defined in What 'Exists' Means · Ontology · Beginner
Existence predicate
The expression "exists" understood as a predicate. On the Fregean analysis it is not a first-order predicate at all: "there are horses" is regimented as saying that something is a horse, so "exists" disappears into the quantifier rather than surviving as a predicate of individuals.Defined in Is Existence a Property? · Ontology · Beginner
Existential dependence
Dependence of one thing on another for its existence. On the standard modal definition, x existentially depends on y when x is distinct from y and, necessarily, if x exists then y exists: there is no possible world containing x but not y.Defined in Ontological Dependence · Metaphysics · Advanced
existential inertia thesis
The claim that things tend to persist in existence on their own, without needing a sustaining cause at each moment. On this view a cause is required to bring a thing into existence and a cause is required to destroy it, but no cause is required for it merely to continue. Persistence is the default, and what calls for explanation is change, not continuation.Defined in Existential Inertia and Divine Conservation · Theism · Advanced
Existential quantifier
The symbol $\exists$, read "for some" or "there is at least one". The formula $\exists x Fx$ is true under an interpretation when at least one object in the domain satisfies $F$, and false when none does. It renders "some", "there is", "at least one", and "a" in its general use.Defined in Predicate Logic · Logic · Intermediate
explanatory power
The extent to which a hypothesis makes the data expected: a hypothesis has high explanatory power with respect to some evidence when, if the hypothesis were true, that evidence is what one would anticipate finding. It is only one virtue among several, and it trades against others. A hypothesis specific enough to make the data highly expected is usually less probable in advance, since it says more and therefore has more ways of being wrong, and the assessment of any explanation requires weighing that trade rather than maximising either side.Defined in Naturalism and Supernaturalism as Frameworks · Theism · Advanced
Explosion
The principle that from $\varphi$ and $\neg \varphi$ any sentence whatever follows, known also by the medieval name ex contradictione quodlibet. It holds in classical and intuitionistic logic alike.Defined in Relevance Logic and Paraconsistency · Logic · Advanced
Externalism
The denial of internalism. On externalist views, what justifies a belief can include facts the believer has no awareness of, such as the reliability of the process that produced it or the believer's causal relation to what the belief is about.Defined in Internalism versus Externalism · Epistemology · Intermediate
Extrinsic property
A property a thing has partly in virtue of how other things are, or how it is related to them. Being the tallest mountain in Wales, being owned by Priya, and being three metres from the door are all extrinsic.Defined in Objects and Properties · Metaphysics · Beginner

F

Fact
A fact is what is the case: that Brutus stabbed Caesar, that seven is prime. On the standard view a fact is not a true sentence or a true proposition but whatever makes such a sentence or proposition true, something in the world and not in language.Defined in Facts, Events, and States of Affairs · Metaphysics · Intermediate
Factive mental state
A mental state that one can be in with respect to a proposition only if that proposition is true. Seeing that it is raining, remembering that the door was locked, and knowing that the shop is closed are factive: none of them can obtain if the proposition is false. Believing and hoping are not factive.Defined in Knowledge-First Epistemology and Anti-Luminosity · Epistemology · Advanced
Factive reason
A reason whose possession entails the truth of what it supports. Seeing that there is a cup is a factive reason for believing there is a cup, since one cannot see that there is a cup unless there is one. Seeming to see a cup is not factive.Defined in Epistemological Disjunctivism and the New Evil Demon · Epistemology · Advanced
Faith
The attitude a religious believer takes toward what they believe, analysed variously as assent to propositions on the authority of the one who revealed them, as trust in a person, or as practical commitment held beyond what the evidence establishes.Defined in Faith and Reason · Theism · Beginner
Fideism
The position that religious faith does not answer to reason, either because it operates where reason has no jurisdiction or because it has standards internal to religious practice that external assessment cannot apply.Defined in Faith and Reason · Theism · Beginner
Field of events
A collection of subsets of a sample space that contains the whole space and is closed under complement and under finite union. Closure under complement and union guarantees closure under intersection as well, so the collection supports all the Boolean operations. Where the closure requirement is extended to countable unions, the collection is called a sigma-field, and that is the form the measure-theoretic treatment uses.Defined in Probability as an Extension of Logic · Logic · Intermediate
Final value
The value something has for its own sake, as an end rather than as a means. Final value is sometimes called intrinsic value, though the two can come apart: something might be valued for its own sake because of a relational property, such as being the first edition of a book.Defined in Epistemic Value and the Swamping Problem · Epistemology · Advanced
Fine-grained event
A fine-grained event is one individuated by its constitutive property (or description), so that distinct properties yield distinct events even when they are exemplified by the same object at the same place and time. On this view Brutus's stabbing of Caesar and Brutus's killing of Caesar are two events.Defined in Facts, Events, and States of Affairs · Metaphysics · Intermediate
Fine-tuning argument
The argument that the constants and initial conditions of physics fall within extremely narrow ranges compatible with the existence of complex structures, and that this is better explained by design than by chance.Defined in Design and Fine-Tuning Arguments · Theism · Intermediate
Finite additivity
The requirement that for any two events that cannot both occur, the probability of their union is the sum of their probabilities, and by repetition the same for any finite collection of pairwise exclusive events. Kolmogorov's own formulation strengthens this to countable additivity, which extends the requirement to infinite sequences of exclusive events, and the two are not equivalent.Defined in Probability as an Extension of Logic · Logic · Intermediate
First incompleteness theorem
For any consistent, recursively axiomatizable theory that represents enough arithmetic, there is a sentence in its language that the theory neither proves nor refutes. No such theory is complete, and adding the undecided sentence as a new axiom yields a theory to which the theorem applies again.Defined in Gödel's Incompleteness Theorems · Logic · Advanced
First philosophy
Aristotle's own name for the enquiry now called metaphysics: the study of being as such, prior to and more general than the study of any particular kind of being.Defined in What Metaphysics Asks · Metaphysics · Beginner
First-order property
A property of individual things: being blue, having a mass of two kilograms, being a mountain. First-order properties are what objects instantiate.Defined in Is Existence a Property? · Ontology · Beginner
First-person authority
The thesis that a subject's sincere reports about their own mental states carry a special weight, so that they are ordinarily taken as settling the matter without needing support.Defined in Introspection and Its Limits · Philosophy of Mind · Beginner
Fission case
A case in which a person at one time is related, by whatever relation is proposed as constitutive of identity, equally well to two later people who are not related to each other in that way. One person goes in, two come out.Defined in Personal Identity · Metaphysics · Intermediate
Fixed-point theory of truth
Kripke's account, on which the truth predicate is interpreted by a pair of sets, its extension and its anti-extension, and the interpretation is grown in stages from the empty pair until it reaches a fixed point, a stage at which adding the sentences now settled adds nothing further. Sentences in neither set at the fixed point receive no truth value.Defined in Undefinability and the Theories of Truth · Logic · Advanced
Formal equality
The requirement that like cases be treated alike: that where two people do not differ in any relevant respect, they be treated the same.Defined in Liberty, Equality, and Justice as Three Demands · Political Philosophy · Beginner
Formal fallacy
An invalid argument form: a pattern of premises and conclusion that fails to guarantee its conclusion no matter what is substituted into it. An argument commits a formal fallacy when it instantiates such a pattern and its arguer takes the pattern to secure the conclusion.Defined in Common Formal Fallacies · Logic · Beginner
Foundationalism
The view that justified beliefs divide into basic beliefs, which are justified without deriving their justification from other beliefs, and non-basic beliefs, which are justified by inference from basic ones. It takes the third horn of the trilemma and denies that stopping is arbitrary.Defined in Foundationalism, Coherentism, Infinitism · Epistemology · Intermediate
Frame
A non-empty set of worlds together with an accessibility relation on that set, written $\langle W, R \rangle$. A frame contains no information about which formulas are true anywhere; it is pure structure, specifying only what points there are and which of them can see which.Defined in Modal Logic: Possible Worlds Semantics · Logic · Intermediate
Frame validity
A formula is valid on a frame when it is true at every world of every model built on that frame, that is, under every assignment of truth values to the atoms. Validity on a frame is therefore a second-order condition, since it quantifies over all subsets of the set of worlds.Defined in Correspondence Theory · Logic · Advanced
Free logic
A predicate logic free of existence assumptions with respect to its singular terms, in which a term may fail to denote and quantifiers range only over what exists. The rule of universal instantiation is restricted, requiring an additional premise asserting that the instantiated term denotes.Defined in Free Logic · Logic · Advanced
Free variable
An occurrence of a variable that is not bound by any quantifier. A formula containing one says nothing determinate, since the variable names nothing; it expresses a condition that objects may or may not satisfy rather than a claim that may be true or false. A formula with no free variables is a sentence, and only sentences have truth values.Defined in Predicate Logic · Logic · Intermediate
Free will defence
The response holding that God's creating agents with genuine freedom is a good sufficient to justify permitting the moral evil those agents choose, and that not even an omnipotent being could create freely choosing agents while guaranteeing what they choose.Defined in Theodicies and Defences · Theism · Intermediate
Full ground
Some facts are a full ground of a further fact when, taken together, they ground it with nothing more needed. The fact that the postbox is red and the fact that it is cylindrical, taken together, are a full ground of the fact that it is red and cylindrical.Defined in Grounding and Metaphysical Explanation · Metaphysics · Advanced
Function
A relation that assigns to each object in one set exactly one object in another. The set the function takes its inputs from is its domain and the set it delivers values into is its codomain, and the value it assigns to $a$ is written $f(a)$. A function is injective when distinct inputs always receive distinct values, surjective when every object in the codomain is the value of something, and bijective when it is both.Defined in Basic Set Theory for Logicians · Logic · Intermediate
Functional completeness
The property a set of connectives has when every truth function of every number of arguments can be expressed by some well-formed formula built using only connectives from that set. The property concerns expressive power alone and says nothing about convenience: a complete set may require enormous formulas for functions a richer set expresses briefly.Defined in Truth-Functional Completeness · Logic · Intermediate
Fundamentality
Being basic in the order of reality. On the account built from grounding, a fact is fundamental when nothing grounds it, fully or partially, so that it holds in virtue of nothing further; one fact is more fundamental than another when it figures among that other's grounds. An entity or property counts as fundamental by way of the facts about it. Some philosophers, Sider among them, attach fundamentality instead to notions, the vocabulary in which the world is described.Defined in Fundamentality and Structure · Metaphysics · Advanced

G

Gaunilo's island
The original parody of the ontological argument: an island than which no greater can be conceived, which by Anselm's reasoning would have to exist, since an existing island is greater than an imaginary one.Defined in Modal Ontological Arguments and Their Parodies · Theism · Advanced
Generality problem
The difficulty that any token belief is produced by a process describable at many levels of generality, each with a different reliability, and that reliabilism must specify the right level without appealing to whether the resulting verdict is the intuitively correct one.Defined in Reliabilism and Virtue Epistemology · Epistemology · Intermediate
Generic dependence
Dependence of one thing on there being something or other of a certain kind, without dependence on any particular member of the kind. In modal form: necessarily, if x exists then some F other than x exists. A living body depends generically on atoms, since it needs some atoms to exist but no atom in particular.Defined in Ontological Dependence · Metaphysics · Advanced
Genetic fallacy
The mistake of inferring that a claim is true or false from facts about how the claim came to be believed or proposed.Defined in Natural Explanations of Religious Belief · Theism · Intermediate
Gettier case
A case in which a person holds a belief that is true and justified but that intuitively fails to count as knowledge, because the feature that makes the belief justified is disconnected from the feature that makes it true.Defined in Gettier Cases and Post-Gettier Repairs · Epistemology · Intermediate
Global supervenience
A family $A$ globally supervenes on a base $B$ if and only if any two possible worlds that are alike in all $B$-respects are alike in all $A$-respects. No difference between worlds in the supervening family without a difference between them in the base.Defined in Supervenience · Metaphysics · Intermediate
God
In the tradition this subject examines, the one personal being that is responsible for the existence of everything else and possesses power, knowledge, and goodness to the maximal degree, existing without depending on anything.Defined in What God Is Claimed to Be · Theism · Beginner
God of the gaps
The strategy of invoking divine action to account for whatever natural science has not yet explained, and, as a term of criticism, the charge that theistic explanation systematically occupies the shrinking territory of current ignorance. The concept was stated by Henry Drummond in the 1890s, criticising those who searched the sciences for unexplained gaps to fill with God, and the phrase is usually credited to Charles Coulson's Science and Christian Belief of 1955. Dietrich Bonhoeffer made the same complaint from a theological direction in the letters written during his imprisonment, arguing that a God found only at the limits of knowledge is a God being pushed steadily out of the world.Defined in Naturalism and Supernaturalism as Frameworks · Theism · Advanced
Gödel numbering
An assignment of distinct natural numbers to the symbols, formulas and finite sequences of formulas of a formal language, computable in both directions, so that syntactic operations on expressions correspond to arithmetical operations on their codes. Under such an assignment a sentence about numbers can be read as a sentence about the language it is written in.Defined in Gödel's Incompleteness Theorems · Logic · Advanced
Gradational accuracy
The idea that credences can be more or less accurate, depending on how close they are to the truth values of the propositions they concern. A credence of 0.9 in a truth is more accurate than a credence of 0.6, and a credence of 0.1 in a falsehood is more accurate than a credence of 0.4.Defined in Accuracy-First Epistemology · Epistemology · Advanced
Gratuitous evil
An instance of suffering that an omnipotent and omniscient being could have prevented without thereby losing some greater good or permitting some equally bad or worse evil.Defined in The Problem of Evil · Theism · Intermediate
Great Pumpkin objection
The charge that if belief in God can be properly basic without argument, so can anything. Plantinga named it after the character in the comic strip Peanuts who awaits the arrival of the Great Pumpkin each Halloween: if the theist may take belief in God as basic, the Great Pumpkin believer may take their belief as basic, and the account gives no way to distinguish them. Generalised, the worry is that a theory of proper basicality with no criterion licenses any belief whatever, which is not a defence of theism but an abandonment of epistemology.Defined in Reformed Epistemology and Proper Function · Theism · Advanced
Great-making property
A property that makes a thing greater than it would be without it, so that a being possessing it is, other things equal, greater than one lacking it.Defined in Ontological Arguments · Theism · Intermediate
Greater good
A good whose existence requires, or is made possible only by, the permitting of some evil, offered as the justifying reason for that evil.Defined in Theodicies and Defences · Theism · Intermediate
Grim Reaper paradox
The Benardete case in which infinitely many reapers are each set to kill a person at their appointed time if the person is still alive, with the appointed times having no earliest, so that the person must die and no reaper can be the one who kills them.Defined in Grim Reaper Paradoxes and Causal Finitism · Theism · Advanced
Groundedness
The property a sentence has when the fixed-point construction settles it at some stage, which happens when its value can be traced back through applications of the truth predicate to sentences not containing that predicate at all. "Snow is white is true" is grounded. The liar is not, and neither is the truth-teller, the sentence saying of itself that it is true.Defined in Undefinability and the Theories of Truth · Logic · Advanced
Grounding
The relation of non-causal determination expressed by "in virtue of" and by the metaphysical use of "because". When one fact grounds another, the second obtains in virtue of the first: the fact that Socrates exists grounds the fact that his singleton set exists, and the fact that it is raining grounds the fact that it is raining or snowing.Defined in Grounding and Metaphysical Explanation · Metaphysics · Advanced
Grounding necessitarianism
The thesis that full grounds necessitate what they ground: if some facts are a full ground of a further fact, then it is metaphysically necessary that whenever those facts obtain, the further fact obtains as well.Defined in Grounding and Metaphysical Explanation · Metaphysics · Advanced
Growing block theory
The view that the past and the present exist but the future does not. Reality grows as new moments are added at the edge, and the present is that edge.Defined in Theories of Time · Metaphysics · Intermediate
Grue
A predicate defined by Nelson Goodman in 1955: an object is grue if it is examined before a certain future time $t$ and is green, or is not examined before $t$ and is blue.Defined in Confirmation Theory, Ravens, and Grue · Epistemology · Advanced

H

Hallucination
An experience that is subjectively like perceiving an ordinary object, but in which no such object is being perceived.Defined in Sensation and Perception · Philosophy of Mind · Beginner
Halting problem
The problem of determining, given a procedure and an input, whether that procedure eventually halts on that input. The set of such pairs is recursively enumerable, since one can simply run the procedure and wait, and it is not decidable, so its complement is not recursively enumerable.Defined in Computability, Decidability, and Church's Theorem · Logic · Advanced
Harm
A setback to a being's interests: a change that leaves it worse off in some respect it has a stake in.Defined in Moral Status · Applied Ethics · Beginner
Henkin construction
The method of proving completeness by first enriching the language with new constants and adding, for every existential formula, an axiom saying that if something satisfies it then a specified new constant does. A set so extended has a name for a witness to each of its existential claims, and the model built out of its constants then satisfies the truth lemma at the quantifier cases as well as the others.Defined in Soundness and Completeness Proofs · Logic · Advanced
Henkin semantics
The interpretation on which a model specifies, alongside its domain, a collection of relations for the second-order variables to range over, required to be closed under the operations definable in the language. Second-order logic so interpreted is a two-sorted first-order logic in disguise.Defined in Second-Order and Higher-Order Logic · Logic · Advanced
Hermeneutical injustice
The wrong done when a gap in the collective interpretive resources of a society leaves someone unable to make sense of, or communicate, a significant area of their own experience, and the gap exists because their group has been excluded from the practices that generate shared meanings.Defined in Epistemic Injustice · Epistemology · Intermediate
Hick's pluralistic hypothesis
John Hick's proposal that there is a single ultimate reality, which he calls the Real, that is never encountered as it is in itself, and that the deities and absolutes of the various traditions are the Real as it appears through different historically conditioned human frameworks. The structure is borrowed from Kant: the Real in itself corresponds to the noumenon and the various described divinities to phenomena, so that no tradition's description applies to the Real as it is, and none is thereby refuted by another. Hick set the hypothesis out at length in An Interpretation of Religion in 1989, an expansion of his Gifford Lectures.Defined in Religious Pluralism and Exclusivism · Theism · Advanced
Higher-order vagueness
The vagueness of the boundary between the clear cases and the borderline cases. If there is no sharp line between the bald and the borderline bald, the classification into three categories is itself vague, and the difficulty reappears one level up without limit.Defined in Vagueness and the Sorites · Logic · Advanced
Hilbert system
A proof system with a small number of rules, often only one, and a stock of axioms carrying the weight the rules do not. The label is retrospective and honours the programme in foundations that Hilbert led rather than any single system he published; systems of this shape were standard well before the name attached to them.Defined in Axiomatic Systems and the Deduction Theorem · Logic · Intermediate
Hilbert's hotel argument
The argument that an actual infinite cannot be instantiated in the world, because a collection with infinitely many members would license operations whose results are absurd, such as adding members without increasing the total.Defined in Grim Reaper Paradoxes and Causal Finitism · Theism · Advanced
Hintikka systems
The family of confirmation functions introduced by Jaakko Hintikka in 1966, which assign positive prior probability to the constituents describing which combinations of properties are instantiated, and thereby give universal generalisations positive probability that rises with evidence. They show that the zero result is a consequence of Carnap's particular priors rather than of the probabilistic framework.Defined in Inductive Logic and the Carnap Programme · Logic · Advanced
horrendous evil
Marilyn McCord Adams's category for evils such that a person's participation in them, whether by suffering them or by doing them, gives that person reason at first sight to doubt whether their life could be a great good to them on the whole. The definition is indexed to the individual participant rather than to the world, and it covers agents as well as victims. Adams introduced the category in a 1989 symposium paper and developed it in Horrendous Evils and the Goodness of God (Cornell University Press, 1999).Defined in Horrendous Evils and Anti-Theodicy · Theism · Advanced
Human rights
Rights held by all human beings simply as such, taken to constrain what any state may do to anyone within its power, and asserted in international law and practice independently of any particular legal system's recognition of them.Defined in Rights, Introduced · Political Philosophy · Beginner
Hume's argument against miracles
The argument of Section X of Hume's Enquiry concerning Human Understanding that testimony can never make belief in a miracle reasonable, since the evidence for the law the miracle violates is always stronger than the evidence supporting any report.Defined in Miracles and Hume · Theism · Intermediate
Hume's problem of induction
The problem posed by the argument that inductive inference cannot be justified deductively, since its conclusions do not follow, nor inductively, since that would presuppose what is at issue.Defined in The Problem of Induction · Epistemology · Intermediate
Hylomorphism
The view that material substances are compounds of matter and form, where the form is a genuine constituent of the thing, not merely a description true of its matter, and is responsible for the thing's being one object of a definite kind with its own conditions of persistence. Neo-Aristotelian versions state the view within a theory of parts, often by counting the form among the thing's parts.Defined in Neo-Aristotelian Hylomorphism · Metaphysics · Advanced
Hyperactive agency detection
The proposed cognitive system that infers the presence of an agent from minimal cues, and that is biased toward over-detection because the costs of the two possible errors are unequal.Defined in Natural Explanations of Religious Belief · Theism · Intermediate
hypothesis of indifference
The hypothesis that neither the nature nor the condition of sentient beings on earth is the result of benevolent or malevolent actions performed by non-human persons. It is not the same as naturalism, and it is deliberately weaker: it does not deny that supernatural beings exist, and it does not deny that they act. It denies only that what happens to sentient creatures here is the product of their caring, one way or the other.Defined in Draper's Argument from Pain and Pleasure · Theism · Advanced
Hypothetical syllogism
The valid form that chains two conditionals sharing a middle term: from $P \rightarrow Q$ and $Q \rightarrow R$, infer $P \rightarrow R$.Defined in Basic Inference Rules · Logic · Beginner
Hypothetico-deductive method
The account of scientific reasoning on which a hypothesis is tested by deducing observable consequences from it, together with auxiliary assumptions, and checking whether they obtain. Evidence confirms a hypothesis if it is a deductive consequence of the hypothesis and the auxiliaries, and disconfirms it if the hypothesis and auxiliaries entail its negation.Defined in Confirmation Theory, Ravens, and Grue · Epistemology · Advanced

I

Identity
The relation each thing bears to itself and to nothing else. To say that a is identical with b is to say that a and b are one thing, not two.Defined in Identity and Individuation · Ontology · Beginner
Identity predicate
The two-place predicate written $=$ and read "is identical to", whose interpretation is fixed in advance rather than varying between interpretations. Where an ordinary predicate applies to whatever objects an interpretation assigns to it, $a = b$ is true exactly when $a$ and $b$ name the same object, on every interpretation without exception. It is conventionally written between its terms rather than in front of them.Defined in Identity and Definite Descriptions · Logic · Intermediate
Immanence
God's being present to and active in every part of the created order, sustaining it from within rather than operating on it from a distance.Defined in Creation, Conservation, and Providence · Theism · Beginner
Immortality of the soul
The view that a person's soul is a distinct thing from the body, capable of existing without it, and continuing after the body's death.Defined in Death and the Afterlife · Theism · Intermediate
Immutability
The doctrine that God cannot undergo change of any kind, since a perfect being could change only for the worse and a being that changes for the better was not perfect before.Defined in Divine Attributes and Their Tensions · Theism · Intermediate
impassibility
The doctrine that God cannot be acted upon by anything outside himself, and in particular cannot be caused to undergo emotional states by what creatures do. An impassible God is not made sorrowful by suffering or gratified by praise. The doctrine is compatible with God's being good and loving, provided love is understood as a settled disposition to will the good of another rather than as a feeling produced in the lover by the beloved.Defined in Simplicity, Timelessness, and Impassibility · Theism · Advanced
Impossible world
A world at which the truth conditions for the connectives do not hold, so that a contradiction may be true, or a classical tautology false. Impossible worlds are used to individuate propositions more finely than sets of possible worlds permit, since any two necessary truths hold at exactly the same possible worlds and are therefore the same proposition on the standard account.Defined in Non-Normal Modal Logics · Logic · Advanced
Imprecise probability
The representation of an epistemic state by a set of probability functions rather than a single one, so that a proposition receives an interval of values rather than a point. Developed systematically by Peter Walley in 1991, it is also known as the theory of lower and upper previsions.Defined in Probability Logic and Uncertain Premises · Logic · Advanced
Incorrigibility
The thesis that a subject cannot be mistaken about their own current mental states, so that a sincere first-person report about them cannot be false.Defined in Introspection and Its Limits · Philosophy of Mind · Beginner
Indeterminism
The thesis that the past and the laws leave more than one future open: at least some events have no sufficient cause in the prior state of the world, and the laws give only probabilities for how things will go.Defined in Free Will and Determinism · Metaphysics · Intermediate
Indexical theory of actuality
The view that "actual" is an indexical term, like "here", "now" and "I": it picks out the world of whoever uses it. For each speaker, the actual world is the world that speaker is part of, and every world is actual from its own point of view.Defined in Modal Realism and Ersatzism · Metaphysics · Intermediate
Indicative conditional
A conditional in the indicative mood, whose antecedent is entertained as a live possibility. "If Oswald did not shoot Kennedy, someone else did" is indicative, and it is true, since someone shot him.Defined in Conditionals and the Triviality Results · Logic · Advanced
Individuation
Marking off one thing from another: determining where one individual ends and the next begins, and what makes it the individual it is rather than some other.Defined in Identity and Individuation · Ontology · Beginner
Induction
Inference from premises that do not entail the conclusion but are taken to support it, typically from observed cases to unobserved ones or from a sample to a population.Defined in The Problem of Induction · Epistemology · Intermediate
Inductive logic
The study of the confirmation relation as a formal relation between sentences, with degree of confirmation playing the role that truth preservation plays in deductive logic. Its central task on Carnap's conception is to select the correct confirmation function from among the infinitely many probability measures that meet the formal constraints.Defined in Inductive Logic and the Carnap Programme · Logic · Advanced
Inductive strength
The degree to which true premises would raise the probability of a conclusion without guaranteeing it. Inductive strength comes in degrees: an argument can be strong, moderate, or weak, and adding a premise can move it in either direction.Defined in Deductive and Inductive Support · Logic · Beginner
Inference
The step from premises to conclusion; the relation an argument claims holds between them.Defined in What an Argument Is · Logic · Beginner
inference to the best explanation
The pattern of reasoning on which, given some data, one accepts the hypothesis that would best explain them if true. It is not deductive, since the data are compatible with other hypotheses, and it is not simple enumerative induction, since it can conclude to entities and processes not observed. Gilbert Harman introduced the label in "The Inference to the Best Explanation", in the Philosophical Review in 1965, and Peter Lipton's Inference to the Best Explanation (Routledge, 1991) is the standard extended treatment.Defined in Naturalism and Supernaturalism as Frameworks · Theism · Advanced
Inferential justification
Justification a belief gets from other beliefs. A belief is inferentially justified when what supports it is something else the person believes, which is offered as a reason for it.Defined in The Regress Problem · Epistemology · Beginner
Infinitism
The view that justification requires an infinite and non-repeating series of reasons, and that having such a series available is what justification consists in. It takes the first horn and denies that endless chains fail to justify.Defined in Foundationalism, Coherentism, Infinitism · Epistemology · Intermediate
Informed consent
A person's authorisation of what is to be done to them, given with adequate disclosure of the material facts, with understanding of them, voluntarily, and with the capacity to decide.Defined in Harm, Benefit, and Consent · Applied Ethics · Beginner
Innate knowledge
Knowledge held to be present in the mind prior to any experience, rather than acquired from it. The traditional rationalist doctrine, argued for by Plato and Descartes and revived in altered form by Chomsky.Defined in A Priori and A Posteriori · Epistemology · Intermediate
Instantiation
The relation that holds in the world between a thing and a property it has, in virtue of which a predication is true. Also called exemplification, or having.Defined in Objects and Properties · Metaphysics · Beginner
Instrumental value
The value something has as a means to something else. Money has instrumental value because of what it can buy. A reliable thermometer has instrumental value because it tends to give accurate readings.Defined in Epistemic Value and the Swamping Problem · Epistemology · Advanced
Intellectual virtue
A stable excellence of a cognitive agent. On reliabilist versions this means a faculty that reliably produces truth, such as good eyesight or a sound memory. On responsibilist versions it means an acquired trait of character, such as open-mindedness, intellectual courage, or thoroughness.Defined in Reliabilism and Virtue Epistemology · Epistemology · Intermediate
Intention and foresight
The distinction between the effects an agent aims at, whether as an end or as a means to their end, and the effects the agent expects to result but does not aim at, which are side effects of what they are doing.Defined in Doing, Allowing, and Double Effect · Applied Ethics · Beginner
Interest
A stake in how things go: something a being has when it can be better or worse off, so that the world can go well or badly from its own point of view.Defined in Moral Status · Applied Ethics · Beginner
Internalism
The family of views on which whether a belief is justified is settled entirely by factors internal to the believer, so that two people alike in all internal respects are alike in what they are justified in believing.Defined in Internalism versus Externalism · Epistemology · Intermediate
Interpretation
An assignment of exactly one truth value to each sentence letter of the language. Since the connectives are truth functions, an interpretation fixes a truth value for every well-formed formula, computed from the values of its letters by the rules for the connectives. For a formula containing $n$ distinct letters, there are $2^n$ interpretations that differ on those letters, and these are the rows of its truth table. In propositional logic an interpretation is nothing more than this; in predicate logic, later in the tier, it becomes a considerably richer object.Defined in Semantic and Syntactic Consequence · Logic · Intermediate
Interventionism
The view that X causes Y when an intervention on X, a change to X made from outside that does not disturb Y by any other route, would change Y. Causation is what would carry the effect of a manipulation.Defined in Theories of Causation · Metaphysics · Intermediate
Intrinsic property
A property a thing has purely in virtue of how it itself is, independently of what anything else is like. Having a mass of two kilograms, and being spherical, are the standard examples.Defined in Objects and Properties · Metaphysics · Beginner
Introduction rule
A rule licensing a formula whose main connective is a given one, on the basis of formulas that do not contain it. The rule states what has to be established in order to assert a compound of that kind, and so functions as an account of what the connective means in the system.Defined in Natural Deduction · Logic · Intermediate
Introspection
The process by which a subject comes to know about their own current mental states, apparently without observing their own behaviour and without inference from anything else.Defined in Introspection and Its Limits · Philosophy of Mind · Beginner
Intuitionistic logic
The logic obtained from classical logic by rejecting the law of excluded middle and the equivalent principles of double negation elimination and classical reductio, while retaining every other rule of natural deduction. It was formalised by Arend Heyting in 1930, following L. E. J. Brouwer's earlier informal criticism of classical reasoning about infinite totalities.Defined in Intuitionistic Logic and Kripke Semantics · Logic · Advanced
Invariantism
The view that "knows" has a single, context-invariant meaning, so that a knowledge attribution expresses the same proposition whoever utters it and wherever. Invariantists differ over what that proposition requires.Defined in Contextualism, Invariantism, and Pragmatic Encroachment · Epistemology · Advanced

J

Jeffrey updating
A generalisation of conditionalization, due to Richard Jeffrey, for cases in which experience changes one's credence in a proposition without making it certain. If experience shifts one's credence in $E$ to a new value, the new credence in $H$ is the old conditional credences in $H$ weighted by the new credences in $E$ and its negation. Also called Jeffrey conditionalization or probability kinematics.Defined in Formal Epistemology: Probabilism and Updating · Epistemology · Advanced
JTB analysis
The account on which a person knows that something is the case when three conditions hold: the claim is true, the person believes it, and the person is justified in believing it. Knowledge is justified true belief.Defined in The JTB Analysis · Epistemology · Beginner
Justification
The positive standing a doxastic attitude has when it is supported by epistemic reasons of sufficient strength. A justified belief is one the believer is, in this sense, entitled to.Defined in What Justification Is · Epistemology · Beginner

K

Kalam cosmological argument
The argument that whatever begins to exist has a cause, that the universe began to exist, and therefore that the universe has a cause of its beginning.Defined in Cosmological Arguments · Theism · Intermediate
Kant's objection
Kant's claim, directed at the ontological argument, that existence is not a determining property of things: saying that a thing exists adds nothing to the concept of it, and so cannot be one of the features a concept includes.Defined in Is Existence a Property? · Ontology · Beginner
Killing and letting die
The medical case at the centre of the dispute: whether ending a patient's life differs in moral character from withholding treatment that would have preserved it, holding the outcome, the motive, and the patient's wishes fixed.Defined in Doing, Allowing, and Double Effect · Applied Ethics · Beginner
Kleene logic
The three-valued scheme introduced by Stephen Kleene in 1938 for partial recursive predicates, in which the third value represents undefinedness. In the strong scheme a compound is defined whenever its value is settled by the defined parts, so a disjunction with a true disjunct is true even if the other is undefined; in the weak scheme any undefined part makes the whole undefined.Defined in Many-Valued Logics · Logic · Advanced
Knowledge
Belief that has both the required relation to truth and something further that a lucky guess lacks. What that further thing is, is the question the rest of this tier and the next builds toward.Defined in Knowledge, Belief, and Opinion · Epistemology · Beginner
Knowledge norm of assertion
The principle that one must assert that p only if one knows that p. Knowledge is the condition an assertion must meet to be proper, so that asserting what one does not know is a violation of the norm constitutive of assertion, even if the assertion is true or reasonable.Defined in Knowledge-First Epistemology and Anti-Luminosity · Epistemology · Advanced
Knowledge-first epistemology
The programme, associated principally with Timothy Williamson, that takes knowledge as explanatorily fundamental rather than as something to be analysed into belief, truth, justification and further conditions. Other epistemic notions, such as evidence, justification, and the norms of assertion and belief, are explained by reference to knowledge.Defined in Knowledge-First Epistemology and Anti-Luminosity · Epistemology · Advanced
Known entailment
The relation holding when a believer knows one proposition, knows that it entails a second, and is in a position to draw the inference. The qualification matters, since no principle is plausible for entailments the believer has not recognised.Defined in Epistemic Closure and Its Denial · Epistemology · Intermediate
Kolmogorov axioms
The three conditions defining a probability measure, given by Kolmogorov in 1933. Every event receives a non-negative value; the whole sample space receives the value one; and the value of a union of events that cannot occur together is the sum of their separate values. Everything else in the mathematical theory of probability is derived from these three.Defined in Probability as an Extension of Logic · Logic · Intermediate
Kripke model
A frame together with a valuation, which assigns to each atomic formula the set of worlds at which it is true. Written $\langle W, R, V \rangle$, a model contains everything needed to evaluate any formula of the language at any of its worlds, since the valuation settles the atomic cases and the clauses for the connectives and the operators settle the rest.Defined in Modal Logic: Possible Worlds Semantics · Logic · Intermediate

L

Lambek calculus
The substructural system obtained by dropping exchange as well as weakening and contraction, introduced by Joachim Lambek in 1958 for the analysis of syntax. Without exchange the antecedent is a sequence, and implication splits into a leftward and a rightward form according to which side the argument is sought on.Defined in Substructural Logics · Logic · Advanced
Law
A system of general rules issued and enforced by an authority claiming jurisdiction over a territory, which purport to bind those subject to them and which officials apply in deciding disputes.Defined in Law and the Rule of Law · Political Philosophy · Beginner
Law of nature
A true generalisation about how things behave that holds without exception, and that supports claims about what would have happened in circumstances that never arose.Defined in Miracles and Hume · Theism · Intermediate
Legal positivism
The position that what the law is depends on social facts alone, so that a rule's legal validity is determined by its sources and by the practices of officials, not by its moral merits.Defined in Law and the Rule of Law · Political Philosophy · Beginner
Legitimacy
The property a state or government has when its exercise of political power is morally justified, so that its claim to authority is a genuine right rather than a pretension.Defined in Authority and Legitimacy · Political Philosophy · Beginner
Leibniz's law
The principle that if a is identical with b, then everything true of a is true of b. Also called the indiscernibility of identicals.Defined in Change and Identity Over Time · Metaphysics · Beginner
Lewis systems
The five systems S1 to S5 developed by C. I. Lewis and C. H. Langford, axiomatising strict implication, defined as the necessity of the material conditional. S4 and S5 are normal and are the ones in wide use; S1, S2 and S3 are not, and S2 and S3 fail the rule of necessitation in the form normal systems require.Defined in Non-Normal Modal Logics · Logic · Advanced
Libertarian free will
The view that we do act freely, that free action is incompatible with determinism, and that therefore at least some human actions are not determined by the past and the laws.Defined in Free Will and Determinism · Metaphysics · Intermediate
Liberty right
A right consisting in the absence of a duty: you have a liberty right to do something exactly when you have no duty not to do it.Defined in Rights, Introduced · Political Philosophy · Beginner
Likelihood ratio
The ratio of how expected a body of evidence is on one hypothesis to how expected the same evidence is on a rival, written $P(e|h_1) / P(e|h_2)$.Defined in Bayesian Natural Theology · Theism · Advanced
Lindenbaum's lemma
The result that every consistent set of formulas is a subset of some maximal consistent set. The extension is not unique and no procedure picks out a canonical one, but at least one exists, which is all the completeness proof requires. The result is attributed to Adolf Lindenbaum, who published very little; it reached print through Tarski, who credited it to him in 1930.Defined in Soundness and Completeness Proofs · Logic · Advanced
Linear logic
The logic obtained by dropping weakening and contraction while retaining exchange, introduced by Jean-Yves Girard in 1987. Its formulas are read as resources consumed by use, and each classical connective splits into two: a multiplicative form combining separate resources and an additive form offering a choice between them.Defined in Substructural Logics · Logic · Advanced
Löb's theorem
The result that if Peano arithmetic proves $\Box A \rightarrow A$, then Peano arithmetic proves $A$. A theory can establish a reflection principle for a particular sentence only in the case where the sentence was available anyway, so the reflection principle is never a route to anything new.Defined in Provability Logic and Löb's Theorem · Logic · Advanced
Lockean thesis
The principle, so named by Richard Foley after a remark of John Locke's, that it is rational to believe a proposition if and only if it is rational to have a sufficiently high credence in it.Defined in Lottery, Preface, and the Threshold View of Belief · Epistemology · Advanced
Logic of paradox
The system LP, introduced by Graham Priest in 1979, sharing the strong Kleene tables but designating the third value as well as truth. It is paraconsistent, since a sentence and its negation can both be designated, and it has exactly the classical tautologies.Defined in Many-Valued Logics · Logic · Advanced
Logical constant
An expression held fixed in the definition of consequence, as against the non-logical vocabulary reinterpreted from model to model. The truth functional connectives, the quantifiers and identity are standardly counted logical; predicates, names and function symbols are not.Defined in What Makes a Constant Logical? · Logic · Advanced
Logical omniscience
The consequence of normality that an agent knows every logical truth and every consequence of what they know. It follows from necessitation and distribution together, and it is false of every actual agent.Defined in Temporal, Deontic, and Epistemic Logic · Logic · Advanced
Logical pluralism
The position that there is more than one correct consequence relation. In the version defended by JC Beall and Greg Restall, the generalised definition of validity, that the conclusion holds in every case in which the premises hold, admits several equally admissible specifications of a case, yielding classical, constructive and relevant consequence together.Defined in What Makes a Constant Logical? · Logic · Advanced
Logical possibility
Possibility judged by consistency alone. A claim is logically possible when it involves no contradiction, whatever else may stand in the way of its being true.Defined in Possibility and Necessity, Informally · Metaphysics · Beginner
Logical probability
A degree of confirmation holding between an evidence sentence and a hypothesis in virtue of their logical forms alone, conceived as the inductive analogue of entailment. Rudolf Carnap developed the notion systematically from the 1940s, following earlier work by Keynes and by W. E. Johnson.Defined in Inductive Logic and the Carnap Programme · Logic · Advanced
Logical problem of evil
The claim that the existence of God and the existence of any evil at all are logically inconsistent, so that theism is not merely improbable but impossible.Defined in The Problem of Evil · Theism · Intermediate
Lottery paradox
The paradox, due to Henry Kyburg in 1961, that in a large fair lottery with one winner, it is rational to believe of each ticket that it will lose, yet it is irrational to believe that every ticket will lose, which is known to be false. Given the Lockean thesis and conjunction closure, rational belief must include a known falsehood.Defined in Lottery, Preface, and the Threshold View of Belief · Epistemology · Advanced
Löwenheim-Skolem theorem
A pair of results about the sizes of models. The downward direction says that a satisfiable set of sentences in a countable language has a countable model. The upward direction says that a set with an infinite model has models of every infinite cardinality at least as large as the language. Together they say that no first-order theory with an infinite model controls how large its models are.Defined in Compactness and Löwenheim-Skolem · Logic · Advanced

M

Main connective
The connective in a formula that applies last, so that the rest of the formula falls inside one or another of its parts. Every formula that is not a single letter has exactly one.Defined in Translating English into Symbols · Logic · Beginner
Many-gods objection
The objection that the wager's reasoning applies equally well to any number of mutually incompatible religious hypotheses that promise an infinite reward, so it cannot single out the one its proponent has in mind.Defined in Pragmatic Arguments for Belief · Theism · Intermediate
Material conditional
The truth function written $P \rightarrow Q$: false in the single case where $P$ is true and $Q$ is false, and true in every other case. $P$ is the antecedent and $Q$ the consequent.Defined in Statements and Connectives · Logic · Beginner
Material constitution
The relation between a material object and what it is made of, when the two share all their matter and occupy exactly the same place: the clay constitutes the statue, the bronze constitutes the bust, the planks constitute the ship. The term is neutral on whether the constituting thing and the constituted thing are one thing or two, and that is the question at issue.Defined in The Problem of Material Constitution · Metaphysics · Advanced
Matter and form
Aristotle's pair of principles for analysing a material thing. The matter is what the thing is made of and what persists when it comes to be: the bronze of a statue, the bricks and timber of a house. The form is what makes that matter into a thing of a definite kind: the shape and organisation in virtue of which the bronze is a statue and the bricks a house, and which Aristotle identifies with the thing's essence.Defined in Neo-Aristotelian Hylomorphism · Metaphysics · Advanced
Maximal consistent set
A consistent set of formulas that cannot be extended: adding any formula not already in it produces an inconsistent set. Equivalently, a consistent set containing, for every formula of the language, either that formula or its negation. Such a set decides every question the language can pose, and it decides them in a way that turns out to mirror the behaviour of a single interpretation.Defined in Soundness and Completeness Proofs · Logic · Advanced
Maximal greatness
The property of having maximal excellence, understood as omnipotence, omniscience, and moral perfection, in every possible world rather than merely in some.Defined in Ontological Arguments · Theism · Intermediate
McTaggart's argument
The argument that time is unreal because it requires change, change requires the A-series, and the A-series is contradictory.Defined in Theories of Time · Metaphysics · Intermediate
meaningful life argument
The central argument for pro-theism, which holds that a range of goods bearing on the significance of human life are available only if God exists: that each person's existence is intended rather than accidental, that suffering is not finally wasted, that moral wrongs are not left permanently unaddressed, that death is not the end of the person, and that each person is known and loved by a being who understands them completely. The argument is not that a godless life is meaningless, which few defend, but that these particular goods are large and that their absence is a large loss.Defined in The Axiology of Theism · Theism · Advanced
Meinongianism
The view, after Alexius Meinong, that there are objects which do not exist, and that such objects genuinely have the properties their descriptions attribute to them.Defined in Existence and Non-Existence · Metaphysics · Beginner
Memory
The retention of information already acquired, and the source of belief when a person believes something because they remember it.Defined in Sources: Perception, Memory, Testimony, Reason · Epistemology · Beginner
Mental state
A condition a subject is in that is characterised in psychological terms: believing something, wanting something, being in pain, attending to something. Mental states are the items a psychological description of a person is made of.Defined in What a Mental State Is · Philosophy of Mind · Beginner
Mentalism
The view that justification supervenes on the believer's mental states, so that any two believers in exactly the same mental states are justified in exactly the same beliefs, whether or not those states are reflectively accessible.Defined in Internalism versus Externalism · Epistemology · Intermediate
mere conservationism
The position that God's causal role in the ordinary course of nature is limited to creating things and keeping them in existence with their powers intact. Given that a creature exists and has the power to do something, its doing it requires no further divine contribution. God sustains the fire; the fire does the burning, unaided. The medieval figure usually named as its representative is Durandus of Saint-Pourçain.Defined in Existential Inertia and Divine Conservation · Theism · Advanced
Mereological fusion
An object made up of some given things and nothing else. An object $z$ is a fusion of some things when each of them is part of $z$, and every part of $z$ overlaps at least one of them. A fusion is also called a mereological sum.Defined in Mereology and Composition · Metaphysics · Intermediate
Mereological nihilism
The view that composition never occurs: no two or more things ever compose an object. Nothing has proper parts, so everything that exists is a simple.Defined in Mereology and Composition · Metaphysics · Intermediate
Mereological universalism
The view that composition always occurs: for any things whatever, there is an object they compose, however scattered, unrelated or unlike one another they may be.Defined in Mereology and Composition · Metaphysics · Intermediate
Mereology
The formal theory of parthood: the principles governing the relation of part to whole, and the further relations that can be defined from it. The name comes from the Greek meros, part.Defined in Mereology and Composition · Metaphysics · Intermediate
Merit
Fitness for a particular position or task: the qualities, skills, and capacities that make someone able to do well what the position requires.Defined in What Justice Requires · Political Philosophy · Beginner
Metaethics
The part of ethics that asks about moral claims rather than making them: what they mean, whether they can be true, what would make them true, and how anyone could know. Its output is claims about morality.Defined in What Metaethics Asks · Ethics · Beginner
Metalanguage
The language in which the object language is described. Here it is English supplemented with some notation, including the variables $\varphi$ and $\psi$ that range over formulas of the object language, and the symbols for the consequence relations introduced in the next article. Statements about which strings are wffs, or about what follows from what, are made in the metalanguage; they are not themselves formulas.Defined in Propositional Logic and Well-Formed Formulas · Logic · Intermediate
Metaphysical explanation
An explanation of why something is the case that cites what it holds in virtue of, rather than what brought it about. Its answers are grounds: the set exists because Socrates does, the act is wrong because it is a betrayal, the disjunction is true because one of its disjuncts is.Defined in Grounding and Metaphysical Explanation · Metaphysics · Advanced
Metaphysical possibility
Possibility judged by the natures of things: what could have been the case given what the things involved actually are, whether or not the laws of nature or logic alone would have permitted it.Defined in Possibility and Necessity, Informally · Metaphysics · Beginner
Metaphysics
The study of the most general features of reality: what kinds of thing there are, what it is for something to be a thing at all, and how the categories we describe the world with fit together.Defined in What Metaphysics Asks · Metaphysics · Beginner
Method of cases
The practice of testing general moral claims against judgements about particular scenarios, treating a clash between a principle and a confident judgement about a case as evidence against the principle.Defined in Moral Intuitions and What to Do With Them · Ethics · Beginner
methodological naturalism
The working rule that scientific inquiry proceeds by seeking natural causes and does not admit supernatural ones among its candidate explanations. It is a constraint on method rather than a claim about what exists, and it is compatible with the truth of theism: a theist can hold that God created a law-governed order and that investigating that order means looking for its regularities rather than invoking its author. Metaphysical naturalism, by contrast, is the substantive claim that there is nothing beyond nature.Defined in Naturalism and Supernaturalism as Frameworks · Theism · Advanced
middle knowledge
God's knowledge of what any possible free creature would freely do in any possible set of circumstances. It is called middle because it falls between two other kinds. Natural knowledge is of necessary truths and of everything that could possibly happen, and God has it independently of any decision. Free knowledge is of what actually happens, and God has it as a consequence of deciding which world to make actual. Middle knowledge is of contingent truths that God does not decide, known prior to the creative decision and therefore available as input to it.Defined in Divine Foreknowledge and Freedom · Theism · Advanced
Mind-body problem
The problem of saying how mental states and processes are related to physical states and processes, and in particular to the body and the brain.Defined in The Mind-Body Problem Stated · Philosophy of Mind · Beginner
Miracle
An event that exceeds what nature can produce, brought about by the action of God, and standardly characterised as a violation of a law of nature by a divine volition.Defined in Miracles and Hume · Theism · Intermediate
Modal account of essence
The view that for a property to be essential to an object is for the object to have it necessarily: to have it at every possible world at which the object exists. An object's essence, on this view, is the collection of properties it has in every world in which it exists, and there is nothing more to being essential than this modal fact.Defined in Essence Is Not Modality · Metaphysics · Advanced
modal collapse objection
The argument that divine simplicity entails that everything that exists exists necessarily. If God's act of creating is identical with God's essence, and God's essence exists of absolute necessity, then God's act of creating is absolutely necessary, and so is everything that act produces. The consequence is that God could not have refrained from creating this world, that no contingency survives anywhere, and that divine freedom is lost.Defined in Simplicity, Timelessness, and Impassibility · Theism · Advanced
Modal ontological argument
An argument that proceeds from the premise that a necessarily existing perfect being is possible to the conclusion that such a being actually exists, using the principle that what is possibly necessary is necessary.Defined in Ontological Arguments · Theism · Intermediate
Modal realism
The view that there exist many possible worlds besides the actual one, each as real as ours and of the same kind as ours, and that modal claims are made true by what goes on in them. "There could have been a talking donkey" is true because, in some other world, there is one.Defined in Modal Realism and Ersatzism · Metaphysics · Intermediate
Modality
The general topic of possibility and necessity, and of the related notions of impossibility and contingency. A modal claim is one that says how a thing is rather than merely that it is.Defined in Possibility and Necessity, Informally · Metaphysics · Beginner
Model
An interpretation on which a given formula, or every member of a given set of formulas, comes out true. A set of formulas that has at least one model is satisfiable, and one with no model is unsatisfiable. The word carries the same sense in the phrase model theory: the models of a set of sentences are the situations in which those sentences hold.Defined in Semantic and Syntactic Consequence · Logic · Intermediate
Model-theoretic consequence
The relation holding between a set of sentences and a sentence when every model of the set is a model of the sentence. Tarski's 1936 paper proposed this as the analysis of following from, replacing the proof-theoretic conception on which consequence is derivability in a system.Defined in What Makes a Constant Logical? · Logic · Advanced
Modus ponens
The valid form that takes a conditional together with its antecedent and yields its consequent: from $P \rightarrow Q$ and $P$, infer $Q$.Defined in Basic Inference Rules · Logic · Beginner
Modus tollens
The valid form that takes a conditional together with the denial of its consequent and yields the denial of its antecedent: from $P \rightarrow Q$ and $\neg Q$, infer $\neg P$.Defined in Basic Inference Rules · Logic · Beginner
Molinism
The account of providence built on middle knowledge, developed by Luis de Molina in the Concordia of 1588. God knows the complete set of counterfactuals of freedom, and with that knowledge chooses which total situation to actualise. What creatures then freely do is not caused by God, but God knew it before deciding, because God knew what they would do in whatever circumstances he might set up. Providence is exercised through the choice of circumstances rather than through the determination of acts, which is why Molinists claim to combine full divine control over history with libertarian freedom for creatures.Defined in Divine Foreknowledge and Freedom · Theism · Advanced
Monism
The view that reality is composed of one fundamental kind of thing, so that mental and physical phenomena are not two basic categories but aspects, arrangements, or instances of a single category.Defined in The Mind-Body Problem Stated · Philosophy of Mind · Beginner
Monopoly on force
The state's claimed exclusive right to authorise the use of physical force within its territory, such that any private use of force is permitted only on terms the state sets.Defined in What a State Is For · Political Philosophy · Beginner
Monotonicity
The requirement that a formula true at a stage remains true at every later stage. Imposed on atoms as a condition on models, it is provable for all formulas, and it encodes the thought that what has been established is not later lost.Defined in Intuitionistic Logic and Kripke Semantics · Logic · Advanced
Moral agent
A being capable of recognising moral reasons and acting on them, and so capable of being held responsible for what it does.Defined in Moral Status · Applied Ethics · Beginner
Moral argument
An argument from the existence or the character of moral facts to the existence of God, in either a theoretical form claiming God is the best explanation of those facts or a practical form claiming that moral commitment rationally requires belief in God.Defined in Moral Arguments · Theism · Intermediate
Moral epistemology
The study of how moral claims could be known or justified, and what the sources of moral knowledge are.Defined in What Metaethics Asks · Ethics · Beginner
Moral evil
Suffering or wrongdoing brought about by the free choices of responsible agents.Defined in The Problem of Evil · Theism · Intermediate
moral insensitivity objection
The charge that constructing justifications for suffering damages the moral perception of the person who constructs them. Someone practised at explaining why a given atrocity was permitted for the sake of a greater good has acquired a habit of looking at other people's worst experiences as instrumental, and that habit is held to be corrupting whether or not the explanations are true. The objection is directed at theodicy as an activity rather than at any particular theodicy's content.Defined in Horrendous Evils and Anti-Theodicy · Theism · Advanced
Moral intuition
A moral judgement about a case or principle that strikes a person as correct without being inferred from anything else. It is how the case seems on considering it, prior to any theory.Defined in Moral Intuitions and What to Do With Them · Ethics · Beginner
Moral metaphysics
