The study of what would have to exist for moral claims to be true, and whether it does: whether there are moral properties and facts, and what sort of thing they could be.Defined in What Metaethics Asks · Ethics · Beginner
Moral obligation
A requirement to act that binds an agent whether or not the agent accepts it and whether or not acting on it serves the agent's interests.Defined in Moral Arguments · Theism · Intermediate
moral paralysis objection
The objection that skeptical theism, if accepted, undermines the reasoning by which we decide what to do. If I cannot tell whether preventing some suffering would forfeit a greater good beyond my grasp, then I cannot tell whether preventing it is the right thing to do, and the same doubt attends every action whose justification runs through its consequences. Michael Almeida and Graham Oppy pressed the objection in "Sceptical Theism and Evidential Arguments from Evil" in the Australasian Journal of Philosophy in 2003.Defined in Skeptical Theism and Its Costs · Theism · Advanced
Moral patient
A being that can be wronged, and to which duties are therefore owed, whether or not it is itself capable of having duties.Defined in Moral Status · Applied Ethics · Beginner
Moral principle
A general normative claim of the form that actions with some feature are right, wrong, or required, in virtue of having it. Principles are the components a theory is assembled from.Defined in What a Moral Theory Is · Ethics · Beginner
Moral responsibility
The status of being an appropriate target of reactive attitudes such as blame, praise, resentment and gratitude, in virtue of what one has done. To say someone is morally responsible for an act is to say that the act can be fairly held against them, or counted in their favour.Defined in Free Will and Determinism · Metaphysics · Intermediate
Moral semantics
The study of what moral claims mean and what kind of speech act is performed in making them: whether they state facts, express attitudes, issue prescriptions, or do something else.Defined in What Metaethics Asks · Ethics · Beginner
Moral status
The property a thing has when it matters morally for its own sake, so that there are reasons to treat it in some ways rather than others which are grounded in what it is or what things are like for it, rather than in anyone else's interests.Defined in Moral Status · Applied Ethics · Beginner
Moral theory
A systematic account of what makes actions right or wrong, stated generally enough to deliver verdicts on cases it was not built from.Defined in What a Moral Theory Is · Ethics · Beginner
Morley's theorem
The result that a countable first-order theory categorical in one uncountable cardinality is categorical in every uncountable cardinality. Proved by Michael Morley in 1965, it establishes that uncountable categoricity is a single property rather than a family of properties indexed by cardinals.Defined in Model Theory: Types, Quantifier Elimination, Categoricity · Logic · Advanced
Motivating reason
The consideration a person actually acts on, whatever its merits. It is the answer to why they did it, in the sense that identifies what they were going for.Defined in Reasons, Oughts, and Normative Force · Ethics · Beginner
Multiverse hypothesis
The hypothesis that our universe is one member of a very large or infinite ensemble of universes in which constants and initial conditions vary.Defined in Design and Fine-Tuning Arguments · Theism · Intermediate
Mystical experience
An experience characterised by a sense of unity, understood either as unity perceived in and through the world of ordinary objects or as unity found by emptying the mind of ordinary content, and typically reported as beyond adequate expression while carrying a conviction of insight.Defined in Religious Experience · Theism · Intermediate

N

Narrative identity
The view that a person's identity is constituted, at least in part, by a story: the account, told by the person or woven from their life by others, in which events are linked into a connected history with a character who endures through it.Defined in Personal Identity · Metaphysics · Intermediate
Natural deduction
A proof system with no axioms, in which every step is licensed by a rule, and in which formulas may be assumed temporarily for the sake of argument and later set aside. The name records the design goal: the rules were chosen to match the moves that mathematical arguments actually make, rather than to minimise the number of primitives.Defined in Natural Deduction · Logic · Intermediate
Natural evil
Suffering brought about by the operation of the natural world, with no responsible agent choosing it.Defined in The Problem of Evil · Theism · Intermediate
Natural law theory
The position that law is connected to morality by more than accident, so that moral standards enter into what makes a rule a law at all rather than merely into whether it is a good law.Defined in Law and the Rule of Law · Political Philosophy · Beginner
Natural rights
Rights held in virtue of what a person is rather than in virtue of any law, agreement, or institution, and therefore held by people whether or not any legal system recognises them.Defined in Rights, Introduced · Political Philosophy · Beginner
Natural theology
The project of investigating claims about God using the faculties natural to human beings, principally reason, perception, and reflection, without appeal to revelation.Defined in Faith and Reason · Theism · Beginner
naturalism
The view that the natural world is all there is: there are no supernatural entities, no minds or agents that exist independently of physical processes, and no explanations that appeal to purposes outside those had by natural organisms. Stating it precisely is harder than it looks, because "natural" is usually explained as "of the kind studied by the natural sciences", which makes the thesis hostage to whatever the sciences turn out to study, and because a science that discovered an intelligent cosmic agent would presumably make that agent natural by definition.Defined in Naturalism and Supernaturalism as Frameworks · Theism · Advanced
Naturalness
An objective distinction among properties between those that mark genuine respects of similarity in the world and those that are gerrymandered or miscellaneous. On Lewis's account it comes in degrees: being green is more natural than being grue, and having a certain charge is more natural than either.Defined in Fundamentality and Structure · Metaphysics · Advanced
Necessary a posteriori
A truth that is necessary but can be known only a posteriori, through experience: it could not have been false, and yet no amount of reflection without investigation would establish it.Defined in Essentialism and the Argument from Origins · Metaphysics · Intermediate
Necessary and sufficient conditions
A condition is necessary for something when that thing cannot hold without it, and sufficient when its holding is enough. A set of conditions that are individually necessary and jointly sufficient picks out exactly the cases in question, admitting no others and excluding none.Defined in The JTB Analysis · Epistemology · Beginner
Necessary being
A being that could not have failed to exist, whose existing is explained by what it is rather than by anything outside it.Defined in Cosmological Arguments · Theism · Intermediate
Necessary condition
A condition without which something cannot occur. Oxygen is a necessary condition for the match to light: no oxygen, no lighting.Defined in Causation, First Pass · Metaphysics · Beginner
Necessity
The status of being unable to fail to be the case. A claim is necessary when there is no way for it to be false.Defined in Possibility and Necessity, Informally · Metaphysics · Beginner
Necessity of identity
The thesis that if $a$ and $b$ are identical, then necessarily they are identical: $a = b \rightarrow \Box\, a = b$. It follows from the reflexivity of identity, Leibniz's law and necessitation, and is therefore available in any quantified modal system retaining all three.Defined in Quantified Modal Logic and the Barcan Formulas · Logic · Advanced
Necessity operator
The one-place operator written $\Box$ and read "it is necessary that" or "necessarily", which attaches to a formula to make a longer formula. Where $\varphi$ is a well-formed formula, so is $\Box \varphi$, and the operator may be applied repeatedly and may occur inside the scope of connectives and quantifiers exactly as negation does.Defined in Modal Logic: Possible Worlds Semantics · Logic · Intermediate
Need
What a person requires in order to reach some threshold of functioning or well-being, independently of what they have done or what they can do.Defined in What Justice Requires · Political Philosophy · Beginner
Negation
The truth function written $\neg P$ and read "not $P$": true when $P$ is false, and false when $P$ is true.Defined in Statements and Connectives · Logic · Beginner
Negative duty
A duty not to do something to someone: an obligation discharged by refraining, which every person can satisfy toward every other person at the same time.Defined in Rights, Duties, and Going Beyond Duty · Applied Ethics · Beginner
Negative existential
A truth saying that there is nothing of a certain kind, or that a certain thing does not exist: "there are no unicorns", "there is no largest prime", "Vulcan does not exist". A negative existential is true because of what is absent, and so it offers no obvious entity to be its truthmaker.Defined in Truthmaker Theory · Metaphysics · Advanced
Negative liberty
Freedom understood as the absence of interference: a person is free to the extent that no one else prevents them from doing what they might otherwise do.Defined in Liberty, Equality, and Justice as Three Demands · Political Philosophy · Beginner
Negative rights
Rights whose corresponding duty is a duty of restraint: that others not do something to the right-holder.Defined in Rights, Introduced · Political Philosophy · Beginner
Neighbourhood semantics
An interpretation assigning to each world a collection of sets of worlds, its neighbourhoods, with $\Box \varphi$ true at a world when the set of worlds satisfying $\varphi$ is one of that world's neighbourhoods. Introduced independently by Dana Scott and Richard Montague in 1970, it is also called Scott-Montague semantics.Defined in Non-Normal Modal Logics · Logic · Advanced
neo-classical theism
Charles Hartshorne's position, on which God has two aspects rather than one. In his abstract essence God is unchanging, necessary, and perfect in the classical way; in his concrete states God is affected by the world, grows in knowledge as events occur, and is enriched by what creatures do. The view is also called dipolar theism, and it is a form of panentheism, since the world is included in God through God's knowledge and love of it without being identical with God.Defined in Classical Theism Against Theistic Personalism · Theism · Advanced
New evil demon problem
The objection, due to Keith Lehrer and Stewart Cohen in 1983 and developed by Cohen in 1984, that externalist theories of justification give the wrong verdict about a subject who is internally identical to a normal perceiver but systematically deceived by a demon. The deceived subject seems just as justified as the normal one, but their belief-forming processes are unreliable, so reliabilism says they are not justified.Defined in Epistemological Disjunctivism and the New Evil Demon · Epistemology · Advanced
New riddle of induction
Goodman's problem of explaining why some predicates, such as green, support inductive generalisation from observed instances while others, such as grue, do not, when the observed instances fit both equally well.Defined in Confirmation Theory, Ravens, and Grue · Epistemology · Advanced
No false lemmas
The proposal that knowledge is justified true belief whose justification does not essentially depend on any false proposition. Smith fails the condition because his reasoning passes through the falsehood that Jones will get the job.Defined in Gettier Cases and Post-Gettier Repairs · Epistemology · Intermediate
no-best-world problem
The difficulty that arises if, for every world an omnipotent being could create, there is a better one that could have been created instead. The series of possible worlds would then be unbounded above, with no maximum, in the way the natural numbers are unbounded. Since perfect goodness is normally understood as requiring that one do the best one can, and there would be no best to do, either the standard for perfect goodness cannot be met or that standard is not the right one.Defined in The No-Best-World Problem · Theism · Advanced
Nominalism
The view that there are no universals: everything that exists is particular, and when two things are alike in some respect, there is no third thing, shared between them, in virtue of which they are.Defined in Universals and Particulars · Metaphysics · Intermediate
Non-normal world
A world of a relational model at which $\Box \varphi$ is stipulated false for every $\varphi$, and correspondingly $\Diamond \varphi$ true for every $\varphi$, regardless of the accessibility relation. Validity is defined as truth at every normal world of every model, so a formula can fail to be valid by failing at a normal world that accesses a non-normal one.Defined in Non-Normal Modal Logics · Logic · Advanced
Nonexistent object
An object that has properties and can be referred to, described, and distinguished from other objects, while not being among the things that exist.Defined in Existence and Non-Existence · Metaphysics · Beginner
nonresistant nonbelief
Nonbelief in God that is not the result of the person's own resistance to relationship with God. It covers the lifelong seeker who investigates in good faith and finds nothing; the former believer who loses belief while wishing it were otherwise; the person raised in a tradition with no concept of the God in question; and anyone who would welcome the relationship if they took it to be available. Schellenberg's argument is stated in terms of this category rather than in terms of reasonable or justified nonbelief, in order to avoid disputes about the standards for rational belief.Defined in The Problem of Divine Hiddenness · Theism · Advanced
Nonstandard element
An element of a nonstandard model larger than the interpretation of every numeral. Such an element is not the value of any closed term of the language, and the model also contains the images of all the numerals, called its standard part.Defined in Nonstandard Models of Arithmetic · Logic · Advanced
Nonstandard model
A model of the first-order theory of the natural numbers that is not isomorphic to the natural numbers. Every such model satisfies exactly the same first-order sentences as the standard one, so no sentence of the language distinguishes it, and it is nonetheless a different structure.Defined in Nonstandard Models of Arithmetic · Logic · Advanced
nontheistic religion
A religious tradition that does not affirm a creator God and whose central claims are not about one. Theravada Buddhism analyses the human situation and prescribes a path without positing a creator, and treats the question as one that does not conduce to liberation. Jainism has no creator and holds the universe to be eternal. Within Indian philosophy, the Mimamsa school developed an elaborate defence of scriptural authority while arguing against the existence of a creator. The category is not a curiosity: it covers a substantial fraction of the world's religious life.Defined in Philosophy of Religion Beyond Monotheism · Theism · Advanced
Normal modal logic
A set of formulas containing every propositional tautology and every instance of the distribution schema, closed under modus ponens, closed under uniform substitution, and closed under the rule of necessitation, which permits inferring $\Box \varphi$ from $\varphi$ whenever $\varphi$ has itself been proved. Every system in this article is normal, and systems failing one of these conditions, which do exist and have uses, are treated in the advanced tier.Defined in The Normal Systems K, D, T, B, S4, S5 · Logic · Intermediate
Normative claim
A claim about how things ought to be, or about what someone has reason to do. It does not report the world; it says something about what the world calls for.Defined in Descriptive and Normative Claims · Ethics · Beginner
Normative ethics
The part of ethics that asks which actions are right, which things are good, and what makes them so. Its output is claims about conduct.Defined in What Metaethics Asks · Ethics · Beginner
Normative reason
A consideration that counts in favour of some action or attitude. It is a reason there is, whether or not anyone has noticed it, and whether or not it moves anyone.Defined in Reasons, Oughts, and Normative Force · Ethics · Beginner
Normative theory
A general account of what makes actions right or wrong, or of what a good life or a good character consists in, offered as the standard against which particular judgements are to be assessed.Defined in From Theory to Cases · Applied Ethics · Beginner
Normativity
The general feature shared by reasons, oughts, values, and standards: the property of favouring, requiring, or grading rather than merely describing.Defined in Reasons, Oughts, and Normative Force · Ethics · Beginner
noseeum inference
Wykstra's label, introduced in his 1996 essay "Rowe's Noseeum Arguments from Evil", for an inference from "so far as I can tell, there is no such thing" to "there is no such thing". Such inferences are ordinary and often good, but their strength depends entirely on a background assumption about detectability: that if the thing existed, one would probably have noticed. Where that assumption fails, the inference carries no weight at all.Defined in The Probabilistic Problem of Evil · Theism · Advanced
Number
A mathematical object such as 7 or π, if there are such objects: the sort of thing numerals appear to name and mathematical statements appear to be about.Defined in Candidate Existents · Ontology · Beginner
Numerical identity
The relation a thing bears to itself and to nothing else. Two names or descriptions pick out numerically identical things when there is one thing there, not two.Defined in Change and Identity Over Time · Metaphysics · Beginner

O

O-minimality
The property a structure with a linear order has when every definable subset of its universe is a finite union of points and open intervals with endpoints in the structure. Definable sets in one variable are as simple as the order permits, and by a theorem of Pillay and Steinhorn the property transfers to every structure elementarily equivalent to the given one.Defined in Model Theory: Types, Quantifier Elimination, Categoricity · Logic · Advanced
Object
A thing that has properties without being a property of anything else: the mug, the mountain, the electron, arguably the number nine. Also called a particular, an individual, or in the older vocabulary a substance.Defined in Objects and Properties · Metaphysics · Beginner
Object language
The language being studied. In propositional logic it contains exactly the sentence letters, the five connectives, and the parentheses, and nothing else. Its expressions are the wffs.Defined in Propositional Logic and Well-Formed Formulas · Logic · Intermediate
occasionalism
The position that creatures have no causal power whatever, and that what look like natural causes are only the occasions on which God produces the effects directly. The fire does not heat the water; God heats the water when the fire is present, and does so with such regularity that we mistake the pattern for a power. On this account there is exactly one cause in the universe.Defined in Existential Inertia and Divine Conservation · Theism · Advanced
Occurrent state
A mental state that is currently active in the subject: a thought being entertained, a pain being felt, a desire currently operating on behaviour.Defined in What a Mental State Is · Philosophy of Mind · Beginner
Ockhamism
The response that denies the second premise, holding that God's past beliefs about the future are not accidentally necessary because they are not really facts about the past alone. A hard fact about a time is one whose obtaining is settled by how things are at that time. A soft fact about a time is one that is partly about later times, as it was a fact in 1900 that a war would begin fourteen years later. Ockhamists argue that God's believing in 1000 that you would have coffee tomorrow is a soft fact about the year 1000, since its obtaining depends on what happens tomorrow, and soft facts about the past carry no accidental necessity.Defined in Divine Foreknowledge and Freedom · Theism · Advanced
Old evidence problem
The difficulty that evidence already known has probability one, so that conditioning on it cannot change any hypothesis's probability, even when that evidence is what convinced everyone in the first place.Defined in Bayesian Natural Theology · Theism · Advanced
Omnibenevolence
Perfect goodness: moral excellence that could not be surpassed, in what God wants, what God is like, and what God does.Defined in What God Is Claimed to Be · Theism · Beginner
Omnipotence
Maximal power: the property of a being whose power could not be exceeded by any other being.Defined in What God Is Claimed to Be · Theism · Beginner
Omnipresence
The property of being present everywhere, ascribed to God despite God's being immaterial and therefore not the kind of thing that occupies a region.Defined in Divine Attributes and Their Tensions · Theism · Intermediate
Omniscience
Maximal knowledge: for every proposition, if it is true then God knows it, and God believes nothing false.Defined in What God Is Claimed to Be · Theism · Beginner
Ontological argument
An argument from the concept or definition of God alone, without appeal to any observation, to the conclusion that God exists.Defined in Ontological Arguments · Theism · Intermediate
Ontological commitment
What a theory must say exists for its claims to be true. A theory is committed to entities of a kind when there is no way for what it asserts to be true unless there are entities of that kind.Defined in Ontological Commitment, Informally · Ontology · Beginner
Ontological inventory
The complete list of what a theory says there is: every kind of entity that has to be on the list for the theory's claims to come out true.Defined in Ontological Commitment, Informally · Ontology · Beginner
Ontology
The study of what there is: which things exist, what kinds they divide into, and what would settle a disagreement about existence when one arises.Defined in What 'Exists' Means · Ontology · Beginner
open theism
The view that the future is genuinely open, so that propositions about what free creatures will do are not yet true, and God therefore does not know them. God is held to know everything that is true, including every possibility and every probability, and to be unsurpassably wise in responding to what happens. What is denied is not omniscience but that infallible knowledge of future free acts is among the things omniscience covers, since there is nothing there to know.Defined in Divine Foreknowledge and Freedom · Theism · Advanced
Opinion
A belief held on grounds the holder does not regard as settling the matter, and about which reasonable disagreement is expected.Defined in Knowledge, Belief, and Opinion · Epistemology · Beginner
Origin essentialism
The thesis that a thing's origin is essential to it: an object could not have originated from anything other than what it actually originated from. For an organism the origin is usually taken to be the particular cells it developed from; for an artefact, the matter it was originally made from.Defined in Essentialism and the Argument from Origins · Metaphysics · Intermediate
Other minds problem
The problem of saying what entitles anyone to believe that beings other than themselves have mental states, given that only behaviour and physical constitution are observable and mental states themselves are not.Defined in The Problem of Other Minds · Philosophy of Mind · Beginner
Ought
The word marking what a person is required or recommended to do. An ought-claim directs action, where an evaluative claim only ranks.Defined in Descriptive and Normative Claims · Ethics · Beginner
Outer domain
A second domain of a model, disjoint from or containing the domain of quantification, providing denotations for terms that do not denote anything existing. Quantifiers range over the inner domain only, while a predicate may hold of an object in the outer one, which is how a positive free logic makes a sentence about Pegasus true.Defined in Free Logic · Logic · Advanced
Overspill
The principle that a formula holding of every standard element of a nonstandard model holds of some nonstandard element. It follows because the set of elements satisfying the formula, if it contained exactly the standard elements, would give a definable set with no least element among the elements failing the formula, contradicting the least number principle that the model satisfies.Defined in Nonstandard Models of Arithmetic · Logic · Advanced

P

panentheism
The view that the world is contained within the divine, which is nonetheless more than the world. It is positioned deliberately between classical theism, which places God wholly outside the world, and pantheism, which identifies them, and it aims to keep divine immanence without surrendering transcendence. The most developed versions are the process theologies descending from Charles Hartshorne, on which God has two aspects: an abstract, unchanging character and a concrete, changing life that includes and is affected by what happens in the world.Defined in Philosophy of Religion Beyond Monotheism · Theism · Advanced
pantheism
The view that the divine is identical with the totality of what exists, so that there is no God distinct from the universe and no universe distinct from God. Spinoza's Ethics of 1677 is the canonical philosophical statement, and his formula Deus sive Natura, God or Nature, marks the identification. Pantheism is not the claim that nature is worthy of reverence, which an atheist may accept; it is the claim that the totality has a unity and a status that make the religious vocabulary appropriate to it.Defined in Philosophy of Religion Beyond Monotheism · Theism · Advanced
Paraconsistent logic
A logic whose consequence relation is not explosive, so that a theory may contain a contradiction without containing every sentence. Relevance logics are paraconsistent, and so are systems reached by other routes, including da Costa's C systems, Priest's logic of paradox and the discussive logic of Jaśkowski.Defined in Relevance Logic and Paraconsistency · Logic · Advanced
Paradox of the stone
The puzzle asking whether an omnipotent being can create a stone too heavy for it to lift, on the ground that either answer seems to identify something the being cannot do.Defined in Divine Attributes and Their Tensions · Theism · Intermediate
Paraphrase
A rewriting of a claim, intended to preserve what it says while removing an apparent commitment. A paraphrase succeeds when the rewritten version says what the original said and requires less.Defined in Ontological Commitment, Informally · Ontology · Beginner
Parody argument
An argument constructed to share the form of a target argument while reaching a conclusion its proponents reject, offered as evidence that the form is defective or that its premises are not as acceptable as they seem.Defined in Modal Ontological Arguments and Their Parodies · Theism · Advanced
Parthood
The relation that holds between $x$ and $y$ when $x$ is part of $y$, written $x \leq y$. Mereology takes it in a broad sense on which every object is part of itself, so that "part" means "part, or the whole thing".Defined in Mereology and Composition · Metaphysics · Intermediate
Partial ground
A fact is a partial ground of another when it belongs to some full ground of it, alone or together with other facts. The fact that the postbox is red is a partial ground of the fact that it is red and cylindrical, since it helps to ground it but needs the fact about the shape to complete the ground.Defined in Grounding and Metaphysical Explanation · Metaphysics · Advanced
Particular
A thing that is not repeatable: it is here rather than there, and it cannot be wholly present in two places at once. This mug, this mountain, and this electron are particulars.Defined in Candidate Existents · Ontology · Beginner
Pascal's wager
The argument that because the reward attached to belief in God is infinite and the cost is finite, wagering for God maximises expected value whatever the probability of theism, provided that probability is not zero.Defined in Pragmatic Arguments for Belief · Theism · Intermediate
Paternalism
Interference with a person's choices or liberty, without their consent, justified by the claim that it will protect them from harm or make them better off.Defined in Harm, Benefit, and Consent · Applied Ethics · Beginner
Peirce arrow
The binary connective false on every row except the one where both arguments are false, written $P \downarrow Q$ and read "neither". It is the negation of disjunction and is often called NOR. Like the Sheffer stroke, it is adequate on its own.Defined in The Sixteen Binary Connectives · Logic · Intermediate
Penumbral connection
A logical relation holding among borderline cases regardless of how the vagueness is resolved. If one man has strictly less hair than another, the sentence saying that the first is bald if the second is comes out true even when both are borderline, because every admissible precisification respects the ordering.Defined in Vagueness and the Sorites · Logic · Advanced
Perception
The uptake of information about the environment through the senses. Perceptual beliefs are those formed directly on the basis of how things look, sound, feel, taste, or smell.Defined in Sources: Perception, Memory, Testimony, Reason · Epistemology · Beginner
Perceptual experience
The conscious episode a subject undergoes when they perceive, or seem to perceive, their surroundings: how things look, sound, or feel to them on an occasion.Defined in Sensation and Perception · Philosophy of Mind · Beginner
Perdurantism
The view that an object persists by having different temporal parts at different times, and so by being extended in time much as it is extended in space. The poker is a four-dimensional object, a kind of spacetime worm, and what is present on Monday is a part of it, not the whole.Defined in Persistence: Endurantism and Perdurantism · Metaphysics · Intermediate
Perfect being theology
The method of determining God's attributes a priori, by identifying God as the greatest possible being and then working out which properties such a being would have.Defined in Divine Attributes and Their Tensions · Theism · Intermediate
Perfectly natural property
A property at the top of the scale of naturalness: one that is intrinsic, whose sharing makes for exact similarity in some respect, and which, on Lewis's view, a completed physics would list among its fundamental properties. Mass and charge are the standard candidates. Lewis suggested that other properties are natural to the degree that they can be simply defined from the perfectly natural ones.Defined in Fundamentality and Structure · Metaphysics · Advanced
Permissibility
The status of an action that may be performed without doing anything wrong, whether or not it must be performed.Defined in What a Moral Theory Is · Ethics · Beginner
Permutation invariance
The criterion on which an expression is logical when its semantic value is unchanged by every permutation of the domain of a model. Suggested by Tarski in a 1966 lecture published posthumously in 1986 and developed by Gila Sher, it derives from Felix Klein's Erlangen programme, which characterised geometries by the transformations their notions are invariant under.Defined in What Makes a Constant Logical? · Logic · Advanced
Persistence
Existing at more than one time. A thing persists when it is there at an earlier time and there at a later one, and it is numerically the same thing on both occasions.Defined in Change and Identity Over Time · Metaphysics · Beginner
Personal autonomy
A person's capacity to govern themselves: to decide, on the basis of their own values and reasoning, how they will act and what shape their life will take.Defined in Harm, Benefit, and Consent · Applied Ethics · Beginner
Personal God
A God that has a mind: beliefs, intentions, and purposes, and the capacity to act for reasons and to stand in relationships with created persons.Defined in What God Is Claimed to Be · Theism · Beginner
Personal identity
In the metaphysical sense, the numerical identity of a person over time: what has to be true of a person at one time and a person at another for them to be one and the same person. It is the persistence question asked about us.Defined in Personal Identity · Metaphysics · Intermediate
Personal identity after death
The problem of specifying what would make a person existing after death the same person as one who died, rather than a duplicate, a successor, or something merely very like them.Defined in Death and the Afterlife · Theism · Intermediate
Phenomenal consciousness
The property a mental state has when there is something it is like to be in it: the experiential or felt character of the state, as distinct from anything it does.Defined in Consciousness Versus Cognition · Philosophy of Mind · Beginner
Physicalism
The view that everything is physical: that the world contains nothing over and above what a completed physics would describe, so that mental states and processes are either identical with physical ones or wholly fixed by them.Defined in The Mind-Body Problem Stated · Philosophy of Mind · Beginner
Political authority
The right to rule: the right to issue directives that are binding on those subject to them, and to enforce those directives, in a way that the directives of a private person are not.Defined in Authority and Legitimacy · Political Philosophy · Beginner
Political obligation
The moral duty of a person subject to a political authority to obey its directives, held in virtue of their relationship to it rather than in virtue of the content of any particular directive.Defined in Authority and Legitimacy · Political Philosophy · Beginner
polytheism
The view that there are several or many divine beings, none of which possesses every perfection and none of which is the sole ultimate. It is not merely a historical stage that monotheism superseded: as a philosophical position it has specific advantages, and it is the conclusion that several of the standard arguments actually support when they are read carefully.Defined in Philosophy of Religion Beyond Monotheism · Theism · Advanced
Popper function
A probability function taking conditional probability as primitive, axiomatised directly rather than defined as a ratio, and permitting conditional probabilities on conditions of probability zero to be well defined and non-trivial. Introduced by Karl Popper in 1955 and studied further by Rényi and by Alan Hájek.Defined in Probability Logic and Uncertain Premises · Logic · Advanced
Positive duty
A duty to do something for someone: an obligation to provide aid, resources, or protection, which cannot be discharged by refraining and which costs whoever bears it something.Defined in Rights, Duties, and Going Beyond Duty · Applied Ethics · Beginner
Positive liberty
Freedom understood as the presence of control: a person is free to the extent that they are the author of their own life, in command of themselves and able to act on their own purposes.Defined in Liberty, Equality, and Justice as Three Demands · Political Philosophy · Beginner
Positive rights
Rights whose corresponding duty is a duty of provision: that others supply the right-holder with something.Defined in Rights, Introduced · Political Philosophy · Beginner
Possibility
The status of being able to be the case. A claim is possible when there is no obstacle of the relevant kind to its being true, whether or not it is in fact true.Defined in Possibility and Necessity, Informally · Metaphysics · Beginner
Possibility operator
The one-place operator written $\Diamond$ and read "it is possible that" or "possibly", formed and used under the same syntactic rules as the box. In the standard systems the two operators are interdefinable, so a language containing either one and negation contains the other by abbreviation.Defined in Modal Logic: Possible Worlds Semantics · Logic · Intermediate
Possibility premise
The premise of a modal ontological argument stating that the property in question is instantiated in at least one possible world.Defined in Modal Ontological Arguments and Their Parodies · Theism · Advanced
Possible world
One of the points at which a formula is evaluated in a modal semantics. For the purposes of the logic a world is nothing but an element of a set, carrying no structure of its own; what makes it behave like a way things might have been is that each world assigns truth values to the atomic formulas, and different worlds may assign different ones. Whether worlds are anything more than this, and what they are if so, is a question of metaphysics rather than of logic.Defined in Modal Logic: Possible Worlds Semantics · Logic · Intermediate
Possible worlds analysis
The analysis of modal claims in terms of possible worlds, understood as complete ways things could have been. Something is possible if it is true at some possible world, necessary if it is true at every possible world, and contingent if it is true at some worlds and false at others.Defined in Modality and Possible Worlds · Metaphysics · Intermediate
Posterior probability
The credence assigned to a proposition after the evidence has been taken into account.Defined in Bayesian Confidence and Credence, Introduced · Epistemology · Intermediate
Power set
The set whose members are all the subsets of a given set, written $\mathcal P(A)$. It includes the empty set and the whole of $A$, since both are subsets. If $A$ has $n$ members then $\mathcal P(A)$ has $2^n$, since each member of $A$ may independently be included in a subset or left out.Defined in Basic Set Theory for Logicians · Logic · Intermediate
Practical reason
Reasoning about what to do, as opposed to reasoning about what is the case. Its conclusion is an action or an intention rather than a belief.Defined in Reasons, Oughts, and Normative Force · Ethics · Beginner
Practical stakes
What a subject stands to lose if they act on a belief and it turns out to be false. In the bank cases, the cost of a bounced cheque raises the stakes on the belief that the bank will be open.Defined in Contextualism, Invariantism, and Pragmatic Encroachment · Epistemology · Advanced
Pragmatic argument
An argument for adopting a belief that appeals to the consequences of holding it rather than to evidence that it is true.Defined in Pragmatic Arguments for Belief · Theism · Intermediate
Pragmatic encroachment
The thesis that practical factors, such as the costs of error, partly determine whether a subject knows or is justified, so that two subjects with the same evidence and the same reliability can differ in what they know because they differ in what hangs on being right.Defined in Contextualism, Invariantism, and Pragmatic Encroachment · Epistemology · Advanced
Predicate
An expression that becomes a sentence when supplied with the right number of names. A predicate taking one name expresses a property, one taking two expresses a relation between two things, and so on, with the number of names required called its arity. Predicates are written with capital letters, and the names they take are written after them, so that $Fa$ says that the object named by $a$ has the property expressed by $F$, and $Rab$ says that $a$ stands in the relation $R$ to $b$.Defined in Predicate Logic · Logic · Intermediate
Predication
The linguistic operation of applying a predicate to a subject: attaching "is chipped" to "the mug" to form a sentence that can be true or false.Defined in Objects and Properties · Metaphysics · Beginner
Preemption
A case in which one cause produces an effect and thereby stops a second, backup cause from producing it. The backup would have produced the effect had the first failed, though in the event it played no part.Defined in Theories of Causation · Metaphysics · Intermediate
Preface paradox
The paradox, due to D. C. Makinson in 1965, that an author can rationally believe each claim in their book while also rationally believing, as they say in the preface, that the book contains at least one error.Defined in Lottery, Preface, and the Threshold View of Belief · Epistemology · Advanced
Premise
A statement offered as a reason for accepting the conclusion of an argument.Defined in What an Argument Is · Logic · Beginner
Presentism
The view that only present things exist. The past and the future are not real, though there were past things and there will be future things.Defined in Theories of Time · Metaphysics · Intermediate
Presumption of atheism
The claim that inquiry into God's existence should start from the absence of belief, so that the theist bears the obligation to make a case and atheism stands if that case fails.Defined in How Arguments About God Work · Theism · Beginner
Primitive conditional probability
The treatment on which the two-place function is the basic notion and the one-place function is recovered by conditioning on a tautology. On this approach the ratio formula holds whenever the denominator is positive and is silent, rather than undefined, when it is not.Defined in Probability Logic and Uncertain Premises · Logic · Advanced
Principle of credulity
The principle that if it seems to a person that something is present, then probably it is present, in the absence of special considerations that would override the appearance.Defined in Religious Experience · Theism · Intermediate
Principle of indifference
The rule that when there is no reason to favour any one of several possibilities over the others, each should receive the same probability. It was standard in the classical period of the subject under the name principle of insufficient reason, and Keynes gave it the name now used in his treatise of 1921.Defined in Probability as an Extension of Logic · Logic · Intermediate
principle of plenitude
The principle that the fullness of being is itself a good, so that a reality containing every kind of thing that could exist is better than a sparser one. Arthur Lovejoy traced its history from the Greeks through the eighteenth century in The Great Chain of Being (Harvard University Press, 1936), where he identified it as one of the organising commitments of Western metaphysics. It functions in this debate as the premise that makes multiverse proposals attractive, since if variety and abundance are goods in themselves, a creator with unlimited power has a reason to make everything worth making.Defined in The No-Best-World Problem · Theism · Advanced
Principle of sufficient reason
The principle that there is an explanation for every fact, or for the existence of every thing, of why it is so rather than otherwise.Defined in Cosmological Arguments · Theism · Intermediate
Principle of testimony
The principle that, in the absence of special considerations, the reports people give of their experiences are probably accurate accounts of how things seemed to them.Defined in Religious Experience · Theism · Intermediate
Prior probability
The credence assigned to a proposition before the evidence in question is taken into account.Defined in Bayesian Confidence and Credence, Introduced · Epistemology · Intermediate
privacy and autonomy objection
The principal argument for anti-theism, which holds that certain goods are unavailable to any creature of an omniscient and omnipotent God. Complete privacy is impossible, since every thought is observed. Genuine independence is impossible, since one exists at every moment by another's sustaining will and one's projects unfold within another's plan. The status of being nobody's subordinate is unavailable, since one is permanently and necessarily in the position of a creature before its maker. The claim is not that these losses outweigh theism's goods but that they are genuine goods, so that even the best theistic world involves a cost.Defined in The Axiology of Theism · Theism · Advanced
Privation theory of evil
The view that evil has no positive existence of its own, and consists instead in the absence of some good that ought to be present, as blindness is the absence of sight rather than a thing in its own right.Defined in Theodicies and Defences · Theism · Intermediate
Privileged access
The thesis that a subject has a way of knowing their own mental states that no one else has and that does not rely on observation of behaviour.Defined in Introspection and Its Limits · Philosophy of Mind · Beginner
Pro tanto reason
A consideration that counts in favour of an action to some degree, and that can be outweighed by others without being cancelled. It contributes to the verdict rather than settling it.Defined in Reasons, Oughts, and Normative Force · Ethics · Beginner
pro-theism
The view that God's existence would make things better, or does make things better, than they otherwise would be. In its strong form it holds that a world with God is better in every respect that matters; in the more defensible weaker form it holds only that a world with God is better on balance, leaving room for particular respects in which it is worse.Defined in The Axiology of Theism · Theism · Advanced
Probabilism
The norm that a rational agent's credences at any time must satisfy the probability axioms. An agent whose credences violate the axioms is said to be incoherent.Defined in Formal Epistemology: Probabilism and Updating · Epistemology · Advanced
Probabilistic argument
An argument whose premises are held to raise or lower the probability of its conclusion without establishing it, so that the conclusion may remain deniable even when the premises are granted.Defined in How Arguments About God Work · Theism · Beginner
Probabilistic causation
The view that causes raise the probability of their effects. One event causes another when it makes the other more likely than it would otherwise have been, without necessarily making it certain.Defined in Theories of Causation · Metaphysics · Intermediate
Probabilistic entailment interval
The interval of values the conclusion's probability may take, given the probabilities of the premises. Computing it is a linear programming problem, since the constraints are linear in the probabilities of the state descriptions, and the interval is generally wide.Defined in Probability Logic and Uncertain Premises · Logic · Advanced
Probabilistic validity
The property an argument has when the uncertainty of its conclusion cannot exceed the sum of the uncertainties of its premises, under every probability assignment. Adams proved that for arguments in the language of conditionals interpreted by his thesis, probabilistic validity coincides with classical validity for arguments without nested conditionals, which is a substantial vindication of classical logic in a probabilistic setting.Defined in Probability Logic and Uncertain Premises · Logic · Advanced
Probability axiom
One of the basic conditions defining a probability function. In the standard formulation due to Andrey Kolmogorov, a function $P$ from propositions to real numbers is a probability function if it satisfies non-negativity, normalisation and finite additivity.Defined in Formal Epistemology: Probabilism and Updating · Epistemology · Advanced
Probability measure
A function assigning to each event in a field a real number between zero and one, subject to the constraints below. It is a function in the sense defined in the previous article, with the field as its domain and the unit interval as its codomain, and the constraints are what distinguish a probability measure from an arbitrary such function.Defined in Probability as an Extension of Logic · Logic · Intermediate
Problem of evil
The difficulty of reconciling the existence of a God who is omnipotent, omniscient, and perfectly good with the existence, quantity, and distribution of suffering in the world.Defined in The Problem of Evil · Theism · Intermediate
Problem of hell
The argument that eternal punishment cannot be reconciled with perfect goodness, since no finite life could merit unending suffering and a being who loved everyone would not permit it.Defined in Death and the Afterlife · Theism · Intermediate
Problem of the priors
The difficulty that Bayes's theorem tells you how to revise a probability but not where the initial probability comes from, so that any posterior at all can be reached by choosing a prior to suit it.Defined in Bayesian Natural Theology · Theism · Advanced
Procedural justice
Justice understood as a property of the process by which an outcome was reached, rather than of the outcome itself.Defined in What Justice Requires · Political Philosophy · Beginner
Process reliabilism
The specific view, due to Alvin Goldman, that a belief is justified when it is produced by a cognitive process that tends to produce true beliefs, and unjustified when the process producing it does not.Defined in Reliabilism and Virtue Epistemology · Epistemology · Intermediate
Projectibility
The property a predicate has when its observed instances confirm generalisations involving it, so that it is legitimate to project it from observed to unobserved cases. Green is projectible; grue is not. Goodman's challenge was to say what projectibility consists in.Defined in Confirmation Theory, Ravens, and Grue · Epistemology · Advanced
Projection theory
The view that religious belief arises by taking human properties, needs, or social facts and projecting them outward as an independent divine being.Defined in Natural Explanations of Religious Belief · Theism · Intermediate
Proof normalization
The process of removing detours from a natural deduction proof, where a detour is an introduction rule immediately followed by the corresponding elimination. Under the correspondence it is exactly beta reduction of the associated term, so simplifying a proof and running a program are the same operation.Defined in The Curry-Howard Correspondence · Logic · Advanced
Proof system
A specification of three things: the language whose formulas the system operates on, a set of axioms taken as derivable without premises, and a set of rules permitting a formula to be written down given formulas already written. The relation of syntactic consequence is defined relative to such a specification, so that a claim of the form $\Gamma \vdash \varphi$ is incomplete until one is fixed.Defined in Natural Deduction · Logic · Intermediate
Proper part
$x$ is a proper part of $y$, written $x < y$, when $x$ is part of $y$ and $x$ is not identical to $y$. The handle is a proper part of the mug; the mug is a part of itself, but not a proper part.Defined in Mereology and Composition · Metaphysics · Intermediate
properly basic belief
A belief held without being inferred from other beliefs, and rationally so. Basicality is a structural matter, concerning where a belief sits in a person's noetic structure rather than what it is about. Propriety is the normative addition: a belief is properly basic when holding it immediately is appropriate rather than reckless. Perceptual, memorial, and other-minds beliefs are the standard examples, and the point of the category is that most of what anyone knows is held this way.Defined in Reformed Epistemology and Proper Function · Theism · Advanced
Property
A way a thing is: being chipped, having a mass of two kilograms, being taller than the fence. Properties are what predicates are true of things in virtue of, and are also called attributes, qualities, or in some contexts features.Defined in Objects and Properties · Metaphysics · Beginner
Property exemplification
A property exemplification is an object's having a property at a time. On Kim's account an event is such an exemplification, written $[x, P, t]$: a constitutive object $x$, a constitutive property $P$, and a time $t$.Defined in Facts, Events, and States of Affairs · Metaphysics · Intermediate
Proposition
What a declarative sentence says: the thing that is true or false. Two sentences express the same proposition when they say the same thing, and one sentence can express different propositions on different occasions of use.Defined in Statements and Connectives · Logic · Beginner
Propositional attitude
A mental state consisting of an attitude taken toward a proposition: believing that the bus is late, hoping that the bus is late, doubting that the bus is late. The state divides into a mode and a content.Defined in What a Mental State Is · Philosophy of Mind · Beginner
Propositional knowledge
Knowing that something is the case: that Ottawa is the capital of Canada, that the bridge will hold, that the patient has an infection. It takes a complete statement as its object rather than a person, a place, or a skill.Defined in Knowledge, Belief, and Opinion · Epistemology · Beginner
Propositions as types
The reading of a formula as the type of its proofs, so that provability is inhabitation: a formula is provable exactly when some closed term has it as a type. Under the reading, conjunction is the product type, disjunction is the sum type, the false constant is the empty type, and the universal quantifier is the dependent function type.Defined in The Curry-Howard Correspondence · Logic · Advanced
Provability logic
The study of the principles governing the formalised provability predicate of a theory of arithmetic, conducted in a modal language whose box is read as "is provable in the theory". The field is distinguished from modal logic generally by the fact that its intended reading is a single fixed predicate rather than a family of informal notions, so that the question of which principles are correct has a determinate answer.Defined in Provability Logic and Löb's Theorem · Logic · Advanced
Providence
God's governing of the created order toward the ends God intends for it, including what God brings about, what God permits, and what God arranges.Defined in Creation, Conservation, and Providence · Theism · Beginner
Psychological continuity
The holding of overlapping chains of strong psychological connections between a person at one time and a person at another. The connections include memories, but also the persistence of beliefs, desires, intentions and character, each of which is carried forward and causally depends on its earlier version.Defined in Personal Identity · Metaphysics · Intermediate
Public goods
Goods whose benefits cannot practicably be withheld from those who did not pay for them, and whose enjoyment by one person does not reduce what is available to anyone else.Defined in What a State Is For · Political Philosophy · Beginner

Q

Qualia
The introspectively accessible qualitative features of experience: the particular way red looks, the particular way a burn feels, what distinguishes one experience from another in respect of how it is.Defined in Consciousness Versus Cognition · Philosophy of Mind · Beginner
Qualitative identity
Exact similarity. Two things are qualitatively identical when they share all their relevant properties, and there are still two of them.Defined in Change and Identity Over Time · Metaphysics · Beginner
Quantifier elimination
The property a theory has when every formula is equivalent, modulo the theory, to a quantifier-free formula in the same free variables. Since quantifier-free formulas are boolean combinations of atomic ones, the definable sets of such a theory are exactly the boolean combinations of the sets defined by atomic formulas.Defined in Model Theory: Types, Quantifier Elimination, Categoricity · Logic · Advanced
Quantifier scope
The portion of a formula a quantifier governs, determined by the punctuation exactly as the scope of a connective is. A quantifier binds every occurrence of its variable within its scope and none outside it, and moving a quantifier across a connective can change the claim entirely.Defined in Predicate Logic · Logic · Intermediate
Quine's circularity argument
The argument that every proposed explanation of analyticity relies on a notion, such as synonymy, definition, or necessity, that can itself be explained only by appeal to analyticity, so that the family of terms is never anchored outside itself.Defined in The Analytic/Synthetic Distinction and Quine's Attack · Epistemology · Intermediate

R

Rational intuition
A non-sensory mental state in which a proposition strikes the thinker as true on the basis of understanding it, offered by rationalists as the source of a priori justification.Defined in A Priori and A Posteriori · Epistemology · Intermediate
Raven paradox
The paradox, formulated by Carl Hempel in 1945, that on apparently innocent principles of confirmation, the observation of a non-black non-raven, such as a white shoe, confirms the hypothesis that all ravens are black.Defined in Confirmation Theory, Ravens, and Grue · Epistemology · Advanced
RCA-zero
The recursive comprehension axiom, the base theory of reverse mathematics. It asserts the existence of sets definable by a condition expressible both with a bounded existential arithmetical formula and with a bounded universal one, which by Post's theorem means the recursive sets, together with induction for existential arithmetical formulas.Defined in Reverse Mathematics · Logic · Advanced
Real definition
A definition of a thing rather than of a word: an account of what the thing is, as opposed to a nominal definition, which says what a term means. A real definition of singleton Socrates says that it is the set whose sole member is Socrates; a nominal definition of "vixen" says that the word applies to female foxes.Defined in Essence Is Not Modality · Metaphysics · Advanced
Realism about universals
The view that there are universals: entities that can be wholly present in many particulars at once, and in virtue of which those particulars are alike. On this view the postbox and the tomato are both red because the very same property, redness, is instantiated in each.Defined in Universals and Particulars · Metaphysics · Intermediate
Reason
The capacity to arrive at beliefs by thinking rather than by observing: deriving conclusions from premises, and grasping truths whose warrant does not depend on any particular experience.Defined in Sources: Perception, Memory, Testimony, Reason · Epistemology · Beginner
Recursive axiomatizability
The property a theory has when its axioms form a decidable set, so that some effective procedure can determine of any given sentence whether it is one of the axioms. The condition is what distinguishes a theory that has been specified from a set of sentences that merely exists, and it is satisfied by every axiom system in ordinary use, including those with infinitely many axioms given by an axiom schema.Defined in Gödel's Incompleteness Theorems · Logic · Advanced
Recursive definition
A definition of a set given in three parts: a base clause listing the simplest members outright, a recursion clause specifying operations that build new members from members already obtained, and a closure clause stating that nothing else belongs. The closure clause is what makes the definition a definition rather than a partial description, since without it the base and recursion clauses would be satisfied by any larger set as well.Defined in Propositional Logic and Well-Formed Formulas · Logic · Intermediate
Recursive function
A function on the natural numbers built from the constant zero, the successor function, and the functions returning one of their arguments, by three operations: composing functions already built, defining a function by recursion on one argument in terms of its value at the predecessor, and searching upward for the least number satisfying a condition already built. The functions obtainable without the search operation are the primitive recursive ones, which are all total; the search operation is what allows a definition to fail to return a value.Defined in Computability, Decidability, and Church's Theorem · Logic · Advanced
Recursively enumerable set
The property a set has when some procedure lists its members, so that everything in the set eventually appears and nothing else does. Equivalently, when some procedure halts exactly on the members and runs forever on everything else. Such a set can be confirmed but not, in general, refuted: waiting is evidence of nothing.Defined in Computability, Decidability, and Church's Theorem · Logic · Advanced
Reductio ad absurdum
The pattern of assuming a formula, deriving a contradiction from it, and concluding its negation. In a natural deduction system it is the introduction rule for negation: assume $\varphi$, derive some formula together with its negation, discharge, and write $\neg \varphi$.Defined in Natural Deduction · Logic · Intermediate
Reductionism about testimony
The view that testimonial justification is not basic but reduces to other sources. A hearer is justified in accepting what a speaker says only when they have independent reasons, ultimately from perception, memory, and inference, for taking the speaker to be reliable on the matter.Defined in Testimony and Disagreement · Epistemology · Intermediate
Reflective access
The capacity to determine, by reflection alone, whether some condition obtains. Access internalists hold that the factors that make a belief justified must be reflectively accessible to the subject.Defined in Epistemological Disjunctivism and the New Evil Demon · Epistemology · Advanced
Reflective equilibrium
The state reached by adjusting principles and judgements against one another until they agree, revising a judgement when a principle is well supported and revising the principle when a judgement is more secure. The method is the process of mutual adjustment; the equilibrium is its endpoint.Defined in Moral Intuitions and What to Do With Them · Ethics · Beginner
Reformed epistemology
The position that belief in God can be properly basic, so that a person may be rational in believing in God without holding that belief on the basis of arguments or evidence. It is called Reformed because it draws on a strand in the Reformed theological tradition that was suspicious of natural theology, and its principal development is the work of Alvin Plantinga, with Nicholas Wolterstorff and William Alston as the other main figures. It does not claim that theistic arguments fail. It claims that their success or failure is not what belief in God stands or falls with.Defined in Reformed Epistemology and Proper Function · Theism · Advanced
Regress argument
The argument that since the chain of reasons must terminate in one of a small number of ways, and each way appears to fail, justified belief is impossible.Defined in The Regress Problem · Epistemology · Beginner
Regularity
The condition that no possible proposition receives probability zero. It secures that the ratio formula is always applicable and is unattainable in any space with uncountably many mutually exclusive possibilities, since only countably many can have positive probability.Defined in Probability Logic and Uncertain Premises · Logic · Advanced
Regularity theory
The view that one event causes another when events of the first kind are always followed by events of the second kind, with nothing more to causation than that pattern.Defined in Theories of Causation · Metaphysics · Intermediate
Reincarnation
The view that a person, or a continuing series causally derived from them, is reborn into another life after death, with the conditions of each life bearing on the next.Defined in Death and the Afterlife · Theism · Intermediate
Relation
A set of ordered pairs. The pair $\langle a, b \rangle$ differs from $\langle b, a \rangle$ unless its two members are the same, which is what distinguishes a pair from a two-membered set. A relation holds between $a$ and $b$ exactly when the pair whose first member is $a$ and whose second is $b$ belongs to it, and the same construction with longer sequences gives relations of any number of places.Defined in Basic Set Theory for Logicians · Logic · Intermediate
Relevance logic
A family of systems requiring that the premises of a valid argument bear on its conclusion, developed principally by Alan Ross Anderson and Nuel Belnap from the 1950s and formalised in the systems E, R and their relatives. Relevance logics are substructural, obtained by dropping weakening, which is the rule licensing the introduction of premises that play no part.Defined in Relevance Logic and Paraconsistency · Logic · Advanced
Relevant alternatives
The view that knowing a proposition requires ruling out only those incompatible possibilities that are relevant in the context, rather than every possibility whatever.Defined in Epistemic Closure and Its Denial · Epistemology · Intermediate
Reliabilism
The family of externalist views on which the justification or warrant of a belief is a matter of its connection to truth, rather than of the believer's evidence or reasons.Defined in Reliabilism and Virtue Epistemology · Epistemology · Intermediate
reliability of cognitive faculties
The property a set of belief-forming faculties has when they produce a high proportion of true beliefs across the range of conditions in which they are used. Reliability in this sense is a matter of frequency rather than of infallibility, and it is domain-relative: a faculty can be reliable about the location of nearby solid objects and unreliable about the origins of the universe, and nothing in the concept requires that a creature's faculties be uniformly good or uniformly bad.Defined in The Evolutionary Argument Against Naturalism · Theism · Advanced
religious disagreement
The problem raised by the fact that religious beliefs are rejected by large numbers of people who appear to be as intelligent, as informed, as careful, and as sincere as those who hold them. The question is what, if anything, awareness of such disagreement does to the rationality of continuing to believe. It is a special case of a general problem in epistemology about disagreement among epistemic peers, and it is not confined to religion, though religion is where the disagreement is most persistent and least resolvable by shared method.Defined in Religious Pluralism and Exclusivism · Theism · Advanced
religious exclusivism
The view that the central claims of one tradition are true and that claims of other traditions incompatible with them are false. In its strict soteriological form it adds that the goods the tradition promises are available only through it. The two components are separable: one can hold that a tradition is uniquely correct about the facts while holding that its benefits are not restricted to its own adherents.Defined in Religious Pluralism and Exclusivism · Theism · Advanced
Religious experience
An experience that seems to the person having it to be of some objective reality, and that has religious significance either in its content or in the interpretation the person places on it.Defined in Religious Experience · Theism · Intermediate
religious inclusivism
The view that one tradition is uniquely correct or complete, but that the goods it identifies are available to people outside it, who may attain them through their own traditions without recognising the source. Karl Rahner's much-discussed notion of anonymous Christianity is the best-known version, and the Second Vatican Council's declaration Nostra Aetate of 1965 took the Catholic Church some distance in this direction while retaining the claim to uniqueness.Defined in Religious Pluralism and Exclusivism · Theism · Advanced
religious pluralism
The view that no tradition is uniquely correct, and that the major traditions are all authentic and roughly equally effective responses to the same ultimate reality, their apparent conflicts arising from differences in the human conceptual and cultural equipment through which that reality is encountered. The position denies exclusivism's uniqueness claim rather than affirming that all religious claims are true, which would be inconsistent on its face.Defined in Religious Pluralism and Exclusivism · Theism · Advanced
Resemblance
The relation of being alike in some respect. On resemblance-based accounts of properties, facts about which things resemble which are taken as basic, rather than being explained by an entity that the resembling things have in common.Defined in Universals and Instances · Ontology · Beginner
Resemblance class
A class of particulars all of which resemble one another in the relevant respect, and which the resemblance nominalist takes to be what the property in question amounts to. The property of being red is the class of things that resemble the paradigm red things closely enough.Defined in Universals and Particulars · Metaphysics · Intermediate
Revealed theology
Theology that proceeds from what is taken to have been divinely revealed, such as scripture, tradition, or direct communication, rather than from what unaided human faculties can establish.Defined in Faith and Reason · Theism · Beginner
Reverse mathematics
The programme of determining, for each theorem of ordinary mathematics, the weakest set-existence axioms sufficient to prove it, by establishing an equivalence between the theorem and those axioms over a fixed weak base theory. Initiated by Harvey Friedman in the 1970s and developed principally by Stephen Simpson and his collaborators.Defined in Reverse Mathematics · Logic · Advanced
Reverse ontological argument
An argument of exactly the same form as the modal ontological argument, starting from the premise that maximal greatness is possibly not instantiated, and concluding that it is necessarily not instantiated.Defined in Modal Ontological Arguments and Their Parodies · Theism · Advanced
Right action
An action that is morally in order: not wrong to perform. The term covers both what is required and what is merely allowed.Defined in What a Moral Theory Is · Ethics · Beginner
Rigid dependence
Dependence of one thing on a particular other thing, which could not be swapped for another of the same kind. In modal form: necessarily, if x exists then y, that very thing, exists. A singleton depends rigidly on its member, and a smile on the face that wears it.Defined in Ontological Dependence · Metaphysics · Advanced
Rowe's evidential argument
The argument that there exist instances of intense suffering that an omnipotent and omniscient being could have prevented without losing some greater good or permitting some equally bad or worse evil; that such a being would prevent any suffering it could prevent without such a loss; and therefore that no such being exists. Its distinctive feature is that the first premise is offered as a reasonable inference from the evidence rather than as something known, which makes the conclusion probable rather than demonstrated.Defined in The Probabilistic Problem of Evil · Theism · Advanced
Rule of law
The ideal that public power be exercised through general, known, and stable rules applied by independent institutions, so that officials as well as citizens are bound by law and no one is subject to arbitrary command.Defined in Law and the Rule of Law · Political Philosophy · Beginner
Russell's theory of descriptions
The account, given in "On Denoting" of 1905, on which a sentence containing a definite description is not about any object named by the description but is instead a general claim with three parts: that something answers to the description, that at most one thing does, and that it has whatever the sentence goes on to attribute. On this account "the" is not a device of reference at all, and the description does not survive as a unit in the analysis.Defined in Identity and Definite Descriptions · Logic · Intermediate

S

Safety condition
The requirement that the believer could not easily have believed falsely. A belief is safe when in all or nearly all close worlds in which the believer forms that belief in the same way, the belief is true.Defined in Safety and Sensitivity Conditions · Epistemology · Intermediate
satisficing creation
The view that a perfectly good creator is required only to create a world that is good enough, rather than the best world available, so that any world above some threshold of value is a permissible choice. The position is what allows a theist to accept that there is no best possible world without concluding that God's goodness has been compromised, since a standard that can actually be met has replaced one that cannot.Defined in The No-Best-World Problem · Theism · Advanced
Saturation
The property a model has when it realises every type over every parameter set of size less than the model's own cardinality. A saturated model realises as many types as its size permits, and is correspondingly homogeneous: any two tuples satisfying the same formulas can be mapped to one another by an automorphism.Defined in Model Theory: Types, Quantifier Elimination, Categoricity · Logic · Advanced
Scope
The portion of a formula that a given connective applies to. Brackets fix scope, and a formula whose brackets are missing may have no determinate meaning at all.Defined in Translating English into Symbols · Logic · Beginner
Scoring rule
A function that measures the inaccuracy of a credence, or a whole credence function, at a given possible world. The most widely used is the Brier score, which sums the squared differences between each credence and the corresponding truth value.Defined in Accuracy-First Epistemology · Epistemology · Advanced
Second incompleteness theorem
No consistent, recursively axiomatizable theory that represents enough arithmetic proves the sentence expressing its own consistency. A theory strong enough to be worth worrying about is therefore not strong enough to settle the worry, and any proof of its consistency must use resources it does not itself contain.Defined in Gödel's Incompleteness Theorems · Logic · Advanced
Second-order logic
The extension of first-order logic with variables for relations and functions on the domain, and quantifiers binding them. A sentence may say that every property with a given closure condition holds universally, or that some relation with a stated feature exists, without the property or relation being named by a formula.Defined in Second-Order and Higher-Order Logic · Logic · Advanced
Second-order property
A property of a property or concept, rather than of an individual: being widely instantiated, being had by exactly nine things, being had by nothing at all.Defined in Is Existence a Property? · Ontology · Beginner
secondary causation
Causation exercised by creatures, so called because it operates under and through the primary causation exercised by God. To affirm secondary causation is to say that when a fire heats water, the fire genuinely does the heating, and not merely that God heats the water on the occasion of the fire being nearby. The term marks a position on which creatures have real causal powers of their own rather than being placeholders in a description of divine activity.Defined in Existential Inertia and Divine Conservation · Theism · Advanced
self-defeat
The condition of a position that, if accepted, supplies a reason to reject it. A self-defeating position is not thereby shown to be false, and this is what distinguishes self-defeat from self-contradiction: the position may be true, but it cannot be rationally believed by someone who sees what it implies. The verification principle of rung 9 failed in this way, and so, on this argument, does naturalism.Defined in The Evolutionary Argument Against Naturalism · Theism · Advanced
Semantic closure
The condition a language meets when it contains names for its own expressions, a predicate applying to those names to say that the sentence named is true, and the resources to assert every instance of the T-schema for its own sentences. Tarski's diagnosis of the liar is that semantic closure, together with ordinary logic, is inconsistent.Defined in Undefinability and the Theories of Truth · Logic · Advanced
Semantic consequence
The relation that holds between a set of formulas and a formula when every interpretation that makes all members of the set true also makes the formula true. It is written $\Gamma \vDash \varphi$, with the double turnstile, where $\Gamma$ is the set of premises. Equivalently, there is no interpretation making every premise true and the conclusion false, which is the beginner tier's account of validity stated exactly.Defined in Semantic and Syntactic Consequence · Logic · Intermediate
Semantic tableau
A tree of formulas built by decomposing a set of formulas into their components according to fixed rules, undertaken to determine whether the set has a model. The root holds the formulas being tested, each rule replaces a formula with the simpler formulas its truth would require, and branching records the alternatives that a formula leaves open. The method is also called the tree method or the method of analytic tableaux.Defined in Semantic Tableaux · Logic · Intermediate
sempiternity
Existence throughout all of time, without beginning or end, as opposed to existence outside time altogether. A sempiternal God has a past and a future, undergoes succession, and knows what time it is now. The position is also called everlastingness or temporal eternity, and it is compatible with God's never having come into being and never ceasing to be.Defined in Simplicity, Timelessness, and Impassibility · Theism · Advanced
Sensation
The raw registering of a stimulus, considered apart from any recognition or classification of what it is: a patch of colour, a pressure, a sound, before it is taken as anything in particular.Defined in Sensation and Perception · Philosophy of Mind · Beginner
Sense datum
An immediate object of perceptual awareness, understood as actually having the qualities the experience presents: a coloured, shaped item of which the perceiver is directly aware and which is distinct from the physical object.Defined in Sensation and Perception · Philosophy of Mind · Beginner
Sensitivity condition
The requirement that had the proposition been false, the believer would not have believed it. A belief meets the condition when it varies with the truth of what is believed.Defined in Safety and Sensitivity Conditions · Epistemology · Intermediate
sensus divinitatis
A supposed human cognitive faculty that produces belief in God directly, in response to circumstances rather than arguments: seeing the night sky, being confronted with the beauty or the scale of the natural world, feeling guilt, coming through danger. On this account belief in God is not the conclusion of an inference from those circumstances; the circumstances are the occasion on which the faculty operates, standing to theistic belief roughly as being appeared to in a certain way stands to perceptual belief.Defined in Reformed Epistemology and Proper Function · Theism · Advanced
Sentience
The capacity for felt experience, and in particular for experiences that feel bad or good to the being having them, such as pain, distress, and pleasure.Defined in Moral Status · Applied Ethics · Beginner
Sequent
