An expression with two lists of formulas separated by an arrow, read as saying that if everything on the left holds then at least one thing on the right holds. The left list is the antecedent and the right list the succedent, and either may be empty. A sequent with an empty succedent says that the antecedent is contradictory; a sequent with an empty antecedent asserts the disjunction of the succedent outright.Defined in Sequent Calculus and Cut Elimination · Logic · Advanced
Set
A collection considered as a single object, determined entirely by which things belong to it. That an object $a$ belongs to a set $A$ is written $a \in A$. Two sets with the same members are the same set, so a set has no order and no repetition: nothing is a member twice, and there is no first member. The set with no members at all is the empty set, and there is only one of it.Defined in Basic Set Theory for Logicians · Logic · Intermediate
Sheffer stroke
The binary connective true on every row except the one where both arguments are true, written $P \mid Q$ and read "not both". It is the negation of conjunction and is often called NAND. It is one of only two binary connectives that form an adequate set on their own.Defined in The Sixteen Binary Connectives · Logic · Intermediate
Simplicity as a prior
The proposal that a hypothesis's probability before any evidence is fixed by how simple the hypothesis is, so that simpler hypotheses start out likelier.Defined in Bayesian Natural Theology · Theism · Advanced
Simply typed lambda calculus
A formal language of terms built from variables, abstraction and application, in which every term carries a type. Types are generated from base types by the arrow constructor, an abstraction $\lambda x^{A}.\, t$ has type $A \rightarrow B$ when $t$ has type $B$ under the assumption that $x$ has type $A$, and an application $t\,u$ has type $B$ when $t$ has type $A \rightarrow B$ and $u$ has type $A$.Defined in The Curry-Howard Correspondence · Logic · Advanced
skeptical spillover
The general worry that the scepticism skeptical theism requires cannot be confined to the case it was introduced for. The theses are about our grasp of value and of the relations between goods and permitted evils, and those matters are not sealed off from the rest of the theist's commitments, so a scepticism strong enough to block the inference from apparent pointlessness is likely to block other inferences the theist wants to keep.Defined in Skeptical Theism and Its Costs · Theism · Advanced
Skeptical theism
The response holding that our failure to identify a justifying reason for some evil is weak evidence that there is none, because our grasp of the available goods, evils, and connections between them is not a representative sample of what an omniscient being would grasp.Defined in Theodicies and Defences · Theism · Intermediate
Skepticism
The position that knowledge of some domain is not available. Global versions deny that anything at all is known; local versions target a particular area, such as the external world, other minds, or the past.Defined in Skepticism, First Encounter · Epistemology · Beginner
Skolem's paradox
The apparent contradiction that arises when the downward theorem is applied to set theory itself. The axioms of Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory are countably many first-order sentences, so if they are consistent they have a countable model. But among their consequences is Cantor's theorem, so that model contains a set it takes to be uncountable, and the model as a whole has only countably many elements.Defined in Compactness and Löwenheim-Skolem · Logic · Advanced
Social epistemology
The study of the social dimensions of knowledge: how knowledge is produced, transmitted, and distributed through relations between people and institutions, and how those relations can support or distort it.Defined in Epistemic Injustice · Epistemology · Intermediate
Sorites paradox
An argument from an evidently true base case and an evidently true tolerance premise, by a long chain of apparently valid steps, to an evidently false conclusion. Attributed to Eubulides of Miletus in the fourth century BC, its name comes from the Greek for heap, the original version concerning how many grains make one.Defined in Vagueness and the Sorites · Logic · Advanced
Sortal
A term or concept that supplies a way of dividing and counting: chair, cat, coin, symphony. A sortal answers what a thing is, and carries with it a way of telling one of them from another.Defined in Identity and Individuation · Ontology · Beginner
Sortal essentialism
The thesis that each thing belongs essentially to its basic kind, the substance sortal that says what it is: a thing could not have existed without falling under that sortal, and so could not have been a thing of a fundamentally different kind.Defined in Essentialism and the Argument from Origins · Metaphysics · Intermediate
Soul-making theodicy
The view that God's purpose is not to maximise happiness but to develop moral and spiritual character, and that a world containing genuine risk, difficulty, and suffering is required for that development.Defined in Theodicies and Defences · Theism · Intermediate
Soundness
An argument is sound when it is valid and all of its premises are in fact true. An argument that is not sound is unsound.Defined in Validity and Soundness · Logic · Beginner
Soundness theorem
The claim that everything derivable is a semantic consequence: whenever a conclusion can be derived from a set of premises, every interpretation making those premises true makes the conclusion true. A proof system with this property never licenses an invalid argument, so a derivation is a guarantee and not merely an indication.Defined in Soundness and Completeness, Informally · Logic · Intermediate
Sovereignty
Supreme authority within a territory: authority not derived from and not answerable to any higher authority of the same kind.Defined in What a State Is For · Political Philosophy · Beginner
Spatiotemporal continuity
The condition of tracing a single unbroken path through space and time, with no gaps and no jumps: at every moment between two times the thing is somewhere, and it gets from each position to the next by passing through the positions in between.Defined in The Ship of Theseus · Metaphysics · Beginner
Spatiotemporal location
Having a position in space and time: being somewhere, at some time, with a determinate distance from other located things.Defined in Abstract and Concrete · Metaphysics · Beginner
Special composition question
The question of what conditions some things must meet for there to be an object that they compose. Peter van Inwagen gave it its name and made it the centre of Material Beings (1990).Defined in Mereology and Composition · Metaphysics · Intermediate
Stalnaker-Lewis semantics
The treatment of the counterfactual on which it is true when the consequent holds at the antecedent worlds most similar to the actual world. Stalnaker's version, from 1968, assumes a unique closest antecedent world; Lewis's, from 1973, quantifies over a sphere of sufficiently close ones and does not assume uniqueness.Defined in Conditionals and the Triviality Results · Logic · Advanced
Standard semantics
The interpretation on which a second-order relation variable ranges over the full power set of the relevant product of the domain, so that every set of elements, definable or not, is in range. Under it, the second-order quantifier means what it appears to mean.Defined in Second-Order and Higher-Order Logic · Logic · Advanced
State
A political association that claims supreme authority over a defined territory and the people in it, exercised through permanent institutions that persist independently of whoever currently occupies them.Defined in What a State Is For · Political Philosophy · Beginner
State of affairs
A state of affairs is a particular thing's having a property, or several things standing in a relation: Brutus's being a conspirator, Caesar's being older than Brutus. Many writers, following Alvin Plantinga's The Nature of Necessity (1974), allow that a state of affairs may fail to obtain, and reserve "fact" for one that does obtain.Defined in Facts, Events, and States of Affairs · Metaphysics · Intermediate
Statistical independence
The relation two events bear when the probability of both occurring is the product of their separate probabilities. It is a definition rather than an intuitive notion made precise, and it is relative to the measure: two events independent under one probability measure may fail to be under another, with no change in the events themselves.Defined in Probability as an Extension of Logic · Logic · Intermediate
Steadfast view
The view that, at least in some cases, one may rationally maintain one's belief in the face of peer disagreement, because the first-order evidence continues to support it and the fact of disagreement does not cancel that support.Defined in Testimony and Disagreement · Epistemology · Intermediate
Strengthened liar
The sentence saying of itself that it is not true, considered in a setting that has assigned it no truth value. The setting's own verdict, that the sentence is not true, is precisely what the sentence says, so the theory appears committed to the sentence's truth at the same time as it denies the sentence a value.Defined in Undefinability and the Theories of Truth · Logic · Advanced
Strong atheism
The condition of a person who believes that God does not exist. Also called positive atheism.Defined in Theism, Atheism, and Agnosticism · Theism · Beginner
Strong supervenience
A family $A$ strongly supervenes on a base $B$ if and only if, for any possible worlds and any things in them, if two things are alike in their $B$-properties then they are alike in their $A$-properties, whether the two things are in the same world or in different ones.Defined in Supervenience · Metaphysics · Intermediate
Structural part
A part of an object that is not one of its material components but its form: the structure, fixed by the object's kind, that its material parts must satisfy for the object to exist. On Kathrin Koslicki's view every composite material object has such a formal component as a proper part, alongside its material parts.Defined in Neo-Aristotelian Hylomorphism · Metaphysics · Advanced
Structural rule
A rule that alters the arrangement of a sequent without mentioning any connective. There are three: weakening, which adds a formula to either side; contraction, which replaces two occurrences of the same formula on one side by one; and exchange, which reorders the formulas on a side. They say, respectively, that unused premises are harmless, that repetition carries no information, and that order carries none either.Defined in Sequent Calculus and Cut Elimination · Logic · Advanced
Structure
Sider's generalisation of naturalness: the objective joint-carving of reality, attributed to notions of any grammatical category, including quantifiers, connectives and operators as well as predicates. A notion carves at the joints when it belongs to the privileged description of the world. Sider takes structure as primitive, and understands fundamentality in its terms rather than in terms of grounding.Defined in Fundamentality and Structure · Metaphysics · Advanced
Subformula property
The feature a proof has when every formula occurring anywhere in it is a subformula of some formula in the sequent being proved. Cut-free proofs in the sequent calculus have it, since every rule other than cut carries its side formulas downward unchanged and introduces only a formula built from what its premises contain.Defined in Sequent Calculus and Cut Elimination · Logic · Advanced
Subject-sensitive invariantism
The view that "knows" is invariant in meaning, but that whether a subject knows depends partly on non-epistemic features of the subject's situation, principally their practical stakes. Also called interest-relative invariantism.Defined in Contextualism, Invariantism, and Pragmatic Encroachment · Epistemology · Advanced
Subjunctive conditional
A conditional whose antecedent is entertained counterfactually, typically marked in English by the subjunctive or by a past-tense construction. "If Oswald had not shot Kennedy, someone else would have" is subjunctive, and it is false unless one holds an unusual view about the assassination.Defined in Conditionals and the Triviality Results · Logic · Advanced
Substance
A particular thing that has properties without being a property of anything, that is a subject of change, and that is in some way more basic than the properties it bears. Aristotle's primary substances in the Categories are the paradigm: this man, this horse, which are neither said of a subject nor present in one.Defined in Substance and Bundle Theories · Metaphysics · Intermediate
Substantive equality
Equality in the actual condition or outcome of people's lives, as against equality only in the rules applied to them.Defined in What Justice Requires · Political Philosophy · Beginner
Substratum
That which underlies the properties of a thing and in which they inhere or to which they belong, conceived as distinct from the properties themselves. The word comes from the Latin for what is spread beneath.Defined in Substance and Bundle Theories · Metaphysics · Intermediate
Substructural logic
A logic obtained by restricting or removing one or more of the structural rules of the sequent calculus. Since the structural rules govern the treatment of premises as a collection rather than the behaviour of any connective, their removal changes what a premise is taken to be.Defined in Substructural Logics · Logic · Advanced
Subsystem of second-order arithmetic
An axiomatic theory in the two-sorted language of second-order arithmetic obtained by restricting the comprehension schema, and correspondingly the induction schema, to a limited class of formulas. Five such subsystems account for the overwhelming majority of the equivalences found.Defined in Reverse Mathematics · Logic · Advanced
Subvenient base
The family of properties on which another family supervenes. In the example, the physical and chemical properties of the paintings form the subvenient base, and beauty is the supervening family.Defined in Supervenience · Metaphysics · Intermediate
Successive addition
The formation of a collection by adding one member at a time, so that at every stage of the process the collection has finitely many members.Defined in Grim Reaper Paradoxes and Causal Finitism · Theism · Advanced
Sufficient condition
A condition whose presence is enough for something to occur. Being decapitated is a sufficient condition for death.Defined in Causation, First Pass · Metaphysics · Beginner
Supererogation
The class of actions that are morally good and praiseworthy but not obligatory, so that performing them is admirable while failing to perform them is not a fault.Defined in Rights, Duties, and Going Beyond Duty · Applied Ethics · Beginner
supernaturalism
The view that there exists at least one thing that is not part of the natural order and that acts on it: minimally, a mind or agent whose existence does not depend on physical arrangement and whose activity is not the operation of a natural law. Theism is one form of it, but not the only one, and the two terms are not interchangeable: a supernaturalism with many limited spirits and no creator would still be supernaturalism.Defined in Naturalism and Supernaturalism as Frameworks · Theism · Advanced
Supertask
The completion of infinitely many tasks within a finite stretch of time.Defined in Grim Reaper Paradoxes and Causal Finitism · Theism · Advanced
Supervaluationism
The theory on which a vague sentence is true when it comes out true on every admissible way of making the language precise, false when it comes out false on every such precisification, and neither when precisifications disagree. Developed by Kit Fine in 1975, following van Fraassen's treatment of presupposition failure.Defined in Vagueness and the Sorites · Logic · Advanced
Supervenience
One family of properties, the supervening family, supervenes on another if and only if there can be no difference in the first without a difference in the second. Equivalently: whatever is alike in the second family is alike in the first.Defined in Supervenience · Metaphysics · Intermediate
Swamping problem
The objection, pressed by Linda Zagzebski, Jonathan Kvanvig and others, that if the value of a reliable process lies wholly in the true beliefs it produces, then a true belief produced by a reliable process has no more value than the same true belief produced by an unreliable one. The value of the truth swamps the value of the reliability.Defined in Epistemic Value and the Swamping Problem · Epistemology · Advanced
Syntactic consequence
The relation that holds between a set of formulas and a formula when there is a finite sequence of formulas ending with that formula, each member of which is either a premise from the set, an axiom of the system, or the result of applying one of the system's rules to earlier members. It is written $\Gamma \vdash \varphi$, with the single turnstile. The relation is always relative to a specified proof system, so that strictly the turnstile should carry a subscript naming it, and does whenever more than one system is in play.Defined in Semantic and Syntactic Consequence · Logic · Intermediate
Synthetic truth
A proposition whose truth depends on how the world is and not on meanings alone, so that understanding it leaves open whether it is true.Defined in The Analytic/Synthetic Distinction and Quine's Attack · Epistemology · Intermediate
System B
T together with the schema $\varphi \rightarrow \Box \Diamond \varphi$, which corresponds to symmetry: whenever one world is accessible from another, the second is accessible from the first. The schema says that whatever is the case is necessarily possible, and the letter is inherited from a traditional association with Brouwer rather than from any doctrine of his about modality.Defined in The Normal Systems K, D, T, B, S4, S5 · Logic · Intermediate
System D
K together with the schema $\Box \varphi \rightarrow \Diamond \varphi$, which corresponds to seriality: every world has at least one world accessible from it, so there are no dead ends. Equivalently, D rules out the worlds at which every formula whatever is necessary.Defined in The Normal Systems K, D, T, B, S4, S5 · Logic · Intermediate
System GL
The normal modal logic obtained by adding to $\mathsf{K}$ the single axiom schema $\Box(\Box A \rightarrow A) \rightarrow \Box A$, known as the Löb axiom. Named for Gödel and Löb, it is also found in the literature as $\mathsf{G}$, $\mathsf{L}$, $\mathsf{KW}$ and $\mathsf{PrL}$.Defined in Provability Logic and Löb's Theorem · Logic · Advanced
System K
The smallest normal modal logic: propositional logic together with the distribution schema and the rule of necessitation, and nothing further. It is sound and complete for the class of all frames, so a formula is a theorem of K exactly when it is valid on every frame whatever, with no condition placed on the accessibility relation.Defined in The Normal Systems K, D, T, B, S4, S5 · Logic · Intermediate
System S4
T together with the schema $\Box \varphi \rightarrow \Box \Box \varphi$, which corresponds to transitivity: whenever one world sees a second and the second sees a third, the first sees the third. The name is inherited from the fourth of the five systems Lewis and Langford numbered in 1932, which is also why the schema is usually called 4.Defined in The Normal Systems K, D, T, B, S4, S5 · Logic · Intermediate
System S5
T together with the schema $\Diamond \varphi \rightarrow \Box \Diamond \varphi$, which corresponds to the euclidean condition: whenever a world sees two worlds, each of those sees the other. Combined with reflexivity this makes the accessibility relation an equivalence relation, so S5 contains both B and S4, and it is the strongest of the six.Defined in The Normal Systems K, D, T, B, S4, S5 · Logic · Intermediate
System T
K together with the schema $\Box \varphi \rightarrow \varphi$, which corresponds to reflexivity: every world is accessible from itself. T contains D, since a reflexive relation is automatically serial, and it is the weakest system in which necessity implies truth.Defined in The Normal Systems K, D, T, B, S4, S5 · Logic · Intermediate

T

T-schema
The schema whose instances take the form: the sentence "p" is true if and only if p, with one instance for each sentence of the language under description. Tarski treated the schema as a condition of adequacy rather than as a definition: any account of truth for a language must entail every instance, and an account that does is materially adequate whatever else it says.Defined in Undefinability and the Theories of Truth · Logic · Advanced
Tautology
A formula whose truth table column is true in every row. A tautology cannot be false, whatever the letters in it stand for.Defined in Truth Tables · Logic · Beginner
Teleological argument
Any argument from the apparent directedness of things toward ends, or from order suited to an outcome, to an intelligence responsible for it.Defined in Design and Fine-Tuning Arguments · Theism · Intermediate
Temporal becoming
The supposed feature of time on which it passes: the present moves, or new reality comes into being, or events change from future to present to past. A-theorists take becoming to be real, and B-theorists deny that it is.Defined in Theories of Time · Metaphysics · Intermediate
Temporal logic
The modal treatment of tense, with operators for what will always be the case, what was always the case, and their duals. Developed by Arthur Prior from 1957, its accessibility relation is the earlier-than ordering on times.Defined in Temporal, Deontic, and Epistemic Logic · Logic · Advanced
Temporal part
A temporal part of an object, relative to a stretch of time, is a part of that object that exists during exactly that stretch, and that overlaps everything which is a part of the object during it. An instantaneous temporal part is the case where the stretch is a single moment.Defined in Persistence: Endurantism and Perdurantism · Metaphysics · Intermediate
Tennenbaum's theorem
The result that no countable nonstandard model of Peano arithmetic is recursive. There is no nonstandard model whose domain is the natural numbers and whose addition and multiplication are both computable functions, and indeed addition alone cannot be computable.Defined in Nonstandard Models of Arithmetic · Logic · Advanced
Testimonial injustice
The wrong done to a speaker when a hearer gives them a credibility deficit because of prejudice against a social group to which the speaker belongs. Fricker's central case is identity-prejudicial credibility deficit, where the prejudice is systematic and tracks the speaker through many areas of life.Defined in Epistemic Injustice · Epistemology · Intermediate
Testimony
The reports of others, taken as a source of belief. Almost everything anyone knows about history, science, geography, and other people's lives rests on it.Defined in Sources: Perception, Memory, Testimony, Reason · Epistemology · Beginner
The argument from illusion
The argument that since illusory experiences present objects as having qualities they do not have, the immediate object of awareness in illusion is not the ordinary object; and since illusory and veridical experiences are of the same kind, the immediate object of awareness is never the ordinary object.Defined in Sensation and Perception · Philosophy of Mind · Beginner
The consequence argument
The argument that if determinism is true, then our acts are the consequences of the remote past and the laws of nature, and since neither of those is up to us, neither are their consequences. Hence we have no choice about what we do.Defined in Free Will and Determinism · Metaphysics · Intermediate
the deceptive appearances objection
The objection that if God may have reasons beyond our grasp for permitting terrible suffering, God may equally have reasons beyond our grasp for permitting us to be systematically deceived. Ordinary confidence that our senses and testimony are not being interfered with rests on the judgement that a good being would not allow large-scale deception without sufficient reason, and skeptical theism removes the basis for that judgement. The result is a general scepticism about appearances, arrived at from inside theism.Defined in Skeptical Theism and Its Costs · Theism · Advanced
The frames of GL
A modal formula is valid on a frame when it holds at every world under every assignment. The Löb axiom is valid on exactly the frames that are transitive and contain no infinite ascending chain of accessible worlds, a condition equivalent, for finite frames, to being transitive and irreflexive.Defined in Provability Logic and Löb's Theorem · Logic · Advanced
The identity of indiscernibles
The principle that if x and y share all their properties, then x and y are identical. Equivalently, there are no two things exactly alike in every respect. Associated with Leibniz, who defended it in the Discourse on Metaphysics (1686).Defined in Substance and Bundle Theories · Metaphysics · Intermediate
The numinous
The distinctive object of religious dread and attraction, described by Rudolf Otto as an overwhelming and wholly other mystery that at once terrifies and compels, and treated by him as a category that cannot be reduced to moral or rational terms.Defined in Religious Experience · Theism · Intermediate
The one over many
The argument that when several distinct things are the same in some respect, there must be a single thing they share, since otherwise their sameness has nothing to consist in.Defined in Universals and Instances · Ontology · Beginner
The principle of alternate possibilities
The principle that a person is morally responsible for what they have done only if they could have done otherwise.Defined in Free Will and Determinism · Metaphysics · Intermediate
The problem of temporary intrinsics
The difficulty for any account of persistence on which a thing is wholly present at each time. Things change in their intrinsic properties, such as shape, and an intrinsic property is one a thing has in virtue of how it is in itself. Yet the poker has the property of being straight and the property of being bent, which are incompatible, and the same wholly present thing seems to have both.Defined in Persistence: Endurantism and Perdurantism · Metaphysics · Intermediate
The ship of Theseus
The puzzle of whether an object that has had every one of its parts replaced, one at a time, is still the object it was.Defined in The Ship of Theseus · Metaphysics · Beginner
Theism
The proposition that God exists, where God is understood as in classical theism: one personal being, responsible for everything else, possessing maximal power, maximal knowledge, and perfect goodness.Defined in Theism, Atheism, and Agnosticism · Theism · Beginner
theistic activism
The more specific account of how that dependence works, on which abstract objects are the products of God's intellective activity. Numbers and propositions exist because God thinks them, and they exist necessarily and eternally because God thinks them necessarily and eternally. The position was developed by Thomas Morris and Christopher Menzel in "Absolute Creation", published in the American Philosophical Quarterly in 1986.Defined in Aseity and the Bootstrapping Problem · Theism · Advanced
theistic multiverse
The proposal that God creates every universe worth creating rather than selecting one, so that the totality of what God makes has no better alternative even though no single universe within it is best. Versions have been developed by Donald Turner, Klaas Kraay, and Timothy O'Connor. Kraay's formulation, in "Theism, Possible Worlds, and the Multiverse" in Philosophical Studies in 2010, holds that God actualises the unique possible world that contains all and only the universes worth creating, which restores a best choice at the level of worlds while denying one at the level of universes.Defined in The No-Best-World Problem · Theism · Advanced
theistic personalism
The family of views on which God is understood as a person, or as personlike, in a sense continuous with our ordinary concept of a person: a bodiless being with beliefs, intentions, and free choices, distinguished from us by having those attributes without limit rather than by belonging to a different order of reality. Brian Davies introduced the label in An Introduction to the Philosophy of Religion to name what he took to be the operating assumption of much analytic philosophy of religion, in contrast with the classical theism of Augustine, Maimonides, Avicenna, and Aquinas.Defined in Classical Theism Against Theistic Personalism · Theism · Advanced
Theodicy
A response to the problem of evil that identifies the reasons God actually has for permitting evil, and argues that those reasons are morally sufficient.Defined in Theodicies and Defences · Theism · Intermediate
theological fatalism
The thesis that divine foreknowledge of a future act is incompatible with that act being free, so that if God knows in advance everything anyone will do, nobody does anything freely. It is not the claim that God's knowledge causes the act. The claim is that a fixed past truth about the act removes the ability to do otherwise, which is what the relevant notion of freedom requires.Defined in Divine Foreknowledge and Freedom · Theism · Advanced
Theory of embodiment
Kit Fine's account of how ordinary things are made up, which supplements the mereological sum with two further modes of composition. A rigid embodiment $a, b, c, \ldots/R$ exists just when the objects $a, b, c, \ldots$ stand in the relation $R$, and has those objects and $R$ as its timeless parts. A variable embodiment $/F/$ is given by a principle $F$ that assigns a manifestation to each time; it exists whenever $F$ has a manifestation, and has that manifestation as a part at that time, so it can change its matter.Defined in Neo-Aristotelian Hylomorphism · Metaphysics · Advanced
Threshold view
The view that binary belief just is credence above some threshold $t$, where $0.5 < t < 1$. On this view, to believe $p$ is to have credence in $p$ of at least $t$, and there is no further state of belief over and above the credence.Defined in Lottery, Preface, and the Threshold View of Belief · Epistemology · Advanced
Token
A particular instance of a type: the specific inscription of "the" third from the left on this line, tonight's performance of the Ninth, the coin in your pocket.Defined in Universals and Instances · Ontology · Beginner
total evidence requirement
The requirement that a probability judgement be made relative to all of one's relevant evidence, and not to some selected portion of it. It is a general constraint on probabilistic reasoning rather than a move within philosophy of religion, and it has an obvious rationale: a probability conditional on part of the evidence can be misleading about the probability conditional on the whole, and there is no rule that the omitted part must point in the same direction.Defined in The Probabilistic Problem of Evil · Theism · Advanced
Tracking account
Robert Nozick's analysis of knowledge, on which knowing requires that the belief be true, that it be sensitive, and that the believer would still believe it were it true but circumstances slightly different, all held fixed for the method actually used.Defined in Safety and Sensitivity Conditions · Epistemology · Intermediate
Transcendence
God's being wholly other than the created order: not an item within the world, not subject to its conditions, and not a member of any kind that its contents belong to.Defined in Creation, Conservation, and Providence · Theism · Beginner
Translation key
An explicit list pairing each capital letter with the English proposition it stands for. The key is written down before any translating begins and does not change while the argument is being handled.Defined in Translating English into Symbols · Logic · Beginner
Transworld depravity
The property an agent has if, in every possible world where that agent exists and is free with respect to morally significant actions, the agent goes wrong at least once.Defined in Theodicies and Defences · Theism · Intermediate
Transworld identity
The identity of an individual across different possible worlds: the sense in which one and the same thing exists in, and has properties at, more than one world.Defined in Modality and Possible Worlds · Metaphysics · Intermediate
Triviality result
A theorem showing that no proposition can have, as its probability, the conditional probability of consequent given antecedent across all probability functions in any sufficiently rich class. Proved by David Lewis in 1976, with numerous strengthenings since.Defined in Conditionals and the Triviality Results · Logic · Advanced
Trolley problem
The problem of identifying a principle that permits diverting the trolley onto one person while forbidding pushing one person into its path, given that both save five at the cost of one.Defined in The Trolley Problem as a Diagnostic · Ethics · Beginner
Trope
A particular instance of a property: not redness in general but this redness, the redness of this postbox, which is located where the postbox's surface is and is not shared with the tomato. Also called an abstract particular, a moment, or a particularised quality.Defined in Universals and Particulars · Metaphysics · Intermediate
Trope theory
The view that tropes, and not universals or bare classes of ordinary things, are the basic constituents of the properties of the world. Two things are alike in colour because their tropes of colour exactly resemble each other, not because anything is wholly present in both.Defined in Universals and Particulars · Metaphysics · Intermediate
Truth
The property a statement has when things are as it says they are. "Snow is white" is true when snow is white.Defined in Knowledge, Belief, and Opinion · Epistemology · Beginner
Truth function
A way of building a compound proposition whose truth value is fixed entirely by the truth values of its parts. Change the parts for others with the same truth values, and the value of the whole cannot change.Defined in Statements and Connectives · Logic · Beginner
Truth supervenes on being
The thesis that there can be no difference in what is true without a difference in being: two possible worlds that differ in which propositions are true must also differ in what things exist, or in which fundamental properties and relations those things have (the perfectly natural ones, in Lewis's version). It is a supervenience claim, with truths as the supervening family and being as the subvenient base.Defined in Truthmaker Theory · Metaphysics · Advanced
Truth table
An exhaustive listing of the possible assignments of truth values to the letters in one or more formulas, with a column showing the value each formula takes under each assignment. A formula with $n$ distinct letters has $2^n$ rows.Defined in Truth Tables · Logic · Beginner
Truth value gap
The status of a sentence assigned neither truth nor falsity, used for presupposition failure, reference failure, future contingents and the borderline cases of vague predicates. The third value in a gap logic is undesignated, so a gappy premise supports nothing.Defined in Many-Valued Logics · Logic · Advanced
Truth value glut
The status of a sentence assigned both truth and falsity, used for the paradoxes by those prepared to accept them. The third value in a glut logic is designated, since a glutty sentence is true, among other things.Defined in Many-Valued Logics · Logic · Advanced
Truthmaker maximalism
The thesis that every truth has a truthmaker: for each true proposition, without exception, there is some entity whose existence makes it true. Armstrong, its leading defender, called it Maximalism, and took it to cover necessary truths, negative truths and general truths as much as "Socrates is pale".Defined in Truthmaker Theory · Metaphysics · Advanced
Type
A repeatable kind, of which there can be many instances: the word "the", the Ninth Symphony, the design of a particular coin.Defined in Universals and Instances · Ontology · Beginner
Type-token distinction
The difference between a repeatable kind and its particular instances: the word "the" as against each printed occurrence of it, the Ninth Symphony as against each performance.Defined in Abstract and Concrete · Metaphysics · Beginner

U

Uncertainty accumulation
The growth of uncertainty in the conclusion of a valid argument as a function of the uncertainty in its premises. Since the uncertainty of a conjunction can be as large as the sum of the uncertainties of its conjuncts, the conclusion of a valid argument from $n$ premises each of probability $1 - \varepsilon$ can have probability as low as $1 - n\varepsilon$.Defined in Probability Logic and Uncertain Premises · Logic · Advanced
Undefinability theorem
Tarski's result that the set of Gödel numbers of true sentences of arithmetic is not definable by any formula of the language of arithmetic. In the form applying to theories: no consistent theory interpreting enough arithmetic contains a predicate it proves to satisfy the T-schema for its own sentences.Defined in Undefinability and the Theories of Truth · Logic · Advanced
undercutting defeater
A consideration that removes the support one's ground gave to a belief without providing any reason to think the belief false. If you learn that the room you are in is lit by lights that make white objects look red, you no longer have grounds for believing the wall is red, but you have not acquired a reason for thinking it is not red. It is contrasted with a rebutting defeater, which supplies positive evidence against the belief itself.Defined in The Evolutionary Argument Against Naturalism · Theism · Advanced
Uniformity of nature
The supposition that unobserved cases resemble observed ones, or that the future will resemble the past. Every inductive inference requires something of this kind as a suppressed premise.Defined in The Problem of Induction · Epistemology · Intermediate
Universal
An entity that can be wholly present in more than one place at the same time, and that different particulars share when they are the same in some respect. Redness, if there is such a thing, is a universal.Defined in Universals and Instances · Ontology · Beginner
Universal quantifier
The symbol $\forall$, read "for all" or "for every". The formula $\forall x Fx$ is true under an interpretation when every object in the domain satisfies $F$, and false when at least one does not. It is the formal counterpart of "every", "all", "each", and "any" in their general uses.Defined in Predicate Logic · Logic · Intermediate
univocal predication
Using a term in exactly the same sense in both applications, so that "wise" means the same in "Solomon is wise" and "God is wise" and differs only in the degree or manner in which it holds. Univocity is what makes ordinary inference possible: if a word shifts sense between premises, the argument equivocates. Its cost in theology is that a term with a single sense across creatures and God appears to place God under a common concept, which is what the doctrine of simplicity was designed to prevent.Defined in Religious Language · Theism · Advanced

V

Validity
An argument is valid when there is no possible situation in which all of its premises are true and its conclusion is false. An argument that is not valid is invalid.Defined in Validity and Soundness · Logic · Beginner
Variable domain semantics
The interpretation on which each world carries its own domain, so that an object may exist at one world and not another. Quantifiers at a world range over that world's domain, and the domains may overlap, nest or be disjoint.Defined in Quantified Modal Logic and the Barcan Formulas · Logic · Advanced
Variable sharing
The necessary condition these systems impose: if $\varphi \rightarrow \psi$ is a theorem, then $\varphi$ and $\psi$ share a propositional variable. The condition rules out the paradoxes of material and strict implication, since $\varphi \rightarrow (\psi \rightarrow \psi)$ and $(\varphi \land \neg \varphi) \rightarrow \psi$ both fail it.Defined in Relevance Logic and Paraconsistency · Logic · Advanced
verification principle
The criterion of meaning proposed by the logical positivists, on which a statement is factually significant only if it is analytic, true or false by the meanings of its terms, or empirically verifiable, capable in principle of being confirmed or disconfirmed by observation. Statements meeting neither condition are not false but meaningless, in the sense of failing to express a proposition at all. Applied to theology, the principle classifies "God exists" and "God does not exist" as equally void of content.Defined in Religious Language · Theism · Advanced
Veritism
The view that truth is the fundamental epistemic good, so that all other epistemic goods, including justification, reliability and rationality, are valuable only as means to true belief and the avoidance of false belief. The term is Alvin Goldman's.Defined in Epistemic Value and the Swamping Problem · Epistemology · Advanced
via negativa
The specific procedure of apophatic theology: reaching a conception of God by removing from an initial description everything that belongs to creatures as such. God is not material, so not extended, not divisible, not located; not changeable, so not temporal; not limited, so not finite in power or knowledge. Each step subtracts rather than adds, and the resulting conception is defined by its exclusions.Defined in Religious Language · Theism · Advanced
Virtue epistemology
The approach on which the primary objects of epistemic evaluation are the believer's stable cognitive qualities, and a belief is justified or knowledgeable in virtue of issuing from a good quality of the believer rather than from a process considered impersonally.Defined in Reliabilism and Virtue Epistemology · Epistemology · Intermediate
Virtue ethics
The family of theories on which the primary subject of moral assessment is character rather than action, and right action is understood by reference to what a person of good character would do.Defined in Consequences, Rules, and Character · Ethics · Beginner

W

Weak atheism
The condition of a person who does not believe that God exists, without thereby believing that God does not exist. Also called negative atheism.Defined in Theism, Atheism, and Agnosticism · Theism · Beginner
Weak König's lemma
The statement that every infinite subtree of the binary tree has an infinite path. The full lemma, for finitely branching trees, is stronger; the restriction to binary branching is what yields the system called WKL-zero when the statement is added to the base theory.Defined in Reverse Mathematics · Logic · Advanced
Weak supervenience
A family $A$ weakly supervenes on a base $B$ if and only if, in any possible world, any two things that are alike in their $B$-properties are alike in their $A$-properties. The comparison is made within each world separately.Defined in Supervenience · Metaphysics · Intermediate
Weakening
The structural rule permitting a sequent to be extended with an additional formula that plays no part in the derivation: from $\Gamma \vdash \varphi$ infer $\Gamma, \psi \vdash \varphi$. It expresses the assumption that unused premises are harmless, and with it comes the theorem $\varphi \rightarrow (\psi \rightarrow \varphi)$ and the derivation of a conclusion from an irrelevant premise.Defined in Substructural Logics · Logic · Advanced
Well-formed formula
A string of the language of propositional logic built according to the following three clauses. First, every sentence letter is a well-formed formula. Second, if $\varphi$ is a well-formed formula then $\neg \varphi$ is one, and if $\varphi$ and $\psi$ are well-formed formulas then $(\varphi \land \psi)$, $(\varphi \lor \psi)$, $(\varphi \rightarrow \psi)$, and $(\varphi \leftrightarrow \psi)$ are each one. Third, nothing else is a well-formed formula. The abbreviation wff is standard and is pronounced as it looks.Defined in Propositional Logic and Well-Formed Formulas · Logic · Intermediate
What it is like
Thomas Nagel's formulation of the subjective character of experience: an organism is conscious in this sense if there is something it is like to be that organism, some way the world seems from its point of view.Defined in Consciousness Versus Cognition · Philosophy of Mind · Beginner
Wholly present
An object is wholly present at a time when everything that the object is, all of it and not merely some portion, exists at that time. Nothing of the object is somewhere else in time, waiting to come or already gone.Defined in Persistence: Endurantism and Perdurantism · Metaphysics · Intermediate
Will to believe
William James's thesis that when an option cannot be settled on intellectual grounds and is living, forced, and momentous, it is legitimate to let considerations other than evidence decide it.Defined in Pragmatic Arguments for Belief · Theism · Intermediate

Z

Zero confirmation of universal laws
The result that on every member of Carnap's continuum, in a language with infinitely many individuals, the probability of a universal generalisation is zero and remains zero after any finite body of confirming evidence. The generalisation is the conjunction of infinitely many instances each with probability less than one, and the product tends to zero.Defined in Inductive Logic and the Carnap Programme · Logic · Advanced
